paras.en: Hence James infers: [[2:24|Do you see|Videtis]] with the inward eye, from what has been proved, [[2:24|that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only?|quoniam ex operibus justificatur homo, et non ex fide tantum]] For both are necessary to salvation, nay, charity most of all, without which neither faith nor any working whatever can be meritorious and acceptable to God. Lastly, a man is said to be justified in two ways. First, by being cleansed of vices and receiving grace and the virtues: which is not done directly and properly by works, since before the infusion of charity and grace there is no meritorious action, nor any that merits grace *de condigno* [that is, by strict desert]. Yet to this justification works good in their kind dispose and fit a man in their own way *de congruo* [that is, by a fittingness, not by strict desert], while he does what is in him. For so attrition too is said to dispose to contrition [that is, sorrow for sin from a lower motive, such as fear, as against sorrow from the love of God]. Secondly, a man is said to be justified by practising just, virtuous and meritorious works, and by growing in grace, gifts and virtues. And it is so that the holy apostle James speaks here.

paras.t: Postremo, ne Judæi ac alii pusillanimes ac pigri, se excusarent, dicendo non posse se tanti Patriarchæ assequi opera tam perfecta, subjungit Apostolus exemplum mulieris peccatricis atque paganæ, quæ tamen per fidem et opera fuit justificata. Nam subditur: Similiter et Rahab meretrix, nonne ex operibus justificata est, inquantum opera illa processerunt ex fide, suscipiens nuntios, id est duos viros exploratores a Josue in Jericho missos, et alia via ejiciens, id est per aliam viam eos ad Josue redire persuadens? Quum enim recepisset eos per ostium suæ domus, et per fenestram exposuisset trans murum, cui domus ejus hærebat, dixit: Ad montana conscendite. Quæ omnia in libro Josue plenius describuntur: ubi fides ejus de Deo Israel, hospitalitas, misericordia, liberatio, quas viris præfatis impendit, diffuse narrantur. Propter quæ omnia meruit populo Israelitico annumerari, et tribui Juda conjugio sociari, genealogiæque inseri Salvatoris, ex ejus semine secundum humanam propaginem descendentis.
paras.en: Lastly, lest the Jews and others faint-hearted and slothful should excuse themselves, saying they could not attain works so perfect as those of so great a Patriarch, the Apostle adds the example of a sinful and pagan woman who was nevertheless justified by faith and works. For it is added: [[2:25|And in like manner also Rahab the harlot, was not she justified by works|Similiter et Rahab meretrix, nonne ex operibus justificata est]], inasmuch as those works proceeded from faith, [[2:25|receiving the messengers|suscipiens nuntios]], that is, the two men, spies sent by Josue into Jericho[[Jos 2:1||]], [[2:25|and sending them out another way|et alia via ejiciens]], that is, persuading them to return to Josue by another way? For when she had received them by the door of her house and let them down through the window beyond the wall to which her house clung, she said: [[Jos 2:16|Get ye up to the mountains|Ad montana conscendite]]. All of which is described more fully in the book of Josue, where her faith in the God of Israel, and the hospitality, mercy and deliverance she bestowed on those men, are told at length. For all which she merited to be numbered among the people of Israel, to be joined in marriage to the tribe of Juda, and to be inserted in the genealogy of the Saviour[[Matt 1:5||]], who descended from her seed according to his human lineage.

paras.t: Postremo, ex præinductis concludit Apostolus: Sicut enim corpus sine spiritu mortuum est, ita et fides sine operibus mortua est, secundum expositionem præhabitam. Sic etiam dici potest, quod fides sine caritate sit mortua, quoniam caritas est forma et vita virtutum. Et tamen sive dicatur sine operibus, sive sine caritate, redit in idem, quoniam caritas otiosa esse non potest: operatur enim magna, si est, quum signum dilectionis sit exhibitio operis. Verumtamen non oportet, nec in vita ista possibile est, ut caritas indesinenter sit in actu seu exercitio actuali. Sed opportuno tempore procedit in actum, operaturque magna, etsi non opera exteriora, tamen interiora desideria et fervores, gaudium, pacem, congratulationem, et elevationem frequenter in Deum. Imo nulla forma tam prompte agit ut caritas.
paras.en: Lastly, from what has been brought forward the Apostle concludes: [[2:26|For even as the body without the spirit is dead: so also faith without works is dead.|Sicut enim corpus sine spiritu mortuum est, ita et fides sine operibus mortua est]] This is according to the explanation already given. So too it can be said that faith without charity is dead, since charity is the form and life of the virtues. And yet whether one says *without works* or *without charity*, it comes to the same, since charity cannot be idle: for it works great things, if it is there, since the sign of love is the showing of the deed. Yet it is not needful, nor possible in this life, that charity be unceasingly in act or actual exercise. But at the fitting time it goes forth into act and works great things: if not outward works, yet inward desires and fervours, joy, peace, rejoicing with others, and frequent lifting up into God. Nay, no form acts so promptly as charity.

3.title: EXPLANATIO CAPITULI TERTII : NOLITE PLURES MAGISTRI FIERI.
3.title_en: Explanation of the third chapter: Be ye not many masters.
3.note: The end of this article is missing from the transcription and will be added from the scan.

paras.t: POSTQUAM instruxit nos sanctus Apostolus, quam necessaria sint opera virtuosa, ad quæ multi sunt pigri, nunc docet quam necessarium sit, vitia vanitatis ac levitatis in docendo ac loquendo vitare, ad quæ multi sunt proni, sicut ad cetera quæ sunt excellentiæ et gloriationis.
paras.en: Having instructed us how necessary are virtuous works, to which many are sluggish, the holy Apostle now teaches how necessary it is to avoid the vices of vanity and levity in teaching and speaking, to which many are prone, as they are to all else that belongs to pre-eminence and boasting.

paras.t: Itaque ait: Nolite plures magistri fieri, fratres mei, id est, ad cathedram magistralem, ad aliorum informationem, ad magisterium non ingeratis vos ipsos importune, vane et inordinate, desiderio commodi proprii aut honoris, et antequam estis idonei. Ut enim ex prologo Lucæ evangelistæ, quem ipsemet evangelio suo præmittit, ex epistolis Pauli, atque ex Actibus patet Apostolorum, multi ad prædicandum nondum idonei, conabantur evangelium scribere, prædicare, et nomen sibi efficere. Quorum etiam aliqui seminaverunt errores, et deceperunt se ipsos ac alios, affirmando legalia cum Evangelio esse servanda: per quod sibi damnationem auxerunt. Ideo subditur: scientes quoniam majus judicium sumitis, id est, graviorem reprobationem et condemnationem a Christo accipietis. Eorum namque quos decepistis, peccata redundabunt in vos. De talibus ad Timotheum habetur: Quidam aberrantes, conversi sunt ad vaniloquium, volentes esse legis doctores, non intelligentes neque quæ loquuntur, neque de quibus affirmant. Denique huic Jacobi verbo consonat, quod apud Matthæum ait Salvator: Nolite vocari Rabbi: unus enim est magister vester: nec vocemini magistri: unus est enim magister vester, Christus.
paras.en: And so he says: [[3:1|Be ye not many masters, my brethren|Nolite plures magistri fieri, fratres mei]], that is, do not thrust yourselves forward to the master's chair, to the instruction of others, to the office of teaching, importunately, vainly and inordinately, out of desire for your own advantage or honour, and before you are fit for it. For, as is clear from the prologue of Luke the evangelist, which he himself sets before his gospel, from the epistles of Paul, and from the Acts of the Apostles, many who were not yet fit to preach tried to write the gospel, to preach it, and to make a name for themselves. Some of these even sowed errors, and deceived themselves and others by affirming that the legal observances [that is, the ceremonies of the Law of Moses] were to be kept together with the Gospel; and by this they increased their own damnation. Therefore it is added: [[3:1|knowing that you receive the greater judgment|scientes quoniam majus judicium sumitis]], that is, you will receive from Christ a heavier reprobation and condemnation. For the sins of those whom you have deceived will redound upon you. Of such men it is written to Timothy: [[1 Tim 1:6|some, going astray, are turned aside unto vain babbling|Quidam aberrantes, conversi sunt ad vaniloquium]], [[1 Tim 1:7|Desiring to be teachers of the law: understanding neither the things they say, nor whereof they affirm|volentes esse legis doctores, non intelligentes neque quæ loquuntur, neque de quibus affirmant]]. Finally, with this word of James agrees what the Saviour says in Matthew: [[Matt 23:8|be not you called Rabbi. For one is your master|Nolite vocari Rabbi: unus enim est magister vester]]: [[Matt 23:10|Neither be ye called masters: for one is your master, Christ|nec vocemini magistri: unus est enim magister vester, Christus]].

paras.t: Per quæ omnia non prohibetur absolute desiderium magistratus aut doctoratus, aut appellatio inde sumpta, sed ne ex vanitate propter nomen sublime aut dignitatem, talia appetantur. Si vero referantur ad debitum finem, ut scilicet actus prædicandi ac docendi caritative, defendendique fidem efficacius expleantur, et ipsa prædicatio ac doctrina salubris a populo diligentius audiantur, sunt licita, quum et Paulus dicat quod Deus dedit quosdam Apostolos, quosdam Prophetas, quosdam doctores. Se ipsum quoque doctorem nominat gentium. Et in Actibus legitur: Erant in Ecclesia Antiochiæ prophetæ et doctores. Præterea, ut super quartum Sententiarum Thomas ostendit, mortaliter peccant, qui prædicationis actum indigne exerceret, non agendo quæ docent.
paras.en: By all this the desire for the office of master or doctor, or for the title taken from it, is not forbidden absolutely; what is forbidden is that such things be sought out of vanity, for the sake of a lofty name or dignity. But if they are referred to their due end, namely that the acts of preaching and teaching be performed in charity and the faith be defended more effectively, and that the wholesome preaching and teaching itself be heard more attentively by the people, they are lawful; for Paul too says that God [[Eph 4:11|gave some apostles, and some prophets|dedit quosdam Apostolos, quosdam Prophetas]], and some doctors. He also calls himself [[1 Tim 2:7|a doctor of the Gentiles|doctorem nominat gentium]]. And in the Acts we read: [[Acts 13:1|there were in the church which was at Antioch prophets and doctors|Erant in Ecclesia Antiochiæ prophetæ et doctores]]. Moreover, as Thomas shows on the fourth book of the Sentences, those who exercise the office of preaching unworthily, not doing what they teach, sin mortally.

paras.t: In multis enim offendimus omnes, id est, non solum vos, fratres nondum perfecti, in multis estis culpabiles, sed et nos qui primitias Spiritus Sancti accepimus, frequenter veniale peccatum incurrimus in cogitatu, verbo, aut opere, seu omissione. Propter quod ait Scriptura: Justus septies cadit in die. Et iterum Salomon contestatur: Non est homo super terram qui faciat bonum, et non peccet. Sanctus quoque Job loquitur: Non justificabitur homo comparatus Deo; si voluerit cum eo contendere, non poterit respondere unum pro mille. Et Propheta oravit: Delicta quis intelligit? ab occultis meis munda me, Domine; itemque, Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo, Domine, etc. Verumtamen pro istis venialibus, ex humana fragilitate manantibus, viri heroici et perfecti quotidie satisfaciunt plene: et ultra hoc, in caritatis fervore, ceterisque virtutibus, donis et fructibus proficiunt valde: corda sua ad Deum sæpissime elevando, orando, meditando, pœnitendo, confitendo, corpus suum multipliciter castigando, dominicam passionem frequenter ac cordialiter revolvendo, Deum laudando, se ipsos profundissime diversisque modis humiliando, accusando, despiciendo, correptiones et correctiones in vita hac libenter suscipiendo. In quibus omnibus nos ipsos quotidie exerceamus.
paras.en: [[3:2|For in many things we all offend|In multis enim offendimus omnes]], that is: not only are you, brethren not yet perfect, blameworthy in many things, but we too, who have received the first-fruits of the Holy Ghost, often fall into venial sin in thought, word or deed, or by omission. Wherefore the Scripture says: [[Prov 24:16|a just man shall fall seven times|Justus septies cadit]] in the day [Denis gives the saying in its common form, with "in the day", which Proverbs does not have]. And again Solomon bears witness: [[Eccles 7:21|there is no just man upon earth, that doth good, and sinneth not|Non est homo super terram qui faciat bonum, et non peccet]]. Holy Job too says: [[Job 9:2|man cannot be justified, compared with God|Non justificabitur homo comparatus Deo]]; [[Job 9:3|If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him one for a thousand|si voluerit cum eo contendere, non poterit respondere unum pro mille]]. And the Prophet prayed: [[Ps 18:13|Who can understand sins? from my secret ones cleanse me, O Lord|Delicta quis intelligit? ab occultis meis munda me, Domine]]; and again: [[Ps 142:2|enter not into judgment with thy servant|Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo]], O Lord, etc. Yet for these venial sins, which flow from human frailty, heroic and perfect men make full satisfaction every day; and beyond this they advance greatly in the fervour of charity and in the other virtues, gifts and fruits: lifting up their hearts to God very often, praying, meditating, doing penance, confessing, chastising their body in many ways, turning over the Lord's passion often and from the heart, praising God, humbling, accusing and despising themselves most deeply and in divers ways, and willingly accepting rebukes and corrections in this life. In all these things let us exercise ourselves daily.

paras.t: Si quis in verbo non offendit, id est, non peccavit inordinate loquendo sive tacendo, ita quod nec protulit non loquenda, nec siluit proferenda: ut nec de indiscreto silentio indigeat pœnitere, illud Isaiæ dicendo: Væ mihi quia tacui: et illud in Psalmo, Quoniam tacui, inveteraverunt ossa mea; neque de illicita locutione habeat dolere, et illud Job proferre: Leviter locutus sum: unum loquutus sum quod utinam non dixissem, et alterum: quibus ultra non addam. Hoc profecto sic fit: non quod in evitatione prolationis verbi illiciti, seu taciturnitate verbi proferendi, essentialiter consistat perfectio hominis, alioqui totaliter muti essent perfecti; sed quia non excessisse in verbo, signum est magnæ custodiæ cordis, magnæ sapientiæ mentis, magnæ perfectionis interioris. Siquidem ea quæ sunt in voce, sunt earum quæ sunt in anima conceptionum affectionumque notæ. Idcirco linguam perfecte reprimere, signum ac opus est affectionis, ac grandis illuminationis mentalis, et supra vires humanas. Propter quod in Proverbiis fertur: Hominis est animum præparare, et Domini gubernare linguam. In Ecclesiastico quoque dicitur: Beatus vir qui non est lapsus in verbo ex ore suo. Et denuo ait Scriptura: Quis est homo qui non est lapsus ex lingua sua?
paras.en: [[3:2|If any man offend not in word|Si quis in verbo non offendit]], that is, has not sinned by speaking or by keeping silence inordinately, so that he has neither uttered what should not be spoken nor kept back what should be uttered: so that he need neither repent of an indiscreet silence, saying that word of Isaias, [[Is 6:5|Woe is me, because I have held my peace|Væ mihi quia tacui]], and that in the Psalm, [[Ps 31:3|Because I was silent my bones grew old|Quoniam tacui, inveteraverunt ossa mea]]; nor have to grieve over unlawful speech and say with Job, as one [[Job 39:34|who hath spoken inconsiderately|Leviter locutus sum]]: [[Job 39:35|One thing I have spoken, which I wish I had not said: and another, to which I will add no more|unum loquutus sum quod utinam non dixissem, et alterum: quibus ultra non addam]]. This is indeed so [that is, such a man is perfect]: not because the perfection of man consists essentially in avoiding the utterance of an unlawful word, or in not keeping silent a word that should be uttered (otherwise those who are wholly dumb would be perfect); but because not to have exceeded in word is a sign of great custody of the heart, of great wisdom of mind, of great inward perfection. For the things that are in the voice are signs of the conceptions and affections that are in the soul [the opening of Aristotle's treatise On Interpretation]. Therefore to restrain the tongue perfectly is the sign and the work of affection and of great enlightenment of mind, and it is above human strength. Wherefore it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 16:1|It is the part of man to prepare the soul: and of the Lord to govern the tongue|Hominis est animum præparare, et Domini gubernare linguam]]. In Ecclesiasticus too it is said: [[Ecclus 14:1|Blessed is the man that hath not slipped by a word out of his mouth|Beatus vir qui non est lapsus in verbo ex ore suo]]. And again the Scripture says: [[Ecclus 19:17|who is there that hath not offended with his tongue?|Quis est homo qui non est lapsus ex lingua sua?]] [the margin gives Ecclus. xxv, 11, which blesses the man that hath not slipped with his tongue; Denis's question is closer to Ecclus 19:17]

paras.t: Potest etiam freno circumducere totum corpus, id est, vir perfectus qui non offendit in verbo, potest totum corpus suum domare, et cetera membra sua, quæ facilius refrenantur quam lingua, compescere: quia qui potest quod majus est, potest et id quod minus est. Hoc facit qui illud implet Apostoli: Non regnet peccatum in vestro mortali corpore; neque exhibeatis membra vestra arma iniquitatis peccato, sed arma justitiæ Deo. Et qui exteriores sensus suos custodit, ne peccet per eos (quemadmodum in Ecclesiastico orat vir sapiens: Domine, pater et dominator vitæ meæ, extollentiam oculorum meorum ne dederis mihi, et omne desiderium pravum averte a me; aufer a me ventris concupiscentiam), potest custodire sua interiora. Hinc oravit Psalmista: Confige timore tuo carnes meas; itemque, Averte oculos meos, ne videant vanitatem. Unde frenum quo totum corpus circumducitur, atque ad Dei servitutem movetur, in perfectis est amor divinus seu timor filialis; in incipientibus, timor servilis aut aliqualiter initialis; in proficientibus, timor initialis, ad filialem timorem propinquus. Potius tamen istud diversis est adscribendum virtutibus, utpote castitati, æquitati ac latriæ. Consequenter Apostolus variis modis refrenationem linguæ persuadet ac docet.
paras.en: [[3:2|He is able also with a bridle to lead about the whole body|Potest etiam freno circumducere totum corpus]], that is, the perfect man, who offends not in word, can tame his whole body and restrain his other members, which are more easily bridled than the tongue: for he who can do the greater can also do the less. This he does who fulfils that word of the Apostle: [[Rom 6:12|Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body|Non regnet peccatum in vestro mortali corpore]]; [[Rom 6:13|Neither yield ye your members as instruments of iniquity unto sin|neque exhibeatis membra vestra arma iniquitatis peccato]], but [[Rom 6:13|instruments of justice unto God|arma justitiæ Deo]]. And he who guards his outward senses so as not to sin through them (as the wise man prays in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 23:1|O Lord, father, and sovereign ruler of my life|Domine, pater et dominator vitæ meæ]], [[Ecclus 23:5|Give me not haughtiness of my eyes, and turn away from me all coveting|extollentiam oculorum meorum ne dederis mihi, et omne desiderium pravum averte a me]] [Denis reads "all evil desire"]; [[Ecclus 23:6|Take from me the greediness of the belly|aufer a me ventris concupiscentiam]]) [the margin gives Ecclus. xxiii, 1, 4–6; the opening words are those of v. 1, which v. 4 repeats with "God" for "sovereign ruler"] can guard his inward parts. Hence the Psalmist prayed: [[Ps 118:120|Pierce thou my flesh with thy fear|Confige timore tuo carnes meas]]; and again: [[Ps 118:37|Turn away my eyes that they may not behold vanity|Averte oculos meos, ne videant vanitatem]]. So the bridle by which the whole body is led about and moved to the service of God is, in the perfect, divine love or filial fear; in beginners, servile fear, or fear that is in some measure initial; in the proficient, initial fear close to filial fear [servile fear shrinks from punishment, filial fear from offending God; initial fear lies between, fearing both]. Yet this is rather to be ascribed to different virtues, such as chastity, equity and latria [that is, the worship due to God alone]. Next the Apostle, in various ways, urges and teaches the bridling of the tongue.

paras.t: Si autem equis frena in ora mittimus ad consentiendum nobis, id est, quia equis ponimus frena in ore, ut dirigamus eos quo volumus, et omne corpus illorum circumferimus, id est, totum corpus equorum freno hinc inde ad libitum movemus: subaudi, Multo plus debemus proprii oris claustra frenare, linguam compescere, labia moderari ad consentiendum Deo ac rationi: quia ut Salomon ait, Qui moderatur labia sua, prudentissimus est; et Propheta testatur: Dixi, Custodiam vias meas, ut non delinquam in lingua mea; posui ori meo custodiam. Et ecce naves quum magnæ sint, et a ventis validis minentur, id est, in anteriora impellantur, circumferuntur tamen a modico gubernaculo, ubi impetus dirigentis voluerit, id est, a gubernatore navigii diriguntur per gubernaculum suum, quo vult: ita et lingua gubernaculo rationis est dirigenda, ne declinet in verba illicita.
paras.en: [[3:3|For if we put bits into the mouths of horses, that they may obey us|Si autem equis frena in ora mittimus ad consentiendum nobis]], that is, since we put bridles in the mouths of horses so as to guide them where we will, [[3:3|and we turn about their whole body|et omne corpus illorum circumferimus]], that is, with the bridle we move the whole body of the horses this way and that at our pleasure: understand, much more ought we to bridle the doors of our own mouth, to restrain the tongue, to govern the lips, so as to obey God and reason [the Latin has the same word, "to consent", for the horses obeying us and for our obeying God]; for, as Solomon says, [[Prov 10:19|he that refraineth his lips, is most wise|Qui moderatur labia sua, prudentissimus est]]; and the Prophet testifies: [[Ps 38:2|I said: I will take heed to my ways: that I sin not with my tongue. I have set a guard to my mouth|Dixi, Custodiam vias meas, ut non delinquam in lingua mea; posui ori meo custodiam]]. [[3:4|Behold also ships, whereas they are great and are driven by strong winds|Et ecce naves quum magnæ sint, et a ventis validis minentur]], that is, are driven forward, [[3:4|yet are they turned about with a small helm, whithersoever the force of the governor willeth|circumferuntur tamen a modico gubernaculo, ubi impetus dirigentis voluerit]], that is, they are steered by the pilot of the ship by means of his helm wherever he will: so too the tongue must be steered by the helm of reason, lest it turn aside into unlawful words.

paras.t: Hinc subditur: Ita et lingua modicum quidem membrum est, id est in substantia parvum. Propterea turpe est nobis si eam non coarctamus, quum magnas circumferamus per rationis industriam naves. Est quoque periculosum. Idcirco subjungitur: et magna exaltat, id est, verba jactantiæ profert, lites concitat, et multa producit pericula, nisi compescatur. Propterea in Ecclesiastico dicitur: Odibilis est, qui procax est ad loquendum; et rursus: Susurro et bilinguis maledictus; multos enim turbavit pacem habentes. Salomon quoque, Os, inquit, fatuorum ebullit stultitiam.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[3:5|Even so the tongue is indeed a little member|Ita et lingua modicum quidem membrum est]], that is, small in substance. Therefore it is shameful for us if we do not keep it in check, when by the industry of reason we turn great ships about. It is also dangerous. Therefore he adds: [[3:5|and boasteth great things|et magna exaltat]], that is, it utters boastful words, stirs up quarrels, and brings forth many dangers, unless it is restrained. Therefore it is said in Ecclesiasticus that there is one [[Ecclus 20:5|that is hateful, that is bold in speech|Odibilis est, qui procax est ad loquendum]]; and again: [[Ecclus 28:15|The whisperer and the double tongue is accursed: for he hath troubled many that were at peace|Susurro et bilinguis maledictus; multos enim turbavit pacem habentes]]. Solomon too: [[Prov 15:2|the mouth|Os]], he says, [[Prov 15:2|of fools bubbleth out folly|fatuorum ebullit stultitiam]].

paras.t: Ecce quantus, id est quam parvus, ignis, quam magnam silvam incendit! utique valde magnam. Nam ignis nunquam dicit, Sufficit; et inter elementa summe activus est et formalis, formam suam in alia celeriter introducens. Et lingua ignis est, id est similis igni: quoniam sicut ignis comburit ligna silvarum, sic lingua inordinate, superflue, vitiose loquendo, actus virtutum mortificat, et animam diversis exponit flagitiis. Propter quod in Proverbiis inducitur: Sicut urbs patens et absque murorum ambitu, ita vir qui non potest in loquendo cohibere spiritum suum. Hinc ait Apostolus: Corrumpunt bonos mores colloquia mala. In Ecclesiastico quoque legitur: Apertio oris illius (qui scilicet multis utitur verbis) inflammatio est.
paras.en: [[3:5|Behold how small|Ecce quantus]] [quantus, literally "how great", which Denis takes here as "how little"], that is, how little, [[3:5|a fire kindleth a great wood|ignis, quam magnam silvam incendit]]! a very great one indeed. For [[Prov 30:16|the fire never saith: It is enough|ignis nunquam dicit, Sufficit]]; and among the elements it is supremely active and formal, swiftly bringing its own form into other things. [[3:6|And the tongue is a fire|Et lingua ignis est]], that is, like fire: for as fire burns up the timber of the forests, so the tongue, by speaking inordinately, superfluously and viciously, kills the acts of the virtues and lays the soul open to divers crimes. Wherefore it is set down in Proverbs: [[Prov 25:28|As a city that lieth open and is not compassed with walls, so is a man that cannot refrain his own spirit in speaking|Sicut urbs patens et absque murorum ambitu, ita vir qui non potest in loquendo cohibere spiritum suum]]. Hence the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 15:33|Evil communications corrupt good manners|Corrumpunt bonos mores colloquia mala]]. In Ecclesiasticus too we read: [[Ecclus 20:15|the opening of his mouth|Apertio oris illius]] (that is, of the man who uses many words) [[Ecclus 20:15|is the kindling of a fire|inflammatio est]] [the margin gives Ecclus. xx, 1; the words are in Ecclus 20:15].

paras.t: Universitas iniquitatis lingua, id est per linguam et ejus loquacitatem ac incustodiam, constituitur in membris nostris. Nam universa peccata ex irrefrenatione linguæ nascuntur: quum et ex verbis inordinate prolatis hæresis incurratur. Detractiones etiam, mendacia, contentiones, susurrationes, et quidquid iniquitatis est, ex linguæ incustodia nascuntur. Idcirco in libro Proverbiorum fertur: Qui custodit os suum, custodit animam suam: qui autem inconsideratus est ad loquendum, sentiet mala. Porro iniquitas dicitur in membris constitui, in quantum exercetur per ea. Ideo sequitur: quæ maculat totum corpus, quia in illud vitia cordis redundant. Carnalia quoque peccata, quæ ex vitiis linguæ, ex verbis procatoriis, ex mulierum alloquio oriuntur, directe inquinant corpus, et ejus inquinamenta vocantur; quoniam teste Apostolo, Qui fornicatur, in proprium corpus peccat. Et inflammat rotam nativitatis nostræ, id est totum vitæ nostræ circuitum, incessabilemque decursum ab infantia usque decrepitam senectutem; quia per omnes ætates, imo per singulos dies, ad inordinate loquendum infeliciter inflammamur, et vitiis linguæ spiritualiter devoramur, juxta illud Job: Etiam si locutus fuerit homo, devorabitur. Hinc ait Scriptura: Os quod mentitur, occidit animam.
paras.en: [[3:6|a world of iniquity|Universitas iniquitatis]], the tongue [Denis reads these words together with what follows: the whole sum of iniquity is placed in our members by the tongue], that is, through the tongue and its talkativeness and want of guard, [[3:6|is placed among our members|constituitur in membris nostris]]. For all sins are born of the unbridling of the tongue, since heresy too is incurred through words uttered inordinately. Detractions also, lies, contentions, whisperings, and whatever iniquity there is, are born of the tongue's want of guard. Therefore it is said in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 13:3|He that keepeth his mouth keepeth his soul: but he that hath no guard on his speech shall meet with evils|Qui custodit os suum, custodit animam suam: qui autem inconsideratus est ad loquendum, sentiet mala]] [the Latin has "he that is inconsiderate in speaking"]. Now iniquity is said to be placed in the members inasmuch as it is exercised through them. Therefore there follows: [[3:6|which defileth the whole body|quæ maculat totum corpus]], since the vices of the heart overflow into it. Carnal sins also, which arise from the vices of the tongue, from wanton words, from talk with women, directly defile the body, and are called its defilements; since, as the Apostle witnesses, [[1 Cor 6:18|he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body|Qui fornicatur, in proprium corpus peccat]]. [[3:6|and inflameth the wheel of our nativity|Et inflammat rotam nativitatis nostræ]], that is, the whole circuit of our life and its unceasing course from infancy to decrepit old age; because through all the ages of life, nay, through every single day, we are unhappily inflamed to speak inordinately, and are spiritually devoured by the vices of the tongue, according to that word of Job: [[Job 37:20|even if a man shall speak, he shall be swallowed up|Etiam si locutus fuerit homo, devorabitur]] [the margin gives Job xxxi, 20; the words are in Job 37:20]. Hence the Scripture says: [[Wis 1:11|the mouth that belieth, killeth the soul|Os quod mentitur, occidit animam]].

paras.t: Hoc ergo instrumentaliter facit lingua, male mota ab anima, et ab homine ipso: lingua, inquam, inflammata a gehenna, id est diabolo habitatore et cive inferni. Sicut enim per terram designantur habitantes in ea, et per civitatem cives, atque per cœlum angeli, sic per gehennam diaboli. Diabolus ergo dicitur linguam inflammare, in quantum ad verba vitiosa incitat hominem. Hoc loco scribit venerabilis Beda: Diaboli ubicumque volitent, in aere, aut in terris, vel sub terris vagentur aut detineantur, suarum semper secum ferunt tormenta flammarum, instar febricitantis, qui etsi in lectis ponatur eburneis, ardorem aut frigus insiti sui languoris vitare non potest. Sic dæmones, quamvis in templis colantur auratis, aut per aera discurrant, igne semper ardent gehennali, atque ex pœnis suis commoniti, fomitem vitiorum hominibus suggeruntur. Econtra sancta Dei civitas nova Jerusalem, puta Ecclesia militans, de cœlo descendere dicitur: quoniam quidquid meritorium et cœleste in terra gerimus, hoc munere cœlesti accepimus.
paras.en: This, then, the tongue does as an instrument, moved amiss by the soul and by the man himself: the tongue, I say, [[3:6|being set on fire by hell|inflammata a gehenna]], that is, by the devil, the dweller and citizen of hell. For as by the earth are signified those who dwell on it, and by the city its citizens, and by heaven the angels, so by hell the devils. The devil, then, is said to set the tongue on fire inasmuch as he incites man to vicious words. On this place the Venerable Bede writes: Wherever the devils fly in the air, or wander or are held on the earth or under the earth, they always carry with them the torments of their flames, like a man in a fever who, even if he be laid on ivory beds, cannot escape the heat or the cold of the sickness within him. So the demons, though they be worshipped in gilded temples or run to and fro through the air, ever burn with the fire of hell, and, spurred by their own pains, suggest to men the tinder of vices [the fomes, the inclination to sin left in fallen nature]. On the other hand the holy city of God, the new Jerusalem, that is, the Church militant, is said to come down from heaven[[Apoc 21:2||]] [the margin gives Apoc. xxi only; the descent of the city is in v. 2], since whatever meritorious and heavenly thing we do on earth, we have received as a heavenly gift.

paras.t: Deinde ostendit quam difficile sit linguam domare. Omnis enim natura bestiarum et volucrum et serpentium, et ceterorum brutorum, domantur, et domita sunt a natura humana, id est, per humanæ rationis industriam aliquo modo possunt domari. Estque distributio ista accommoda, et pro generibus singulorum, non pro singulis generum, suo modo intelligenda. Nec dubium quin virtute divina, per gratiam Christi fideique virtutem, ista copiosius atque frequentius sint peracta: quemadmodum etiam ait discipulis suis Salvator, Ecce dedi vobis potestatem calcandi super serpentes et scorpiones. Unde et in Psalmo: Super aspidem et basiliscum ambulabis, etc. Denique maxima bestia, elephantus, humana capitur, domatur et informatur industria, ut et regem adoret. Ait demum hic Beda: Legimus in Plinio immanissimam aspidem in Ægypto, a quodam patrefamilias domitam, quæ de caverna sua quotidie exiens, a mensa illius suam accepit annonam, etc. Legimus item, scribente comite Marcellino, mansuefactam tigridem, ab India Anastasio principi missam. Sic et leo beneficii exhibitione domatur. Vult ergo Apostolus per hæc verba insinuare, quod pravorum hominum lingua bestiis sit ferocior, avibus levior, serpentibus venenosior. Feris namque assimilantur, de quibus fertur in Psalmo, Exacuerunt ut gladium linguas suas; volucribus, de quibus Psalmista, Posuerunt in cœlum os suum; serpentibus, de quibus idem, Venenum aspidum sub labiis eorum.
paras.en: Next he shows how hard it is to tame the tongue. [[3:7|For every nature of beasts and of birds and of serpents and of the rest is tamed and hath been tamed, by the nature of man|Omnis enim natura bestiarum et volucrum et serpentium, et ceterorum brutorum, domantur, et domita sunt a natura humana]] [Denis adds "brute beasts": "of the rest of the brute beasts"], that is, by the industry of human reason they can in some way be tamed. And this distribution is apt, and is to be understood in its own way of the kinds of individuals, not of the individuals of the kinds [that is, some of every kind, not every one of every kind]. Nor is there any doubt that by divine power, through the grace of Christ and the virtue of faith, these things have been done more abundantly and more often: as the Saviour too says to his disciples: [[Luke 10:19|Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions|Ecce dedi vobis potestatem calcandi super serpentes et scorpiones]]. Hence also in the Psalm: [[Ps 90:13|Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk|Super aspidem et basiliscum ambulabis]], etc. Indeed the greatest of beasts, the elephant, is caught, tamed and trained by human industry, so that it even does homage to the king. Bede, lastly, says here: We read in Pliny of a most monstrous asp in Egypt, tamed by a certain householder, which came out of its hole every day and took its food from his table, etc. We read likewise, as Count Marcellinus writes, of a tame tigress sent from India to the Emperor Anastasius. So too the lion is tamed by the showing of kindness. By these words, then, the Apostle means to suggest that the tongue of wicked men is fiercer than the beasts, more fickle than the birds, more venomous than the serpents. For they are likened to wild beasts, of whom it is said in the Psalm, [[Ps 63:4|they have whetted their tongues like a sword|Exacuerunt ut gladium linguas suas]]; to birds, of whom the Psalmist says, [[Ps 72:9|They have set their mouth against heaven|Posuerunt in cœlum os suum]] [the verse number in the margin cannot be read; the words are Ps 72:9. The Latin in cœlum is literally "into heaven", whence the likeness to birds]; to serpents, of whom the same says, [[Ps 13:3|the poison of asps is under their lips|Venenum aspidum sub labiis eorum]].

paras.t: Linguam autem nullus hominum domare potest. Quod dupliciter potest intelligi: Primo, quod nullus hominum propriam potest compescere linguam, quin interdum venialiter peccet per eam. Sed contra objici potest, quia quum peccatum sit voluntarium, si impossibile est linguam domare, indomantia linguæ non erit culpabilis. Ad hoc potest duplex dari responsio: Prima, quod nullus hominum dicitur posse linguam domare, non propter omnimodam impossibilitatem, sed difficultatem prægrandem. Juxta quem modum Christus in Evangelio ait quibusdam: Hypocritæ, quomodo potestis loqui bona, quum sitis mali? Et apud Jeremiam dicitur: Si Æthiops potest mutare pellem suam, et pardus varietates suas, et vos poteritis benefacere, quum didiceritis malum, id est, assueti sitis in malis. Secunda responsio est, quia etsi singulæ oris culpæ queant vitari, non tamen forsitan omnes. — Secunda expositio hujus est, quod nullus etiam sapientium potest linguam pravorum domare: quia etsi ad horam compescantur a verbis illicitis, tamen occasione opportunitateque data, excedent loquendo. Sed et boni contra propositum, subinde ex fragilitate peccant in verbis. Propter quod in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Est qui labitur lingua sua, sed non ex animo. Hinc quidam gentilium sapientium dixit: Quoties inter homines fui, minor homo redii. — Ex quibus constat quantum vitanda sint inordinata, inutilia et non necessaria colloquia, ei qui cupit vere proficere, et Deo in sanctitate ac justitia deservire.
paras.en: [[3:8|But the tongue no man can tame|Linguam autem nullus hominum domare potest]]. This can be understood in two ways. First, that no man can so restrain his own tongue as never to sin venially by it. But against this it may be objected that, since sin is voluntary, if it is impossible to tame the tongue, the untamedness of the tongue will not be blameworthy. To this a twofold answer can be given. The first, that no man is said to be able to tame the tongue, not because of an utter impossibility, but because of very great difficulty. In this manner Christ says to certain men in the Gospel: Hypocrites, [[Matt 12:34|how can you speak good things, whereas you are evil?|quomodo potestis loqui bona, quum sitis mali?]] [the Gospel has "O generation of vipers"] And in Jeremias it is said: [[Jer 13:23|If the Ethiopian can change his skin, or the leopard his spots: you also may do well, when you have learned evil|Si Æthiops potest mutare pellem suam, et pardus varietates suas, et vos poteritis benefacere, quum didiceritis malum]], that is, when you have grown used to evil. The second answer is that, although each single fault of the mouth can be avoided, perhaps not all of them can. — The second explanation of this is that no man, even of the wise, can tame the tongue of the wicked: for although for a time they are restrained from unlawful words, yet when occasion and opportunity are given they will exceed in speaking. And even the good sin in words now and then through frailty, against their purpose. Wherefore it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 19:16|There is one, that slippeth with the tongue, but not from his heart|Est qui labitur lingua sua, sed non ex animo]]. Hence one of the wise men of the gentiles said: As often as I have been among men, I have come back less a man [Seneca, Letter 7]. — From this it is plain how much inordinate, useless and unnecessary conversation is to be avoided by him who desires truly to advance and to serve[[Luke 1:74||]] God [[Luke 1:75|In holiness and justice|in sanctitate ac justitia]].

paras.t: Inquietum malum, id est, lingua est membrum, non utique substantialiter, sed ex abusione propria, malum atque culpabile, inquietans mentem prave loquentis ac alios. Multæ enim perturbationes et inquietudines ex vitiis linguæ nascuntur. Nec quietem mentis habet in Deo, qui linguam suam non reprimit. Hinc lingua in lubrico posita dicitur. Et in Ecclesiastico asseritur: Lingua tertia multos commovit, et dispersit illos de gente in gentem. Apostolus quoque ad Timotheum: Lingua, inquit, vaniloquorum ut cancer serpit. Plena veneno mortifero, id est verbis infectivis, mortalibusque peccatis, utpote detractoriis, discordiæ seminativis, contumeliosis et pungitivis, nisi efficaciter reprimatur. Quamvis mortale peccatum formaliter sit in anima, in qua est aversio mentis a Deo; in lingua vero sunt ista, quasi in instrumento et causa. Verba autem vocalia subjective esse in ore cognoscuntur. Juxta hunc sensum in Jeremia habetur: Sagitta vulnerans lingua eorum. Qui enim detractoria, lasciva, prohibitaque verba effatur, non solum se ipsum, sed audientes quoque (si consentiant) spiritualiter trucidare censetur. Hinc multi se ipsos male loquendo occidunt, prout in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Multi interierunt in ore gladii, sed non sic ut qui interierunt per linguam suam.
paras.en: [[3:8|an unquiet evil|Inquietum malum]], that is, the tongue is a member that is evil and blameworthy, not indeed in its substance but by its own abuse, disquieting the mind of him who speaks wickedly, and others too. For many disturbances and disquiets are born of the vices of the tongue. Nor has he quiet of mind in God who does not restrain his tongue. Hence the tongue is said to be set in a slippery place. And in Ecclesiasticus it is affirmed: [[Ecclus 28:16|The tongue of a third person hath disquieted many, and scattered them from nation to nation|Lingua tertia multos commovit, et dispersit illos de gente in gentem]] ["a third tongue": a talebearer who comes between two]. The Apostle too, writing to Timothy: The tongue, he says, of vain talkers [[2 Tim 2:17|spreadeth like a canker|ut cancer serpit]] [Denis reads "the tongue of vain talkers" where the Vulgate has "their speech"]. [[3:8|full of deadly poison|Plena veneno mortifero]], that is, of infecting words and mortal sins, such as words of detraction, words that sow discord, insulting and stinging words, unless it is effectively restrained. For although mortal sin is formally in the soul, in which is the turning of the mind away from God, these things are in the tongue as in an instrument and a cause; and spoken words are known to be in the mouth as in their subject. In this sense it is said in Jeremias: [[Jer 9:8|Their tongue is a piercing arrow|Sagitta vulnerans lingua eorum]]. For he who utters words of detraction, lewd and forbidden words, is judged to slay spiritually not only himself but his hearers too (if they consent). Hence many kill themselves by speaking evil, as it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 28:22|Many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not so many as have perished by their own tongue|Multi interierunt in ore gladii, sed non sic ut qui interierunt per linguam suam]].

paras.t: Consequenter ostendit qualiter lingua sit plena veneno mortifero. In ipsa, id est per linguæ locutionem, benedicimus, id est laudamus, Deum Patrem propter bonitatem et beneficia ejus, et in ipsa maledicimus homines, qui ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei facti sunt. Per quod venenatam habere linguam probamur : quia per talem maledictionem in primis proprias occidimus animas, et etiam animas aliorum, quantum in nobis est. Siquidem iis quibus maledicimus, rancoris, iræ, detractionis et remaledictionis, contra nos occasionem præstamus. Proximis quoque maledicendo, Deum offendimus : primo, quoniam contra ejus præceptum hoc agimus ; secundo, quia injuriatio imaginis redundat in eum cujus existit imago. Ex ipso ore procedit benedictio Dei, et maledictio proximi. Non oportet, fratres mei, hæc ita fieri. Minus dicit, et majus significat, ut sit sensus : Ista linguæ peccata prorsus illicita sunt, videlicet mala bonis ita miscere. Ideo subdit :
paras.en: Next he shows how the tongue is full of deadly poison. [[3:9|By it|In ipsa]], that is, through the speech of the tongue, [[3:9|we bless|benedicimus]], that is, we praise, [[3:9|God and the Father|Deum Patrem]] for his goodness and his benefits, [[3:9|and by it we curse men who are made after the likeness of God|et in ipsa maledicimus homines, qui ad imaginem et similitudinem Dei facti sunt]][[Gen 1:26||]][[Gen 1:27||]] [Denis reads "to the image and likeness of God", after Gen 1:26; the Vulgate of St James has only "likeness"]. By this we are proved to have a poisoned tongue: for by such cursing we first of all slay our own souls, and also the souls of others, as far as lies in us. For to those whom we curse we give occasion of rancour, anger, detraction and cursing in return against us. By cursing our neighbours we also offend God: first, because we do this against his commandment[[Matt 5:22||]][[Matt 5:44||]]; secondly, because an injury done to the image redounds upon him whose image it is. [[3:10|Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing|Ex ipso ore procedit benedictio]] of God, [[3:10|and cursing|et maledictio]] of one's neighbour. [[3:10|My brethren, these things ought not so to be|Non oportet, fratres mei, hæc ita fieri]]. He says less and means more [that is, he understates for emphasis], so that the sense is: these sins of the tongue, namely so to mingle evil with good, are utterly unlawful. Therefore he adds:

paras.t: Numquid fons de eadem foramine emanat dulcem et amaram aquam ? Non utique, nisi fons corrumpatur. Numquid potest, fratres mei : ecce quam dulciter, quam amorose atque humiliter loquitur in tota epistola sua sanctus iste Apostolus, quam crebro subditos suos nominat fratres ! Numquid itaque potest, o fratres mei, ficus uvas facere, id est arbor ficorum, seu ficuum, producere uvas, aut vitis producere ficus ? Nequaquam. Sic neque salsa aqua dulcem potest facere aquam. Conformiter contra rationem est, et contra legem divinam, ut eadem lingua verba bona et mala, verba benedictionis et verba maledictionis pronuntiet, quum lingua divinitus sit instituta et data ad usum laudabilem, ad verba virtutum. Verumtamen, nonnunquam ex zelo justitiæ et debita atque legitima auctoritate, viri sancti et prælati leguntur transgressoribus maledixisse, non appetitu ultionis aut livore rancoris : quemadmodum princeps Apostolorum dixit ad Simonem magum, Pecunia tua sit tecum in perditionem. Denique verbis his Jacobi consonat quod loquitur Christus : Numquid colligunt de spinis uvas, aut de tribulis ficus ? Præterea, quemadmodum si aqua dulcis et aqua amara in eodem vasculo misceantur, dulcis in amaritudinem vertitur, non amara dulcis efficitur ; sic benedictio ejus qui Deum benedicit, a maledictione corrumpitur qua proximo maledicit, sicut et virtus peccato aufertur. Ideo ait Apostolus : Modicum fermentum totam massam corrumpit. Et rursus ait Scriptura : Non est speciosa laus in ore peccatoris.
paras.en: [[3:11|Doth a fountain send forth, out of the same hole, sweet and bitter water?|Numquid fons de eadem foramine emanat dulcem et amaram aquam]] Not at all, unless the fountain be corrupted. [[3:12|Can|Numquid potest]], [[3:12|my brethren|fratres mei]]: see how sweetly, how lovingly and humbly this holy Apostle speaks throughout his whole epistle, how often he calls those under him brethren! Can then, O my brethren, [[3:12|the fig tree|ficus]] [[3:12|bear grapes|uvas facere]], that is, that a tree of figs should produce grapes, [[3:12|Or the vine, figs?|aut vitis producere ficus ?]] By no means. [[3:12|So neither can the salt water yield sweet|Sic neque salsa aqua dulcem potest facere aquam]]. In the same way it is against reason, and against the divine law, that the same tongue should utter good words and evil, words of blessing and words of cursing, since the tongue was instituted and given by God for a praiseworthy use, for words of virtue. Nevertheless, holy men and prelates are sometimes read to have cursed transgressors out of zeal for justice and by due and lawful authority, not from desire of vengeance or the spite of rancour: as the prince of the Apostles said to Simon the magician, [[Acts 8:20|Keep thy money to thyself, to perish with thee|Pecunia tua sit tecum in perditionem]]. Finally, what Christ says agrees with these words of James: [[Matt 7:16|Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?|Numquid colligunt de spinis uvas, aut de tribulis ficus]] Moreover, just as when sweet water and bitter water are mixed in the same vessel, the sweet is turned to bitterness and the bitter is not made sweet; so the blessing of him who blesses God is corrupted by the cursing with which he curses his neighbour, as virtue too is taken away by sin. Therefore the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 5:6|a little leaven corrupteth the whole lump|Modicum fermentum totam massam corrumpit]]. And again Scripture says: [[Ecclus 15:9|Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner|Non est speciosa laus in ore peccatoris]].

paras.t: Jam audivimus, quam vehementissime sanctissimus iste Apostolus irrefrenationem linguæ vituperet, quanta mala dicat de lingua, et quanta vitia oriantur ex ea. Ideo custoditi simus in verbis, præmeditantes quid et qualiter sit loquendum, ut sermo noster, juxta doctrinam Pauli, semper in gratia sale discretionis sit conditus. Et Deum pro virtute et gratia moderandi loquelam in omnibus fervide deprecemur, cum Propheta dicentes : Pone, Domine, custodiam ori meo, et ostium circumstantiæ labiis meis. Hinc ait Hugo de S. Victore : Lingua dicitur, quoniam lingit adulando, mordet detrahendo, occidit mentiendo ; ligat, et ligari non potest. Labilis est, et teneri non valet ; sed labitur et fallit. Labitur ut anguilla, penetrat ut sagitta ; tollit amicos, multiplicat inimicos, movet rixas, seminat discordias ; uno ictu percutit occiditque plurimos ; blanda est et subdola, lata et parata ad exhaurienda bona, et mala miscenda. Mors et vita in potestate linguæ est. Ait quoque S. Bernardus : Levis sermo leviter volat, sed non leviter vulnerat ; leviter transit, sed graviter urit ; leviter penetrat animum, sed non leviter exit eum ; leviter profertur, sed non leviter revocatur ; facile volat, ideo facile caritatem violat. Quum ergo tot vitia pariat lingua non refrenata, merito Sapiens exclamat : Quis dabit ori meo custodiam, et super labia mea signaculum certum, ut non cadam ab ipsis, et lingua mea me perdat ? Hinc sancti Patres consultissime statuerunt, sacra silentia a religiosis servari. Et certe religiosi qui suam linguam refrenant, silentiumque stricte observant, varias evadunt tentationes, inquietudines et ruinas, atque facile possunt valde proficere. Qui autem incontinentis linguæ sunt, frequenter turbantur et turbant ; peccant, et alios ad peccandum inducunt ; potiusque deficiunt, quam proficiunt ut tenentur.
paras.en: We have now heard how very vehemently this most holy Apostle condemns the unbridling of the tongue, what great evils he speaks of the tongue, and how many vices arise from it. Let us therefore be guarded in our words, considering beforehand what is to be said and how, so that, according to the teaching of Paul, our speech may [[Col 4:6|be always in grace|semper in gratia]], [[Col 4:6|seasoned with salt|sale]] of discretion. And let us fervently beseech God for the strength and grace to govern our speech in all things, saying with the Prophet: [[Ps 140:3|Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth: and a door round about my lips|Pone, Domine, custodiam ori meo, et ostium circumstantiæ labiis meis]]. Hence Hugh of St Victor says: The tongue (*lingua*) is so called because it licks (*lingit*) by flattering [a play on words lost in English], bites by detracting, kills by lying; it binds, and cannot be bound. It is slippery, and cannot be held; it slips away and deceives. It slips away like an eel, it pierces like an arrow; it takes away friends, multiplies enemies, stirs up quarrels, sows discords; with one stroke it strikes and kills very many; it is smooth and crafty, broad and ready to drain away good things and to mingle evil. [[Prov 18:21|Death and life are in the power of the tongue|Mors et vita in potestate linguæ est]]. St Bernard also says: A light word flies lightly, but wounds not lightly; it passes lightly, but burns heavily; it enters the mind lightly, but leaves it not lightly; it is uttered lightly, but not lightly recalled; it flies easily, and so it easily violates charity. Since then the unbridled tongue brings forth so many vices, rightly does the Wise Man cry out: [[Ecclus 22:33|Who will set a guard before my mouth, and a sure seal upon my lips, that I fall not by them, and that my tongue destroy me not?|Quis dabit ori meo custodiam, et super labia mea signaculum certum, ut non cadam ab ipsis, et lingua mea me perdat]] Hence the holy Fathers most wisely laid down that sacred silence be kept by religious. And certainly religious who bridle their tongue and keep silence strictly escape various temptations, disquiets and falls, and can easily make great progress. But those who are of an unrestrained tongue are often troubled and trouble others; they sin, and lead others into sin; and they fall back rather than go forward, as they are bound to do.

paras.t: Præterea, quia apostolus Jacobus jam instruxit nos quantæ insipientiæ sit linguam non coarctare, consequenter docet quid ad verum pertineat sapientem. Quis sapiens in cognitione Dei et contemplationibus divinorum, et disciplinatus, id est moralibus virtutibus institutus, moribusque compositus, seu debitis observantiis exercitatus, vel in Scripturis bene instructus, inter vos ? Ostendat ex bona conversatione operationem suam, id est, virtuose conversando, non inaniter se jactando, demonstret se opera sancta juxta evangelicæ legis doctrinam habere. Et hoc ostendat, virtuoseque vivat, in mansuetudine sapientiæ, id est, cum mansuetudine ex sapientia progrediente omnia faciendo, juxta illud Ecclesiastici : Fili, in mansuetudine opera tua perfice, et super hominum gloriam diligeris. Mansuetudo namque facit hominem Deo ac proximis specialiter esse amabilem. Unde in epistola ad Demophilum monachum divinus Dionysius protestatur, quod Joseph, Moyses et David maximam apud Deum gratiam invenerunt, quoniam mansueti fuerunt. Ideo Christus : Discite, inquit, a me, quia mitis sum et humilis corde. Unde Psalmista ait de Deo : Exaltabit mansuetos in salutem. Et Judith ait : Humilium et mansuetorum semper tibi placuit deprecatio, Domine. Denique, sicut ira in sinu stulti, sic mansuetudo in sinu sapientis requiescit. Et sapientia mansuetudine in suis actibus dirigitur.
paras.en: Moreover, since the apostle James has now taught us how foolish it is not to restrain the tongue, he next teaches what belongs to the truly wise man. [[3:13|Who is a wise man|Quis sapiens]] in the knowledge of God and in the contemplation of divine things, [[3:13|and endued with knowledge|et disciplinatus]] [Latin *disciplinatus*, "disciplined", "trained"], that is, formed in the moral virtues and well ordered in his conduct, or practised in the observances due, or well instructed in the Scriptures, [[3:13|among you? Let him shew, by a good contestation, his work|inter vos ? Ostendat ex bona conversatione operationem suam]]: that is, by living virtuously, not by vainly boasting of himself, let him show that he has holy works according to the teaching of the law of the Gospel. And let him show this, and live virtuously, [[3:13|in the meekness of wisdom|in mansuetudine sapientiæ]], that is, doing all things with a meekness that proceeds from wisdom, according to that saying of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 3:19|My son, do thy works in meekness, and thou shalt be beloved above the glory of men|Fili, in mansuetudine opera tua perfice, et super hominum gloriam diligeris]]. For meekness makes a man especially lovable to God and to his neighbours. Hence in the letter to the monk Demophilus the divine Dionysius declares that Joseph, Moses and David found the greatest favour with God because they were meek. Therefore Christ says: [[Matt 11:29|learn|Discite]], he says, [[Matt 11:29|of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart|a me, quia mitis sum et humilis corde]]. Hence the Psalmist says of God: [[Ps 149:4|he will exalt the meek unto salvation|Exaltabit mansuetos in salutem]]. And Judith says: [[Jdt 9:16|the prayer of the humble and the meek hath always pleased thee|Humilium et mansuetorum semper tibi placuit deprecatio]], O Lord. Finally, as [[Eccles 7:10|anger resteth in the bosom of a fool|ira in sinu stulti]] [the margin gives Ecclus. xx, 10, which does not fit; the words are from Eccles 7:10], so meekness rests in the bosom of the wise. And wisdom is directed in its acts by meekness.

paras.t: Itaque nemo se putet vere sapientem et disciplinatum, nisi inveniat se reformatum, fractum et mitem, divina præcepta implentem, virtutibus præditum et exemplarem : quia ut ait Scriptura, In malevolam animam non introibit sapientia; atque ut Job asserit, Non invenitur sapientia in terra suaviter viventium, id est in cordibus carnalium hominum, oblectamenta carnis quærentium. Propter quod loquitur Isaias : Quem docebit Dominus scientiam? et quem intelligere faciet auditum? Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere. Et Sapiens ait : Qui amat vinum et pinguia, non erit sapiens. Hæc autem de sapientia quæ est donum, præsertim intelliguntur. Hinc et Leo papa fatetur : Christianæ, inquiens, sapientiæ altitudo, non in abundantia verbi, non in astutia disputandi, sed in vera humilitate consistit.
paras.en: So let no one think himself truly [[3:13|wise|sapientem]] and [[3:13|endued with knowledge|disciplinatum]] unless he finds himself reformed, broken and gentle, fulfilling the divine commandments, endowed with virtues and an example to others: for, as Scripture says, [[Wis 1:4|wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul|In malevolam animam non introibit sapientia]]; and, as Job asserts, [[Job 28:13|neither is it found in the land of them that live in delights|Non invenitur sapientia in terra suaviter viventium]], that is, in the hearts of carnal men who seek the pleasures of the flesh. For which reason Isaias says: [[Is 28:9|Whom shall he teach knowledge? and whom shall he make to understand the hearing? them that are weaned from the milk, that are drawn away from the breasts|Quem docebit Dominus scientiam? et quem intelligere faciet auditum? Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere]]. And the Wise Man says: [[Prov 21:17|he that loveth wine, and fat things|Qui amat vinum et pinguia]] shall not be wise [the Vulgate, Prov 21:17, ends "shall not be rich"]. These things are understood above all of the wisdom that is a gift [that is, the gift of the Holy Ghost]. Hence Pope Leo too declares: The height of Christian wisdom, he says, consists not in abundance of words, not in cleverness in disputing, but in true humility.

paras.t: Quod si zelum amarum, id est indiscretum, sive livorem et irrationabilem mentis amaricationem contra vos invicem, habetis, et contentiones sunt in cordibus vestris; nolite gloriari, sed potius flete propter tantos excessus : quid enim gloriaris in malitia? et mendaces esse adversus veritatem, æstimando aut asserendo quod talia placeant Deo, ut per ea salutem consequi valeatis. Qui enim amaro zelo afficiuntur contra alium, et contra eum contendunt, solent justificare se ipsos, et suam partem insipienter defendere, propriis vitiis excæcati. Non est illa sapientia desursum descendens, id est, talis opinio ac falsa sapientia non datur a Deo, sed error est ab homine adinventus, atque a dæmone persuasus. Ideo sequitur : sed terrena, id est temporalia ac transitoria quærens, animalis, id est sensuales delicias cupiens, et diabolica, quia a diabolo inspirata, et quasi honoris ac prælationis est avida. Vel dicitur terrena, prout oritur ex concupiscentia oculorum; animalis, in quantum procedit ex concupiscentia carnis; diabolica, in quantum nascitur ex superbia vitæ. — De hac sapientia falsa (per quam homo statuit sibi finem in divitiis, deliciis et honoribus mundi, et media sua astute disponit ad obtinenda talia) scriptum est ad Romanos : Prudentia carnis, mors est; et rursus : Prudentia carnis inimica est Deo; legi enim Dei non est subjecta. De his sapientiæ filiis loquitur Jeremias : Sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nescierunt; et Christus in Evangelio, Filii hujus sæculi prudentiores filiis lucis in generatione sua sunt. Unde et Baruch ait propheta : Filii Agar qui exquirunt prudentiam quæ de terra est, viam sapientiæ nescierunt.
paras.en: [[3:14|But if you have bitter zeal|Quod si zelum amarum]], that is, indiscreet zeal, or envy and an irrational embittering of mind against one another, [[3:14|you have|habetis]], [[3:14|and there be contention in your hearts|et contentiones sunt in cordibus vestris]]; [[3:14|glory not|nolite gloriari]], but rather weep for such great excesses: for [[Ps 51:3|Why dost thou glory in malice|quid enim gloriaris in malitia]]? [[3:14|and be not liars against the truth|et mendaces esse adversus veritatem]], by judging or asserting that such things please God, so that through them you may be able to attain salvation. For those who are moved with bitter zeal against another, and contend against him, are wont to justify themselves and foolishly to defend their own side, blinded by their own vices. [[3:15|this is not wisdom, descending from above|Non est illa sapientia desursum descendens]], that is, such an opinion and false wisdom is not given by God, but is an error devised by man and urged on by the devil. Therefore there follows: [[3:15|but earthly|sed terrena]], that is, seeking temporal and passing things, [[3:15|sensual|animalis]], that is, desiring the delights of the senses, [[3:15|devilish|et diabolica]], because it is inspired by the devil, and is, as it were, greedy for honour and for preferment. Or it is called earthly inasmuch as it arises from the concupiscence of the eyes; sensual, inasmuch as it proceeds from the concupiscence of the flesh; devilish, inasmuch as it is born of the pride of life. Of this false wisdom (by which a man sets his end in riches, delights and the honours of the world, and craftily arranges his means for obtaining such things) it is written to the Romans: [[Rom 8:6|the wisdom of the flesh is death|Prudentia carnis, mors est]]; and again: [[Rom 8:7|the wisdom of the flesh is an enemy to God. For it is not subject to the law of God|Prudentia carnis inimica est Deo; legi enim Dei non est subjecta]]. Of these children of this wisdom Jeremias says: [[Jer 4:22|they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge|Sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nescierunt]]; and Christ in the Gospel: [[Luke 16:8|the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light|Filii hujus sæculi prudentiores filiis lucis in generatione sua sunt]]. Hence the prophet Baruch too says: [[Bar 3:23|The children of Agar|Filii Agar]] [[Bar 3:23|that search after the wisdom that is of the earth|qui exquirunt prudentiam quæ de terra est]], [[Bar 3:23|the way of wisdom they have not known|viam sapientiæ nescierunt]].

paras.t: Ubi enim zelus, id est amaritudo, indignatio seu livor, et contentio, ibi inconstantia, id est fluctuatio cordis, et agitatio passionum, perturbatio, aversio, multiplexque corrosio ac distractio mentis. Animus enim inordinatus, sibi ipsi est gravis. Atque ut asserit Isaias, Impii sunt quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest. Optimum ergo est, juxta Apostolum, gratia stabiliri cor, et virtutibus illud firmare in Deo, ne per errores et vitia distrahatur. Specialiter vero vitia ista, videlicet zelus et contentio, sunt inquietudinis causa et animæ afflictiva, quia putredo ossium invidia, et contentiosus turbat se ipsum. Nec solum est ibi inconstantia, sed et omne opus pravum ; non quod omnia opera mala sint actualiter ac inseparabiliter zelo et contentioni annexa, sed quia ex eis procedere possunt ac solent, imo plerumque diversa vitia sunt eis conjuncta.
paras.en: [[3:16|For where envying|Ubi enim zelus]], that is, bitterness, indignation or envy, [[3:16|and contention is: there is inconstancy|et contentio, ibi inconstantia]], that is, wavering of heart, and the tossing of the passions, disturbance, aversion, and a manifold gnawing and distraction of the mind. For a disordered mind is a burden to itself. And as Isaias asserts, [[Is 57:20|the wicked are like the raging sea, which cannot rest|Impii sunt quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest]]. It is best therefore, according to the Apostle, [[Heb 13:9|that the heart be established with grace|gratia stabiliri cor]], and to make it firm in God by the virtues, lest it be distracted by errors and vices. But these vices in particular, namely envy and contention, are a cause of disquiet and an affliction of the soul, because envy is the rottenness of the bones, and the contentious man troubles himself. And not only is there inconstancy there, but [[3:16|and every evil work|et omne opus pravum]]: not that all evil works are actually and inseparably joined to envy and contention, but because they can and commonly do proceed from them; indeed, for the most part various vices are joined with them.

paras.t: Porro contentio proprie dicta, quam Apostolus inter mortalia peccata annumerat, et de qua nunc loquitur Jacobus, est impugnatio veritatis cum confidentia clamoris, secundum Ambrosium. Contentio autem quæ est impugnatio falsitatis cum moderata acrimonia vocis, est laudabilis. Quod si modus excedatur, erit culpabilis. Contentio autem quæ non est cum intentione impugnandi veritatem, sed dum quisque defendit quod sibi verum aut bonum apparet, non est perfecta contentio nec mortale peccatum. Contentio vero de qua nunc sermo, in Scripturis valde vituperatur. Ait enim ad Timotheum Apostolus : Noli verbis contendere; ad nihil enim utile est, nisi ad subversionem audientium. Et rursus ad Corinthios scribit : Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio, nonne carnales estis? In Ecclesiastico quoque jubetur : Abstine te a lite; et in Job, Respondete absque contentione. Est quoque inhonestum et aliorum scandalizativum, contendere. Propter quod ait Scriptura : Honor est homini quum separat se a contentione. Postremo, contentio ex superbia aut vana gloria generatur. Propter quod Salomon protestatur : Inter superbos sunt semper jurgia.
paras.en: Now [[3:16|contention|contentio]] properly so called, which the Apostle numbers among the mortal sins[[2 Cor 12:20||]], and of which James is now speaking, is, according to Ambrose, the assailing of the truth with confident clamour. But contention that is the assailing of falsehood with a moderate sharpness of voice is praiseworthy; though if the measure be exceeded, it will be blameworthy. And contention that is not with the intention of assailing the truth, but where each defends what seems to him true or good, is not contention in the full sense, nor a mortal sin. But the contention now spoken of is strongly condemned in the Scriptures. For the Apostle says to Timothy: [[2 Tim 2:14|Contend not in words: for it is to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers|Noli verbis contendere; ad nihil enim utile est, nisi ad subversionem audientium]]. And again he writes to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 3:3|whereas there is among you envying and contention, are you not carnal|Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio, nonne carnales estis]]? In Ecclesiasticus too it is commanded: [[Ecclus 28:10|Refrain from strife|Abstine te a lite]]; and in Job: [[Job 6:29|Answer|Respondete]] [[Job 6:29|without contention|absque contentione]]. It is also unseemly, and a cause of scandal to others, to contend. For which reason Scripture says: [[Prov 20:3|It is an honour for a man to separate himself from quarrels|Honor est homini quum separat se a contentione]]. Lastly, contention is born of pride or vainglory. For which reason Solomon declares: [[Prov 13:10|Among the proud there are always contentions|Inter superbos sunt semper jurgia]].

paras.t: Vitemus ergo hæc vitia, et dulci caritatis affectu in alterutrum efficiamur. Sed et discretum habeamus zelum justitiæ absque animi perturbatione. Accendamur quoque zelo divini honoris, et zelum amarum penitus a corde nostro repellamus, quum in Ecclesiastico dicatur : Non est sensus ubi abundat amaritudo : et in Deuteronomio, Non sit inter vos radix germinans fel et amaritudinem. Hinc ad Hebræos dicitur : Pacem sequimini cum omnibus, contemplantes ne qua radix amaritudinis sursum germinans impediat, et per illam inquinentur multi. Et rursus ait Apostolus : Si invicem mordetis et comeditis, videte ne ab invicem consumamini.
paras.en: Let us therefore shun these vices, and be disposed towards one another with the sweet affection of charity. But let us also have a discreet zeal for justice, without disturbance of mind. Let us also be kindled with zeal for the honour of God, and drive [[3:14|bitter zeal|zelum amarum]] utterly from our heart, since it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 21:15|there is no understanding where there is bitterness|Non est sensus ubi abundat amaritudo]]; and in Deuteronomy: Let there not be among you [[Deut 29:18|a root bringing forth gall and bitterness|radix germinans fel et amaritudinem]]. Hence it is said to the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:14|Follow peace with all men|Pacem sequimini cum omnibus]], [[Heb 12:15|Looking diligently|contemplantes]] [[Heb 12:15|lest any root of bitterness springing up do hinder and by it many be defiled|ne qua radix amaritudinis sursum germinans impediat, et per illam inquinentur multi]]. And again the Apostle says: [[Gal 5:15|if you bite and devour one another: take heed you be not consumed one of another|Si invicem mordetis et comeditis, videte ne ab invicem consumamini]].

paras.t: Consequenter describit Apostolus veram sapientiam, illam præcipue quæ est unum et primum inter septem dona Spiritus Sancti. Illam ergo describit per proprietates et operationes ipsius, subdendo : Quæ autem desursum est sapientia, puta sapientia spiritualis, supernaturalis, infusa : per quam homo contemplatur Deum per gustum internum, et bene sentit ac judicat de eo per connaturalitatem et conformitatem affectus ad eum, videlicet quod ei soli sit finaliter adhærendum tanquam summo et incomparabili bono, finique ultimo : primum quidem pudica est, id est peccati fœditatem turpitudinemque detestans ac erubescens. Et ita sapientia ista facit a malo recedere, seu peccata vitare. Nempe per hoc quod summæ veritatis ac primæ lucis puritatem ac pulchritudinem contemplatur, parit in mente castum pudorem, quo homo erubescit se in divinæ majestatis præsentia et aspectu viliter turpiterque habere, cogitatione, affectione, verbo, actu, aut omissione peccando. Iste est sapientialis ac optimus pudor, de quo scriptum est : Est confusio adducens gratiam et gloriam. Facit quoque sapientia ista hominem habere de præteritis culpis suis salubrem pudorem, qui ad deletionem peccati, etiam quoad pœnam, non mediocriter confert. Rursus sapientia ista dicitur esse pudica, quia ad contemplationem Dei reverenter accedit, non præsumptuose, impudenter aut temerarie ingerens se ad divinorum ac incomprehensibilium perscrutationem. Est demum et vituperabilis pudor, quo homo sua peccata fateri, et pro eis corripi ac corrigi erubescit. De quo dictum est : Est confusio adducens peccatum; et rursus, Non confundaris confiteri peccata tua.
paras.en: Next the Apostle describes true wisdom, above all that which is one, and the first, among the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]]. He describes it, then, by its properties and operations, adding: [[3:17|But the wisdom that is from above|Quæ autem desursum est sapientia]], namely spiritual, supernatural, infused wisdom: by which a man contemplates God by an inward taste, and rightly perceives and judges of him through a connaturality and conformity of affection towards him [that is, a likeness of the will to God that lets it judge of divine things as by kinship rather than by reasoning], namely, that to him alone one must finally cleave as to the supreme and incomparable good and the last end: [[3:17|first indeed is chaste|primum quidem pudica est]] [Latin *pudica*, "modest", "having a sense of shame": Denis goes on to explain it of *pudor*, shame], that is, detesting and blushing at the foulness and baseness of sin. And so this wisdom makes one depart from evil, or avoid sins. For in that it contemplates the purity and beauty of the supreme truth and the first light, it brings forth in the mind a chaste shame, by which a man blushes to behave himself vilely and basely in the presence and sight of the divine majesty, sinning by thought, affection, word, deed or omission. This is the shame that belongs to wisdom, and the best shame, of which it is written: [[Ecclus 4:25|there is a shame that bringeth glory and grace|Est confusio adducens gratiam et gloriam]] [the margin note here could not be read]. This wisdom also makes a man have a wholesome shame of his past faults, which contributes not a little to the blotting out of sin, even as to its penalty. Again, this wisdom is said to be chaste because it approaches the contemplation of God with reverence, not thrusting itself presumptuously, shamelessly or rashly into the searching of divine and incomprehensible things. There is, lastly, a blameworthy shame too, by which a man blushes to confess his sins and to be reproved and corrected for them. Of this it is said: [[Ecclus 4:25|there is a shame that bringeth sin|Est confusio adducens peccatum]]; and again: [[Ecclus 4:31|Be not ashamed to confess thy sins|Non confundaris confiteri peccata tua]].

paras.t: Deinde pacifica, id est tranquillitatem seu pacem internam gignens in sapiente : quia per hanc sapientiam quiescit, tranquillatur et figitur mens in Deo, juxta illud Sapientiæ : Intrans in domum meam, conquiescam cum illa : non enim habet amaritudinem conversatio illius, nec tædium convictus illius, sed gaudium et lætitiam. Pax autem idem est quod gaudium imperturbatum. Ideo ait Scriptura : Vir sapiens suavis est animæ suæ. Et ad Romanos habetur : Prudentia spiritus vita et pax. Dicitur quoque sapientia ista pacifica, quia per eam fideles concordant in bonis, nec per elationem se ab invicem dividunt, quemadmodum per humanam et naturalem sapientiam sæpe contingit : quia in ea invenitur opinionum diversitas, nec est tanta in ea certitudo sicut in ista ; et parit elationem, hæc vero humiliationem spontaneam, Salomone attestante, Ubi sapientia, ibi humilitas.
paras.en: [[3:17|then peaceable|Deinde pacifica]], that is, begetting tranquillity or inward peace in the wise man: because by this wisdom the mind rests, is calmed and is fixed in God, according to that saying of Wisdom: [[Wis 8:16|When I go into my house, I shall repose myself with her: for her conversation hath no bitterness, nor her company any tediousness, but joy and gladness|Intrans in domum meam, conquiescam cum illa : non enim habet amaritudinem conversatio illius, nec tædium convictus illius, sed gaudium et lætitiam]]. Now peace is the same as undisturbed joy. Therefore Scripture says: The wise man [[Ecclus 37:22|is sweet to his own soul|suavis est animæ suæ]] [the Vulgate has "the skilful man"]. And in Romans we have: [[Rom 8:6|the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace|Prudentia spiritus vita et pax]]. This wisdom is also called peaceable because through it the faithful agree together in good things, and do not divide themselves from one another through pride, as often happens through human and natural wisdom: for in that there is found diversity of opinions, nor is there such certainty in it as in this; and it brings forth pride, whereas this brings forth a willing humility, as Solomon testifies: Where wisdom is, there is humility[[Prov 11:2||]] [Prov 11:2 reads: where humility is, there also is wisdom].

paras.t: Est quoque sapientia ista modesta, id est moderamen servans in omnibus, quum sapientis sit ordinare, secundum Philosophum. Facitque hominem circumspectum, non impetuosum. Ideo monet Apostolus : In sapientia ambulate ad eos qui foris sunt. Et Sapiens : Est enim in illa spiritus intelligentiæ sanctus, unicus et modestus. Suadibilis, id est docilis ac dirigibilis : quemadmodum et juxta philosophos, prima pars prudentiæ est docilitas. Qui ergo in suo sensu sunt pertinaces, sapientiæ sunt expertes. Bonis consentiens, id est rationabilibus verbis præbens assensum. Non enim qui veraciter est sapiens, proprium judicium aliorum judicio immansive præponit. Hinc princeps Apostolorum, increpationi informationique Pauli humiliter acquievit. Propter quod in Proverbiis asseritur : Argue sapientem, et diliget te; doce justum, et festinabit accipere. Propterea iterum Salomon loquitur : Non sis sapiens apud temetipsum. Et ad Romanos fertur : Nolite esse prudentes apud vosmetipsos.
paras.en: This wisdom is also [[3:17|modest|modesta]], that is, keeping measure in all things, since it belongs to the wise man to set in order, according to the Philosopher. And it makes a man circumspect, not headlong. Therefore the Apostle warns: [[Col 4:5|Walk with wisdom towards them that are without|In sapientia ambulate ad eos qui foris sunt]]. And the Wise Man: [[Wis 7:22|For in her is the spirit of understanding; holy, one|Est enim in illa spiritus intelligentiæ sanctus, unicus]] and modest [the Vulgate has no "modest" here]. [[3:17|easy to be persuaded|Suadibilis]], that is, teachable and ready to be directed: as also, according to the philosophers, the first part of prudence is docility. Those then who are obstinate in their own opinion have no share in wisdom. [[3:17|consenting to the good|Bonis consentiens]], that is, giving assent to reasonable words. For he who is truly wise does not obstinately [the print reads *immansive*, an unclear word; "obstinately" is a guess from the sense] set his own judgment above the judgment of others. Hence the prince of the Apostles humbly accepted the rebuke and instruction of Paul. For which reason it is asserted in Proverbs: [[Prov 9:8|Rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee|Argue sapientem, et diliget te]]; [[Prov 9:9|Teach a just man, and he shall make haste to receive it|doce justum, et festinabit accipere]]. Therefore Solomon says again: [[Prov 3:7|Be not wise in thy own conceit|Non sis sapiens apud temetipsum]]. And in Romans it is said: [[Rom 12:16|Be not wise in your own conceits|Nolite esse prudentes apud vosmetipsos]].

paras.t: Plena misericordia et fructibus bonis. Hæc enim sapientia facit hominem compassivum atque beneficum aliis : quoniam intuetur quod Deo sit proprium misereri ac subvenire, quod etiam omnis homo ex se ipse sit fragilis, atque in magno periculo constitutus. Idcirco condolet aliis, ac subvenit eis pro posse, ne tanta beatitudine ad quam conditi sunt, priventur. Judicans sine simulatione, id est sincere se habens in judicando; nec vitia sub colore virtutum exercens, quemadmodum qui ex odio, ira, aut impatientia corripiunt proximos, ex caritate et zelo justitiæ id se facere confingentes. Idcirco Sapiens ait : Spiritus sanctus disciplinæ effugiet fictum. Hinc Christus docuit, ut simus simplices sicut columbæ : qui hypocrisim in Evangelio specialissime reprobat et condemnat.
paras.en: [[3:17|full of mercy and good fruits|Plena misericordia et fructibus bonis]]. For this wisdom makes a man compassionate and beneficent to others: because it sees that it is proper to God to have mercy and to help, and also that every man is frail of himself[[Gen 8:21||]] and set in great peril.
