Therefore it suffers with others, and helps them as far as it can, lest they be deprived of the great beatitude for which they were created. Judging [[3:17|without dissimulation|sine simulatione]] [Denis reads *judicans sine simulatione*, "judging without dissimulation"; the Vulgate has *non judicans*, "without judging"], that is, behaving sincerely in judging; and not practising vices under the colour of virtues, like those who rebuke their neighbours out of hatred, anger or impatience, pretending that they do it out of charity and zeal for justice. Therefore the Wise Man says: [[Wis 1:5|the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful|Spiritus sanctus disciplinæ effugiet fictum]]. Hence Christ taught that we should be [[Matt 10:16|simple as doves|simplices sicut columbæ]]: he who in the Gospel most especially reproves and condemns hypocrisy[[Matt 6:2||]][[Matt 6:5||]][[Matt 6:16||]][[Matt 23:13||]][[Luke 12:1||]] [the margin gives Matt. vi, 2, 5, 16; xxiii, passim; Luke xii, 1; etc.].

paras.t: Fructus autem justitiæ in pace seminatur. Fructus justitiæ interdum vocatur operatio virtuosa, ex justitia manans. Et hujus fructus, merces ac finis, est vera felicitas, juxta illud Apostoli : Habetis fructum vestrum in sanctificatione, finem vero vitam æternam. Unde in Joanne ait Salvator discipulis : Posui vos ut eatis, et fructum afferatis. Joannes quoque Baptista : Omnis, inquit, arbor quæ non facit fructum bonum, excidetur. Hic itaque fructus seminatur in pace, id est, exercetur cum pace pectoris, sine qua nemo Deo placere potest, quia oportet mentem concordare cum Deo in observantia præceptorum et caritatis tenore. Cujus effectus est pax, quemadmodum scriptum est : Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam. Hinc in libro Job docetur : Acquiesce Deo, et habeto pacem, et per hæc habebis fructus optimos. Seminatur itaque fructus justitiæ in pace, facientibus pacem, id est ad meritum præmiumque eorum; vel, Facientibus, id est a facientibus, pacem, puta a pacificis, de quibus dicitur : Beati pacifici, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur.
paras.en: [[3:18|And the fruit of justice is sown in peace|Fructus autem justitiæ in pace seminatur]]. The fruit of justice is sometimes the name given to virtuous work flowing from justice. And the reward and end of this fruit is true happiness, according to that saying of the Apostle: [[Rom 6:22|you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end life everlasting|Habetis fructum vestrum in sanctificatione, finem vero vitam æternam]]. Hence in John the Saviour says to the disciples: [[John 15:16|have appointed you, that you should go and should bring forth fruit|Posui vos ut eatis, et fructum afferatis]]. John the Baptist also: [[Matt 3:10|Every|Omnis]], he says, [[Matt 3:10|tree therefore that doth not yield good fruit, shall be cut down|arbor quæ non facit fructum bonum, excidetur]]. This fruit, then, is sown in peace, that is, it is practised with peace of heart, without which no one can please God, since the mind must agree with God in keeping the commandments and in the constancy of charity. And the effect of this is peace, as it is written: [[Ps 118:165|Much peace have they that love thy law|Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam]]. Hence it is taught in the book of Job: [[Job 22:21|Submit thyself then to him, and be at peace: and thereby thou shalt have the best fruits|Acquiesce Deo, et habeto pacem, et per hæc habebis fructus optimos]]. So the fruit of justice is sown in peace [[3:18|to them that make peace|facientibus pacem]], that is, for their merit and reward; or [[3:18|to them that make|Facientibus]], that is, by those that make, peace, namely by the peacemakers, of whom it is said: [[Matt 5:9|Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God|Beati pacifici, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur]].

paras.t: Denique unusquisque facere debet pacem in primis sibi ipsi cum Deo, eum sibi per pœnitentiam reconciliando, atque per contemplationem et dilectionem cor suum in ipso figendo ac tranquillando. Propter quod ait Apostolus ad Romanos : Justificati ex fide, pacem habeamus ad Deum ; et iterum : Obsecramus pro Christo, reconciliamini Deo. Secundo, debet unusquisque sibi pacem facere et servare pro posse cum proximo suo, sicut in Evangelio præcipit Dominus : Vade, reconciliare fratri tuo. Et Paulus : Si fieri potest, quod in vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus pacem habete. Deinde debemus ex caritate fraterna proximis nostris pace carentibus, pacem cum Deo et hominibus procurare, orando, hortando, confœderando, ac aliis viis.
paras.en: Finally, each one ought to make peace first for himself with God, reconciling him to himself by penance, and fixing and calming his heart in him by contemplation and love. For which reason the Apostle says to the Romans: [[Rom 5:1|Being justified therefore by faith, let us have peace with God|Justificati ex fide, pacem habeamus ad Deum]]; and again: [[2 Cor 5:20|for Christ, we beseech you, be reconciled to God|Obsecramus pro Christo, reconciliamini Deo]]. Secondly, each one ought to make peace for himself and keep it, as far as he can, with his neighbour, as the Lord commands in the Gospel: [[Matt 5:24|go first to be reconciled to thy brother|Vade, reconciliare fratri tuo]]. And Paul: [[Rom 12:18|If it be possible, as much as is in you, have peace with all men|Si fieri potest, quod in vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus pacem habete]]. Then we ought, out of fraternal charity, to procure for our neighbours who lack peace, peace with God and with men, by praying, exhorting, reconciling and other ways.

paras.t: Insuper fructus justitiæ nominatur interim æterna felicitas, juxta illud Sapientiæ : Bonorum laborum gloriosus est fructus. Porro operatio vitæ præsentis, est seminatio respectu futuræ remunerationis […]
paras.en: Moreover, [[3:18|the fruit of justice|fructus justitiæ]] is at times the name given to eternal happiness, according to that saying of Wisdom: [[Wis 3:15|the fruit of good labours is glorious|Bonorum laborum gloriosus est fructus]]. Further, the work of the present life is a sowing with respect to the future reward […]

4.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI QUARTI : UNDE BELLA ET LITES IN VOBIS ?
4.title_en: Exposition of the fourth chapter: From whence are wars and contentions among you?

paras.t: HOC capitulo hortatur Apostolus, ne inordinati sint nostri affectus, et ne ex eis ad ea quæ aliis nociva sunt, procedamus.
paras.en: In this chapter the Apostle exhorts us that our affections be not disordered, and that we go not on from them to things that are harmful to others.

paras.t: Unde bella et lites in vobis? id est, ex qua radice oriuntur pugnæ reales atque verbales, quibus vos invicem impugnatis? Nonne ex concupiscentiis vestris, id est terrenis, inordinatis, mundanis et sensualibus affectionibus, quæ militant in membris vestris, id est, ministerio membrorum ducuntur ad opus iniquum? Sic militant seu dominantur in membris, quia juxta concupiscentiarum inclinationem ac impetum, membra moventur in actum, quamvis concupiscentiæ sint subjective in appetitivis potentiis. Sumitur ergo nomen concupiscentiæ hoc loco, communiter pro quovis inordinato affectu divitiarum, deliciarum sive honorum. Hinc ad Romanos hortatur Apostolus: Sicut exhibuistis membra vestra servire immunditiæ et iniquitati ad iniquitatem, ita nunc exhibete membra vestra servire justitiæ in sanctificationem. Certum est autem quod mali effectus ex pravis procedant affectibus, et quidquid culpæ in verbis aut factis consistit, ex interiori inordinatione dependet ac profluit. Propter quod princeps Apostolorum hortatur: Obsecro vos abstinere a carnalibus desideriis, quæ militant adversus animam.
paras.en: [[4:1|From whence are wars and contentions among you?|Unde bella et lites in vobis?]] that is, from what root spring the fights, in deed and in word, with which you assail one another? Are they not [[4:1|from your concupiscences|ex concupiscentiis vestris]], that is, from earthly, disordered, worldly and sensual affections, [[4:1|which war in your members|quæ militant in membris vestris]]? that is, which are carried into wicked work by the service of the members. They war, or hold sway, in the members in this way: the members are moved to act according to the bent and drive of the concupiscences, though the concupiscences are seated, as in their subject, in the appetitive powers. The word *concupiscence* is therefore taken here in a general sense, for any disordered affection for riches, pleasures or honours. Hence the Apostle exhorts the Romans: [[Rom 6:19|as you have yielded your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity, unto iniquity: so now yield your members to serve justice, unto sanctification|Sicut exhibuistis membra vestra servire immunditiæ et iniquitati ad iniquitatem, ita nunc exhibete membra vestra servire justitiæ in sanctificationem]]. Now it is certain that evil effects proceed from wicked affections, and that whatever fault lies in words or deeds depends and flows from the disorder within. For this reason the prince of the Apostles exhorts: [[1 Pet 2:11|I beseech you|Obsecro vos]] [[1 Pet 2:11|to refrain yourselves from carnal desires which war against the soul|abstinere a carnalibus desideriis, quæ militant adversus animam]].

paras.t: Concupiscitis carnalia et mundana, et non habetis ea. Et sic solo inordinato affectu fœdamini; et non habituri effectum operis, præcipitatis vos in vitia impiæ voluntatis: quia voluntas inordinata deliberata, reputatur pro opere. Sic multi quum in egestate vivant, voluntariæ paupertatis privantur mercede, et cum divitibus voluptuariis, superbis atque avaris damnantur, quia terrenam abundantiam, delectationem sensualem ac mundanum præoptant honorem. Isti sunt miseri in præsenti sæculo et futuro: quia nec hic, nec ibi obtinent quæ affectant. Ideo scriptum est: Est dives, quum nihil habeat; et est pauper, quum in divitiis multis sit. Occiditis, vel corporaliter alios, vel spiritualiter vosmetipsos: quia ex vitiosis desideriis, quibus homo in primis spiritualiter necat se ipsum, interdum corporale homicidium oritur; et zelatis, id est, aliis invidetis. Quod enim quis sibimet cupit, hoc invidere aliis solet. Et non potestis adipisci quod vitiose appetitis, quia multi consequi nequeunt, nec valent implere, quod damnabiliter quærunt et cupiunt. Idcirco in libro Job asseritur: Deus consilium pravorum dissipat: qui dissipat cogitationes malignorum, ne possint implere manus eorum quod cœperant. Unde et in Isaia legitur: Dat scrutatores secretorum quasi non sint, et consiliarios in stultum finem adducit. Istud tamen frequenter misericorditer accidit, quia non expedit pravis hominibus obtinere quod optant illicite. Idcirco per Osee Dominus loquitur: Ecce ego sepiam viam tuam spinis.
paras.en: [[4:2|You covet|Concupiscitis]] carnal and worldly things, [[4:2|and have not|et non habetis]] them. And so you are defiled by the disordered affection alone; and, though you will not have the effect of the deed, you cast yourselves headlong into the vices of an impious will: for a deliberate disordered will is reckoned as the deed. So many who live in want are deprived of the reward of voluntary poverty, and are damned with the rich who are given to pleasure, pride and avarice, because they long for earthly abundance, sensual delight and worldly honour. These are wretched in this world and in the world to come: for neither here nor there do they obtain what they aim at. Therefore it is written: [[Prov 13:7|One is as it were rich, when he hath nothing and another is as it were poor, when he hath great riches|Est dives, quum nihil habeat; et est pauper, quum in divitiis multis sit]]. [[4:2|you kill|Occiditis]], either others in body, or yourselves in spirit: for out of vicious desires, by which a man first of all kills himself spiritually, bodily murder sometimes springs; [[4:2|and envy|et zelatis]], that is, you envy others. For what a man covets for himself, that he is wont to envy others. [[4:2|and cannot obtain|Et non potestis adipisci]] what you viciously crave, for many cannot attain nor are able to fulfil what they damnably seek and covet. Therefore it is asserted in the book of Job: God [[Job 5:13|disappointeth the counsel of the wicked|consilium pravorum dissipat]]: [[Job 5:12|Who bringeth to nought the designs of the malignant, so that their hands cannot accomplish what they had begun|qui dissipat cogitationes malignorum, ne possint implere manus eorum quod cœperant]]. And so too we read in Isaias: [[Is 40:23|He that bringeth the searchers of secrets to nothing|Dat scrutatores secretorum quasi non sint]], and he [[Job 12:17|bringeth counsellors to a foolish end|consiliarios in stultum finem adducit]] [these last words are from Job 12:17, not Isaias; the margin gives no reference for either]. Yet this often happens in mercy, because it is not good for wicked men to obtain what they unlawfully desire. Therefore the Lord says through Osee: [[Osee 2:6|behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns|Ecce ego sepiam viam tuam spinis]].

paras.t: Litigatis verbis, et belligeratis in opere contra proximos pro terrenis, et non habetis ea, scilicet necessaria vitæ, propter quod non postulastis, id est, Deum humiliter atque ordinate pro eis habendis non rogastis: primo ac principaliter exorando pro spiritualibus, Dei honorem ac animarum salutem concernentibus; deinde pro corporalibus, prout ad spiritualia necessaria sunt sive accommoda, sicuti Christus in Evangelio docet: Primum, inquiens, quærite regnum Dei et justitiam ejus, et hæc omnia adjicientur vobis.
paras.en: [[4:2|You contend|Litigatis]] in words, [[4:2|and war|et belligeratis]] in deed against your neighbours for earthly things, [[4:2|and you have not|et non habetis]] them, namely the necessaries of life, [[4:2|because you ask not|propter quod non postulastis]], that is, you have not besought God humbly and in due order to have them: praying first and chiefly for spiritual things, which concern God's honour and the salvation of souls; then for bodily things, so far as they are necessary or helpful for spiritual ones, as Christ teaches in the Gospel, saying: [[Matt 6:33|first|Primum]], he says, [[Matt 6:33|Seek ye|quærite]] [[Matt 6:33|the kingdom of God, and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you|regnum Dei et justitiam ejus, et hæc omnia adjicientur vobis]].

paras.t: Petitis, et non accipitis, id est, inordinate Deum rogatis, idcirco non audit vos; eo quod male petatis, non obediendo in primis Dei præceptis. Qui enim declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis. Temporalia quoque magis quam spiritualia postulatis. Unde apud Joannem ait Christus discipulis adhuc carnalibus: Usque modo non petistis quidquam in nomine meo, id est pertinentia ad salutem. Ut in concupiscentiis vestris insumatis: id est, temporalia quæ petitis, non ordinatis ad debitum finem, scilicet ad moderatam et necessariam corporis sustentationem, sed ad superfluitatem ac voluptatem, ut ea insumatis, id est, intra vos accipiatis et consumatis, in concupiscentiis vestris, scilicet juxta impetum concupiscentiarum, non secundum rationis judicium. Contra quod Paulus hortatur: Curam carnis ne feceritis in desideriis; itemque, Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus. Christus quoque: Attendite, inquit, vobis, ne graventur corda vestra crapula et ebrietate et curis hujus vitæ.
paras.en: [[4:3|You ask and receive not|Petitis, et non accipitis]], that is, you beseech God in a disordered way, and so he does not hear you; [[4:3|because you ask amiss|eo quod male petatis]], not obeying God's commandments in the first place. For [[Prov 28:9|He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination|Qui enim declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis]]. You also ask for temporal things more than for spiritual ones. Hence in John Christ says to his disciples, who were still carnal: [[John 16:24|Hitherto, you have not asked any thing in my name|Usque modo non petistis quidquam in nomine meo]], that is, things pertaining to salvation. [[4:3|that you may consume it on your concupiscences|Ut in concupiscentiis vestris insumatis]]: that is, the temporal things you ask for you do not direct to their due end, namely the moderate and necessary sustenance of the body, but to excess and pleasure, [[4:3|that you may consume it|ut ea insumatis]], that is, take them into yourselves and consume them, [[4:3|on your concupiscences|in concupiscentiis vestris]], namely according to the drive of the concupiscences, not according to the judgement of reason. Against this Paul exhorts: [[Rom 13:14|make not provision for the flesh in its concupiscences|Curam carnis ne feceritis in desideriis]]; and again: [[1 Tim 6:8|having food and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content|Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus]]. Christ too: [[Luke 21:34|take heed|Attendite]], he says, [[Luke 21:34|to yourselves, lest perhaps your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness and the cares of this life|vobis, ne graventur corda vestra crapula et ebrietate et curis hujus vitæ]].

paras.t: Adulteri, id est mente a Deo aversi. Quæ aversio, spiritualis fornicatio est, juxta illud Psalmographi: Qui elongant se a te, peribunt; perdidisti omnes qui fornicantur abs te; et illud Osee, Fornicati sunt a Deo suo. Omnis etenim anima, aut est Dei sponsa, aut diaboli adultera. Dei equidem sponsa est, quæ ei fide et caritate conjungitur. Unde per Osee effatur: Sponsabo te mihi in fide. Talis anima Deum spirituali amore amplectitur, atque ab ipso cœlesti semine (quod est verbum Dei) ac lumine gratiæ fecundatur. Porro diaboli perhibetur adultera, quæ ei perversæ voluntatis miscetur consensu. Spiritualis quoque sapientia, præsertim æterna et increata, sponsa est hominis justi, juxta illud Sapientiæ: Hanc amavi et exquisivi, et quæsivi sponsam mihi eam assumere, et amator factus sum formæ illius.
paras.en: [[4:4|Adulterers|Adulteri]], that is, turned away from God in mind. This turning away is spiritual fornication, according to that word of the Psalmist: [[Ps 72:27|they that go far from thee shall perish: thou hast destroyed all them that are disloyal to thee|Qui elongant se a te, peribunt; perdidisti omnes qui fornicantur abs te]] [the Latin *fornicantur*, which the Douay-Rheims renders "are disloyal", means "commit fornication"]; and that of Osee: [[Osee 4:12|they have committed fornication against their God|Fornicati sunt a Deo suo]]. For every soul is either the spouse of God or the adulteress of the devil. She is the spouse of God who is joined to him by faith and charity. Hence he declares through Osee: [[Osee 2:20|I will espouse thee to me in faith|Sponsabo te mihi in fide]]. Such a soul embraces God with spiritual love, and is made fruitful by him with the heavenly seed (which is the word of God[[Luke 8:11||]]) and with the light of grace. But she is called the adulteress of the devil who is mingled with him by the consent of a perverse will. Spiritual wisdom too, above all eternal and uncreated Wisdom, is the spouse of the just man, according to that word of Wisdom: [[Wis 8:2|Her have I loved, and have sought her out|Hanc amavi et exquisivi]], [[Wis 8:2|and have desired to take for my spouse, and I became a lover of her beauty|et quæsivi sponsam mihi eam assumere, et amator factus sum formæ illius]].

paras.t: Qui ergo hanc sponsam relinquit, et ei terrena præponit, atque carnalia amplexatur, recte adulter vocatur. Judæi etiam ad corporalia adulteria erant proclives, sicut per Jeremiam loquitur Deus: Unusquisque ad uxorem proximi sui hinniebat.
paras.en: He, then, who forsakes this spouse, and sets earthly things before her, and embraces carnal ones, is rightly called an adulterer. The Jews too were prone to bodily adulteries, as God says through Jeremias: [[Jer 5:8|every one neighed after his neighbour's wife|Unusquisque ad uxorem proximi sui hinniebat]].

paras.t: Nescitis quia amicitia hujus mundi, id est amor carnalis ac mundanus, inordinatus, et sensualis affectio ad complacendum hominibus non in Deo, atque ad obtinendum mundi honores, voluptates et opes, inimica est Deo, id est divinæ legi contraria, ac displicens Deo, et caritati repugnans? Quicumque ergo voluerit esse amicus hujus sæculi, id est hominum mundanorum, secundum quod tales sunt, inimicus Dei constituitur, id est Deo contrarius, et ab eo aversus. De quo ait Propheta: Odisti omnes qui operantur iniquitatem. Unde Sapiens: Odio sunt Deo impius et impietas ejus. Itaque quicumque se mundanis conformat hominibus, et eis consentit ac placere quærit in rebus illicitis, eo ipso quo talis est et ita se habet, Dei inimicus efficitur. Hoc est quod S. Joannes docet: Nolite diligere mundum, neque ea quæ in mundo sunt: quia si quis diligit mundum, non est caritas Patris in eo. Hinc loquitur et Paulus: Nolite conformari huic sæculo; itemque: An quæro hominibus placere? Si hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem. Hoc est quod terribiliter ait Propheta regius: Quoniam dissipavit Deus ossa eorum qui hominibus placent; confusi sunt, quoniam Deus sprevit eos. Verumtamen debemus mundanos homines spirituali amore diligere, sicut et inimicos, et orare pro eis, eis quoque in bonis velle placere, eo modo quo ait Apostolus, Unusquisque proximo suo placeat in bonum, ad ædificationem: quum etiam jubeat Dominus, Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona facta vestra, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in cœlis est.
paras.en: [[4:4|know you not that the friendship of this world|Nescitis quia amicitia hujus mundi]], that is, carnal and worldly love, a disordered and sensual affection for pleasing men not in God, and for gaining the world's honours, pleasures and riches, [[4:4|is the enemy of God|inimica est Deo]]? that is, contrary to the divine law, displeasing to God, and at war with charity. [[4:4|Whosoever therefore will be a friend of this world|Quicumque ergo voluerit esse amicus hujus sæculi]], that is, of worldly men, in so far as they are such, [[4:4|becometh an enemy of God|inimicus Dei constituitur]], that is, opposed to God and turned away from him. Of such the Prophet says: [[Ps 5:7|Thou hatest all the workers of iniquity|Odisti omnes qui operantur iniquitatem]]. Hence the Wise Man: [[Wis 14:9|to God the wicked and his wickedness are hateful|Odio sunt Deo impius et impietas ejus]]. And so whoever conforms himself to worldly men, and consents to them and seeks to please them in unlawful things, by the very fact that he is such and so disposed, is made an enemy of God. This is what St John teaches: [[1 John 2:15|Love not the world, nor the things which are in the world. If any man love the world, the charity of the Father is not in him|Nolite diligere mundum, neque ea quæ in mundo sunt: quia si quis diligit mundum, non est caritas Patris in eo]]. Hence Paul too says: [[Rom 12:2|be not conformed to this world|Nolite conformari huic sæculo]]; and again: [[Gal 1:10|Or do I seek to please men?|An quæro hominibus placere?]] [[Gal 1:10|If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ|Si hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem]]. This is what the royal Prophet says so fearfully: [[Ps 52:6|For God hath scattered the bones of them that please men: they have been confounded, because God hath despised them|Quoniam dissipavit Deus ossa eorum qui hominibus placent; confusi sunt, quoniam Deus sprevit eos]]. Nevertheless we ought to love worldly men with a spiritual love, as we do our enemies too, and to pray for them[[Matt 5:44||]], and also to wish to please them in good things, in the way the Apostle says: [[Rom 15:2|Let every one of you Please his neighbour unto good, to edification|Unusquisque proximo suo placeat in bonum, ad ædificationem]]; since the Lord too commands: [[Matt 5:16|So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven|Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona facta vestra, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in cœlis est]].

paras.t: [An putatis] quia inaniter Scriptura dicit (id est, nequaquam hoc æstimare debetis, quum verba Scripturæ, verba sint Spiritus Sancti), Ad invidiam concupiscit spiritus qui habitat in vobis? Hoc tripliciter potest intelligi. Primo, de Spiritu Sancto. Sicque legendum est interrogative et negative, ut sit sensus: Spiritus Sanctus corda vestra gratiose inhabitans, nequaquam concupiscit, id est, concupiscere vos non facit ad invidiam, hoc est, non movet vos ad invidendum alicui, quum sacra Scriptura ubique doceat Spiritum Sanctum esse spiritum puræ dilectionis. De quo in libro Sapientiæ habetur: Benignus est spiritus sapientiæ; et in Psalmo, Spiritus tuus bonus deducet me in terram rectam. — Secundo exponitur assertive de spiritu hominis, id est anima rationali habitante in corpore suo, quæ ad invidiam prona est, et aliis invidet quod affectat. Sicque scriptura ista accipitur ex eo quod in Genesi habetur: Sensus et cogitatio cordis humani proni sunt in malum ab adolescentia sua. — Tertio exponitur de Spiritu Sancto assertive. Et est sensus: Spiritus Sanctus in vobis per fidem et gratiam habitans, concupiscit, movet, et concupiscere facit vos ad invidiam exstirpandam: quia ad hoc instigat Spiritus Sanctus, secundum Scripturas, ut invidiam eradicemus. Juxta hunc modum loquendi fertur in Psalmo: Ex ore infantium et lactentium perfecisti laudem propter inimicos tuos, scilicet destruendos ac reprobandos.
paras.en: [[4:5|Or do you think|An putatis]] [the words *An putatis* are lost at the foot of the page and are supplied from the verse] [[4:5|that the scripture saith in vain|quia inaniter Scriptura dicit]] (that is, you must by no means think this, since the words of Scripture are the words of the Holy Ghost): [[4:5|To envy doth the spirit covet which dwelleth in you?|Ad invidiam concupiscit spiritus qui habitat in vobis?]] This can be understood in three ways. First, of the Holy Ghost. And so it is to be read as a question expecting the answer no, so that the sense is: the Holy Ghost, dwelling by grace in your hearts, by no means covets, that is, does not make you covet, unto envy; that is, he does not move you to envy anyone, since sacred Scripture everywhere teaches that the Holy Ghost is the spirit of pure love. Of him it is said in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 1:6|the spirit of wisdom is benevolent|Benignus est spiritus sapientiæ]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 142:10|Thy good spirit shall lead me into the right land|Spiritus tuus bonus deducet me in terram rectam]]. Secondly, it is expounded as a statement, of the spirit of man, that is, of the rational soul dwelling in its body, which is prone to envy and envies others what it desires for itself. And so this scripture is taken from what is found in Genesis: [[Gen 8:21|the imagination and thought of man's heart are prone to evil from his youth|Sensus et cogitatio cordis humani proni sunt in malum ab adolescentia sua]]. Thirdly, it is expounded as a statement, of the Holy Ghost. And the sense is: the Holy Ghost, dwelling in you by faith and grace, covets, moves you, and makes you covet, unto envy, that is, unto the rooting out of envy: for the Holy Ghost, according to the Scriptures, urges us to this, that we uproot envy. According to this manner of speaking it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 8:3|Out of the mouth of infants and of sucklings thou hast perfected praise, because of thy enemies|Ex ore infantium et lactentium perfecisti laudem propter inimicos tuos]], namely, that they may be destroyed and cast off [as *because of thy enemies* means "for the destroying of thy enemies", so *unto envy* means "for the rooting out of envy"].

paras.t: Si autem quæratur, quomodo in his habitavit Spiritus Sanctus quos paulo ante vocavit adulteros, litigiosos, cupidos, ac male petentes: respondendum, quod in Judæis quibus scripsit, erant carnales et spirituales, boni ac mali: quemadmodum et inter Corinthios, quibus scripsit inter cetera Paulus, Nihil vobis deest in ulla gratia; et post pauca, Non potui vobis loqui quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus. Sicque diversa ad diversos sunt referenda. Præterea viri sancti parva peccata quasi magna in suis subditis reprehendunt, ut eos magis humilient, exerceant et accendant.
paras.en: But if it is asked how the Holy Ghost dwelt in those whom he has just called adulterers, contentious, covetous, and asking amiss, the answer is that among the Jews to whom he wrote there were carnal and spiritual, good and wicked: just as there were among the Corinthians, to whom Paul wrote, among other things: [[1 Cor 1:7|nothing is wanting to you in any grace|Nihil vobis deest in ulla gratia]]; and a little after: I [[1 Cor 3:1|could not speak to you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal|Non potui vobis loqui quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus]]. And so different things are to be referred to different persons. Moreover, holy men rebuke small sins in their subjects as though they were great, so as to humble, exercise and kindle them the more.

paras.t: Prima demum expositio horum verborum litteralior esse videtur, quia subjungitur: Majorem autem dat gratiam, scilicet Spiritus qui habitat in vobis, puta Spiritus Sanctus, qui dat gratiam majorem quam mundus vel amicitia ejus. Dat enim dona supernaturalia atque gratuita. Propter quod dicit Scriptura in Proverbiis, secundum translationem Septuaginta interpretum: Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam. Sic enim Septuaginta transtulerunt, ubi Hieronymus transtulit: Illusores Deus deludet, mansuetis autem dabit gratiam. Vel sumitur ista scriptura ex eo, quod alio loco in Proverbiis habetur: Superbum sequitur humilitas (quia videlicet humiliatur atque dejicitur a judice Deo), et humilem spiritu suscipiet gloria.
paras.en: The first exposition of these words, however, seems the more literal, because there follows: [[4:6|But he giveth greater grace|Majorem autem dat gratiam]], namely the Spirit [[4:5|which dwelleth in you|qui habitat in vobis]], that is, the Holy Ghost, who gives a greater grace than the world or its friendship. For he gives supernatural and gratuitous gifts. [[4:6|Wherefore he saith|Propter quod dicit]], that is, Scripture says in Proverbs, according to the translation of the Seventy interpreters: [[4:6|God resisteth the proud and giveth grace to the humble|Deus superbis resistit, humilibus autem dat gratiam]][[1 Pet 5:5||]]. For so the Seventy translated it, where Jerome translated: [[Prov 3:34|He shall scorn the scorners, and to the meek he will give grace|Illusores Deus deludet, mansuetis autem dabit gratiam]]. Or this scripture is taken from what is found in another place in Proverbs: [[Prov 29:23|Humiliation followeth the proud|Superbum sequitur humilitas]] (because, that is, he is humbled and cast down by God the judge), [[Prov 29:23|and glory shall uphold the humble of spirit|et humilem spiritu suscipiet gloria]].

paras.t: Præterea valde pensandum, quod in verbis istis apostolus Jacobus insinuat Spiritum Sanctum esse Deum. Quum enim de eo dixisset, Majorem autem dat gratiam, mox ad probandum hoc ipsum, allegat Scripturam canonicam, asserentem: Deus superbis resistit. Quæ probatio non valeret, nisi in illa auctoritate allegata, per Deum, intelligeretur Spiritus Sanctus seu Trinitas Deus, et per consequens, quælibet divina, æterna, increata, adoranda Persona.
paras.en: Moreover, it is much to be weighed that in these words the apostle James implies that the Holy Ghost is God. For when he had said of him: [[4:6|But he giveth greater grace|Majorem autem dat gratiam]], he straightway, to prove this very thing, cites canonical Scripture, which asserts: [[4:6|God resisteth the proud|Deus superbis resistit]]. And this proof would not hold unless, in the authority cited, *God* were understood to mean the Holy Ghost, or God the Trinity, and consequently any divine, eternal, uncreated and adorable Person.

paras.t: Sed quum Deus omnem vitiosum detestetur, damnet et puniat, cur specialiter superbis resistere perhibetur? Et respondendum, quod quia superbi specialiter se extollunt, seque Deo opponunt, et quod Deo debetur, videlicet gloriam et honorem, sibi usurpant, et quia superbia omnium vitiorum regina et mater est, idcirco Deus eis specialiter resistere fertur, eos dejicere, humiliare, comprimere. Et hoc sibi proprium esse testatur, loquens ad Job: Si habes brachium sicut Deus, et simili voce tonas, disperge superbos in furore tuo, et respiciens omnem arrogantem humilia; respice cunctos superbos, et confunde eos, et contere impios in loco suo; absconde eos in pulvere simul, et facies eorum demerge in foveam: et ego confitebor, quod salvare te possit dextera tua. Absit ergo a nobis omnis elatio, quæ tam est odibilis Deo, et cui resistit Omnipotens. Non conveniat alicui nostrum id, quod in libro Job scribitur: Quid tumet contra Deum spiritus tuus? Nec illud: Cucurrit impius adversus Deum erecto collo.
paras.en: But since God detests, condemns and punishes every vicious man, why is he said in particular to resist the proud? The answer is that, because the proud in particular exalt themselves and set themselves against God, and usurp for themselves what is due to God, namely glory and honour, and because pride is the queen and mother of all vices, therefore God is said in particular to resist them, to cast them down, to humble and to crush them. And he testifies that this is proper to himself, speaking to Job: [[Job 40:4|hast thou an arm like God, and canst thou thunder with a voice like him?|Si habes brachium sicut Deus, et simili voce tonas]] [[Job 40:6|Scatter the proud in thy indignation, and behold every arrogant man, and humble him|disperge superbos in furore tuo, et respiciens omnem arrogantem humilia]]; [[Job 40:7|Look on all that are proud, and confound them, and crush the wicked in their place|respice cunctos superbos, et confunde eos, et contere impios in loco suo]]; [[Job 40:8|Hide them in the dust together, and plunge their faces into the pit|absconde eos in pulvere simul, et facies eorum demerge in foveam]]: [[Job 40:9|Then I will confess that thy right hand is able to save thee|et ego confitebor, quod salvare te possit dextera tua]]. Far from us, then, be all exaltation, which is so hateful to God, and which the Almighty resists. Let not that befit any of us which is written in the book of Job: [[Job 15:13|Why doth thy spirit swell against God|Quid tumet contra Deum spiritus tuus?]]? Nor that: [[Job 15:26|He hath run against him with his neck raised up|Cucurrit impius adversus Deum erecto collo]] [Denis's text has *impius*, "the wicked man", and *against God* for "against him"].

paras.t: Porro humilibus Deus dat gratiam: quia et peccatoribus se ipsos ex corde accusantibus, ac Deo subjicientibus, veniamque petentibus, Deus peccata remittit, et gratiarum charismata elargitur, ut patet in publicano. Humilibus vero jam in caritate exsistentibus, dat gratiarum augmenta. Et quanto se Deo profundius subdunt, humiliusque substernunt ac supplicant, tanto gratiæ opulentioribus charismatibus perfunduntur. Semper igitur simus viles ac imperfecti in propriis oculis, et coram Altissimo in omni timore ac humilitate jugiter ambulemus.
paras.en: Further, God [[4:6|giveth grace to the humble|humilibus Deus dat gratiam]]: for to sinners too who accuse themselves from the heart, submit themselves to God and ask pardon, God remits their sins and bestows the gifts of graces, as is plain in the publican[[Luke 18:13||]][[Luke 18:14||]]. And to the humble who are already in charity he gives increase of graces. And the more deeply they submit themselves to God, and the more humbly they lay themselves low and make supplication, the more richly are they filled with the gifts of grace. Let us therefore always be vile and imperfect in our own eyes, and walk continually before the Most High in all fear and humility.

paras.t: Subditi igitur estote Deo per veram ac profundam humilitatem, ac divinorum præceptorum exsecutionem. Quemadmodum enim quidquid habemus ac sumus, a Deo accepimus; sic totum ei subjicere et ejus obsequio mancipare debemus, sicut et Psalmista hortatur: Subditus esto Domino, et ora eum. Siquidem, quis restitit ei, et habuit pacem?
paras.en: [[4:7|Be subject therefore to God|Subditi igitur estote Deo]] by true and deep humility and the carrying out of the divine commandments. For as whatever we have and are we have received from God[[1 Cor 4:7||]], so we ought to subject the whole of it to him and give it over to his service, as the Psalmist too exhorts: [[Ps 36:7|Be subject to the Lord and pray to him|Subditus esto Domino, et ora eum]]. For indeed, [[Job 9:4|who hath resisted him, and hath had peace?|quis restitit ei, et habuit pacem?]]

paras.t: Resistite autem diabolo, id est, ejus suggestionibus non consentiatis, sed eas despicite. Porro diabolo debemus resistere: primo, totam spem nostram in Dei adjutorio collocando, nihil de propriis viribus præsumendo; secundo, nos ipsos in omnibus humiliando, et propriam infirmitatem, imperfectionem, vitiositatem humiliter recognoscendo; tertio, divinæ pietatis subsidium jugiter invocando; quarto, dominicam passionem cordialiter ac frequenter reminiscendo; quinto, quatuor novissima diligenter atque assidue adspiciendo; sexto, tanto ferventius devotis insistendo exercitiis, quanto acrius diabolicis impugnamur tentationibus. Sunt et alii modi resistendi quamplurimi. Debemus quippe rite perpendere, quantis periculis simus expositi, quantis laqueis circumdati, quanta atrocitate invidentiaque infatigabiliter a dæmonibus impugnemur, quanta felicitate nos privare, ad quantam miseriam nos pertrahere conantur. Ex quorum omnium vivaci consideratione debemus esse semper solliciti, custoditi, timorati, ac fortiter tanquam Dei milites contra aciem vitiorum ac dæmonum præliantes, quum teste Apostolo, non coronetur nisi qui legitime certaverit.
paras.en: [[4:7|But resist the devil|Resistite autem diabolo]], that is, do not consent to his suggestions, but despise them. Now we ought to resist the devil: first, by placing all our hope in God's help and presuming nothing of our own strength; secondly, by humbling ourselves in all things, and humbly acknowledging our own weakness, imperfection and viciousness; thirdly, by continually calling on the help of the divine mercy; fourthly, by remembering the Lord's Passion heartily and often; fifthly, by looking diligently and constantly at the four last things; sixthly, by pressing on with devout exercises the more fervently, the more sharply we are assailed by the devil's temptations. There are very many other ways of resisting too. For we ought duly to weigh to how great dangers we are exposed, by how many snares surrounded, with what ferocity and envy we are tirelessly assailed by the demons, of what happiness they try to deprive us, into what misery to drag us. From a lively consideration of all these things we ought to be always watchful, guarded and fearful, fighting bravely as soldiers of God against the battle line of vices and demons, since, as the Apostle witnesses, he [[2 Tim 2:5|is not crowned, except he strive lawfully|non coronetur nisi qui legitime certaverit]].

paras.t: Et fugiet a vobis, videns vos sibi tam viriliter ac perseveranter resistere. Qui enim modis prætactis resistit diabolo, suis resistentiis tam virtuosis ac fervidis ineffabiliter illum tam contumacem ac perversum affligit, incendit, exagitat. Ideo fugit. Quocirca quæri potest, an postmodum ad tentandum eumdem hominem redeat. Et videtur quod non, quia communiter dicitur quod diabolus ab aliquo victus, nunquam redeat ad tentandum eumdem, saltem de eodem peccato. Ad hanc insuper quæstionem Thomas respondet in prima parte Summæ suæ, dicendo: Aliqui dicunt, quod dæmon semel victus ab aliquo, nunquam postea tentet nec illum nec alium, nec de eodem peccato, nec de alio. Sed huic non consonat quod in Matthæo de diabolo scriptum est: Revertar in domum meam unde exivi. Alii dicunt, quod diabolus superatus, posset tentare alium, sed non eumdem. Quod probabilius dicitur, si tamen intelligatur, quantum ad certum tempus, quia de Christo habetur: Consummata omni tentatione, diabolus recessit ab eo ad tempus. Quod autem ad tempus a tentatione desistat, congruit divinæ clementiæ, quæ in hoc infirmitati condescendit humanæ, ne nimium infestetur. Congruit quoque dæmonis astutiæ: quia, secundum Ambrosium super Lucam, dæmon formidat instare, quia formidat succumbere. Hæc est S. Thomæ responsio.
paras.en: [[4:7|and he will fly from you|Et fugiet a vobis]], seeing you resist him so manfully and perseveringly. For he who resists the devil in the ways just touched on afflicts, inflames and harasses him beyond words, stubborn and perverse as he is, by resistance so virtuous and fervent. Therefore he flees. Hence it may be asked whether he afterwards returns to tempt the same man. And it seems not, because it is commonly said that the devil, once overcome by anyone, never returns to tempt the same man, at least with the same sin. To this question, moreover, Thomas answers in the First Part of his Summa [I, q. 114, a. 5], saying: Some say that a demon once overcome by anyone never afterwards tempts either him or another, either with the same sin or with another. But with this does not agree what is written of the devil in Matthew: [[Matt 12:44|I will return into my house from whence I came out|Revertar in domum meam unde exivi]]. Others say that the devil, once overcome, could tempt another, but not the same man. And this is said with more probability, provided it is understood of a certain time, since it is said of Christ: [[Luke 4:13|all the temptation being ended, the devil departed from him for a time|Consummata omni tentatione, diabolus recessit ab eo ad tempus]]. That he desists from temptation for a time befits the divine clemency, which in this condescends to human weakness, lest it be assailed too much. It befits the cunning of the demon too, because, according to Ambrose on Luke, the demon fears to press on, because he fears to be defeated. This is St Thomas's answer.

paras.t: Porro, quod diabolus ab aliquo victus, redeat ad tentandum eumdem de eodem peccato, videtur multipliciter posse probari. Primo, quia de beato Job habetur, quod diabolus a sancto Job in prima impugnatione devictus est, ita quod diabolus nequivit eum ad impatientiam aut maledictionem Dei, seu verborum excessum inducere. Deinde de eodem habetur, quod Satan semel sic victus, secundo tentavit sanctum Job acrius. Rursusque victus, tentavit eum per suam uxorem, deinde per amicos et alios. Et omnes istæ tentationes ad idem peccatum tendebant. Ad idem posset adduci, quod S. Athanasius scribit de B. Antonio, qualiter sæpe a dæmonibus cæsus est, et semper prævaluit. Et satis innuitur in illa Legenda, quod utique ab eisdem. Simile refert B. Hieronymus de S. Hilarione. Multa quoque similia de aliis Sanctis leguntur. Papa S. Gregorius dicit in homilia, quod diabolus contra duos bellum movet: unum, incitans ut injurias inferat; alium, ut injuriis acceptis, contumelias reddat. Quem dum in primo conflictu superare nequivit, interim ab aperto certamine cessans, post modicum redit, et illum eumdem acrius quam ante impugnat, etiam de eodem peccato, puta de impatientia et vindicta. Cassiodorus quoque ait: Bellum grave est contra diabolum, quia occultum, quia cum fortiore, quia hostis insidiæ non videntur; adversarius nec labore deficit, nec victus aliquando discedit (videlicet omnino), sed tanto acrior redit quanto per gratiam Dei debellatus fortius fuit. Postremo, creditur quod sicut unusquisque habet angelum bonum pro sui custodia in tota hac vita, ita et angelum malum pro sua exercitatione et probatione: qui, durante hac vita, quantumcumque vincatur, non recedit in toto. — Istud ergo verius reor. Idcirco post unam victoriam non simus securi, sed ad acriorem conflictum accincti. Militia enim, vel (ut alia habet translatio) tentatio est vita hominis super terram. Propter quod loquitur Augustinus: Persevera usque in finem, quia tentatio perseverat usque in finem.
paras.en: Yet that the devil, once overcome by anyone, returns to tempt the same man with the same sin, seems capable of proof in many ways. First, because it is related of blessed Job that the devil was overcome by holy Job in the first assault[[Job 1:13||]], so that the devil could not lead him to impatience, or to cursing God, or to excess in words. Then it is related of the same Job that Satan, once overcome in this way, tempted holy Job a second time and more sharply[[Job 2:7||]][[Job 2:8||]]. And overcome again, he tempted him through his wife[[Job 2:9||]], then through his friends and others [the margin gives Job 2:9 and following]. And all these temptations tended to the same sin. To the same effect could be brought what St Athanasius writes of blessed Antony, how he was often beaten by the demons and always prevailed. And it is quite plainly implied in that Life that it was indeed by the same demons. Blessed Jerome relates something similar of St Hilarion. Many like things too are read of other Saints. Pope St Gregory says in a homily that the devil wages war against two men: one he incites to inflict injuries, the other to return insults when injuries have been received. And when he has not been able to overcome this man in the first conflict, he ceases for a while from open combat, returns after a little, and assails that same man more sharply than before, even with the same sin, that is, with impatience and revenge. Cassiodorus too says: Grievous is the war against the devil, because it is hidden, because it is with one stronger, because the enemy's ambushes are not seen; the adversary neither fails through labour, nor, when overcome, ever departs (that is, altogether), but returns the fiercer the more strongly he has been vanquished by the grace of God. Lastly, it is believed that, as each man has a good angel for his guard through the whole of this life, so he has a bad angel too, for his exercise and testing: who, while this life lasts, however often he is overcome, does not withdraw altogether. This, then, I judge to be the truer view. Therefore let us not be secure after one victory, but girded for a sharper conflict. For the [[Job 7:1|life of man upon earth|est vita hominis super terram]] [[Job 7:1|is a warfare|Militia]], or (as another translation has it) a temptation [*tentatio*, "temptation" or "trial"; the Vulgate has *militia*, "warfare"]. For which reason Augustine says: Persevere unto the end, because temptation perseveres unto the end.

paras.t: Appropinquate Deo, et appropinquabit vobis. Huic simile est quod per Zachariam loquitur Deus: Convertimini ad me, et convertar ad vos. Ex quibus sequi videtur, quod gratia Dei insit hominibus ex eorum prævio merito, principiumque merendi sit a libero arbitrio, et non a Deo: quum tamen dicat Salvator, Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum; et alibi, Sine me nihil potestis facere. Atque Apostolus ait: Quid habes quod non accepisti?
paras.en: [[4:8|Draw nigh to God: and he will draw nigh to you|Appropinquate Deo, et appropinquabit vobis]]. Like this is what God says through Zacharias: [[Zach 1:3|Turn ye to me|Convertimini ad me]], [[Zach 1:3|and I will turn to you|et convertar ad vos]]. From these words it seems to follow that the grace of God is in men from their own previous merit, and that the beginning of meriting is from free will and not from God: whereas the Saviour says: [[John 6:44|No man can come to me, except the Father, who hath sent me, draw him|Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum]]; and elsewhere: [[John 15:5|without me you can do nothing|Sine me nihil potestis facere]]. And the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 4:7|what hast thou that thou hast not received|Quid habes quod non accepisti]]?

paras.t: Ad istud Thomas, Petrus de Tarento, Richardus de Mediavilla, et alii dicunt, quod sicut Deus communi influxu universa convertit ad se, tanquam ad finem ultimatum, secundum esse eorum naturale, sic rationalem creaturam convertit ad se speciali influxu, tanquam ad finem supernaturalem. Nec iste influxus est aliqua gratia habitualis, sed divina motio, et instinctus qui ad dona gratiæ movet hominem, atque ad meritorium bonum. Et omnibus offertur, ac vicissim influit iste instinctus. Cui quidam consentiunt, et per hoc ad gratiam habitualem de congruo disponuntur: quibus tunc gratia mox confertur. Et de ista dispositione potest intelligi verbum istud Apostoli, ut sit sensus: Appropinquate Deo, ad ejus gratiam vos aptando, et ejus instinctui acquiescendo. Aliqui vero huic instinctui resistunt. Nihilo minus dispositionem istam de congruo præcedit divinus instinctus, ut patuit. Ideoque principium meriti simpliciter est a Deo.
paras.en: To this Thomas, Peter of Tarentaise [later Pope Innocent V], Richard of Middleton and others say that, as God by a common influence turns all things to himself as to their last end, according to their natural being, so he turns the rational creature to himself by a special influence, as to a supernatural end. Nor is this influence any habitual grace [that is, sanctifying grace abiding in the soul as a quality], but a divine motion, an impulse which moves man to the gifts of grace and to meritorious good. And this impulse is offered to all, and flows into them in turn. Some consent to it, and by this are disposed *de congruo* [that is, by a fitting disposition which God rewards of his liberality, not by merit in strict justice] for habitual grace: and to these grace is then at once given. And the Apostle's word can be understood of this disposition, so that the sense is: [[4:8|Draw nigh to God|Appropinquate Deo]], by making yourselves fit for his grace and yielding to his impulse. But some resist this impulse. Nevertheless the divine impulse goes before this disposition *de congruo*, as has been shown. And therefore the beginning of merit is simply from God.

paras.t: Sed advertendum, quod verba hæc dupliciter possunt exponi: Primo, quantum ad eos qui nondum in caritate et gratia sunt, qui a Deo aversi sunt, et elongantur ab eo dissimilitudine culpæ. Ideo dicitur eis: Appropinquate Deo, pœnitendo, confitendo, satisfaciendo, sicque quod in vobis est faciendo, et appropinquabit vobis, id est, gratiose applicabit se vobis, dona gratiæ infundendo. Secundo potest exponi de exsistentibus in gratia et caritate, qui licet a Deo non distent dissimilitudine culpæ, saltem mortalis, distant tamen ab eo minoratione perfectionis ad quam in hac vita pertingere valent. Ideo dicitur eis ut Deo propinquent, id est, similiores fiant, eum ardentius diligendo, quotidie proficiendo, et ei se omni hora intimius sive devotius uniendo. Verumtamen, propinquatio sive conversio utraque fit ex prævio quodam Dei instinctu ac munere. Ad quod insinuandum in Threnis scriptum est: Converte nos, Domine, ad te, et convertemur. Et rursus Jeremias loquitur: Converte me, Domine, et convertar, quia tu es Dominus Deus meus: postquam enim convertisti me, egi pœnitentiam; et postquam ostendisti mihi, percussi femur meum. Istis Deo sic appropinquantibus, Deus propinquat per gratiæ incrementa, et eis se clarius ostendendo, atque intimius uniendo per donum sapientiæ et caritatis augmentum, divinorumque gustum et interiorem amplexum.
paras.en: But note that these words can be expounded in two ways. First, as regards those who are not yet in charity and grace, who are turned away from God and are far from him by the unlikeness of sin. So it is said to them: [[4:8|Draw nigh to God|Appropinquate Deo]], by repenting, confessing and making satisfaction, and so doing what is in you, [[4:8|and he will draw nigh to you|et appropinquabit vobis]], that is, he will graciously apply himself to you, pouring in the gifts of grace. Secondly, it can be expounded of those who are in grace and charity, who, though they are not distant from God by the unlikeness of sin, at least of mortal sin, are yet distant from him by falling short of the perfection which they are able to reach in this life. So they are told to draw near to God, that is, to become more like him, by loving him more ardently, advancing daily, and uniting themselves to him every hour more inwardly or more devoutly. Yet both kinds of drawing near, or turning, come from a certain prevenient impulse and gift of God. To intimate this it is written in Lamentations: [[Lam 5:21|Convert us, O Lord, to thee, and we shall be converted|Converte nos, Domine, ad te, et convertemur]]. And again Jeremias says: [[Jer 31:18|Convert me, and I shall be converted, for thou art the Lord my God|Converte me, Domine, et convertar, quia tu es Dominus Deus meus]]: [[Jer 31:19|For after thou didst convert me, I did penance: and after thou didst shew unto me, I struck my thigh|postquam enim convertisti me, egi pœnitentiam; et postquam ostendisti mihi, percussi femur meum]]. To those who thus draw near to God, God draws near by increases of grace, and by showing himself to them more clearly and uniting himself to them more inwardly through the gift of wisdom and the increase of charity, the taste of divine things and the inward embrace.

paras.t: Insuper, Deus (qui per Jeremiam iterum protestatur, Numquid non cœlum et terram ego impleo?) distat a creatura rationali, non loco, sed perfectione; et culpa distat ab eo illa. Propterea in Proverbiis fertur, Longe est Dominus ab impiis; et Jeremias fatetur, Longe Dominus apparuit mihi. Si autem de similitudine, seu de defectu perfectionis sit sermo, certum est quod omnis creatura distet in infinitum a Creatore, qui per Isaiam sciscitatur: Cui me similem fecistis et adæquastis, dicit Sanctus? A cujus contemplatione in tantum deficimus, ut apud Job dicatur: Unusquisque intuetur eum procul.
paras.en: Moreover God (who again protests through Jeremias: [[Jer 23:24|do not I fill heaven and earth|Numquid non cœlum et terram ego impleo]]?) is distant from the rational creature not in place but in perfection; and it is by sin that the creature is distant from him. Hence it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 15:29|The Lord is far from the wicked|Longe est Dominus ab impiis]]; and Jeremias confesses: [[Jer 31:3|The Lord hath appeared from afar to me|Longe Dominus apparuit mihi]]. But if we speak of likeness, or of the lack of perfection, it is certain that every creature is infinitely distant from the Creator, who asks through Isaias: [[Is 40:25|to whom have ye likened me, or made me equal, saith the Holy One?|Cui me similem fecistis et adæquastis, dicit Sanctus?]] And we fall so far short of contemplating him that it is said in Job: [[Job 36:25|every one beholdeth afar off|Unusquisque intuetur eum procul]].

paras.t: Emundate manus, o peccatores. Per manum, quæ est organum organorum, potestas et operatio designantur. Manus ergo, id est opera nostra, emundare debemus, ut ex sincera intentione procedant, nec vitiis misceantur, ne illud Isaiæ nobis conveniat, Manus vestræ sanguine plenæ sunt; sed quod in Psalmo dicitur, Innocens manibus et mundo corde, hic accipiet benedictionem a Domino. Unde et in Job habetur : Salvabitur innocens; salvabitur autem munditia manuum suarum.
paras.en: [[4:8|Cleanse your hands, ye sinners|Emundate manus, o peccatores]]. By the hand, which is the instrument of instruments, power and working are signified. Our hands, then, that is, our works, we must cleanse, so that they proceed from a sincere intention and are not mixed with vices; lest that word of Isaias fit us: [[Is 1:15|your hands are full of blood|Manus vestræ sanguine plenæ sunt]]; but rather what is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 23:4|The innocent in hands, and clean of heart|Innocens manibus et mundo corde]], [[Ps 23:5|He shall receive a blessing from the Lord|hic accipiet benedictionem a Domino]]. Hence also in Job we have: [[Job 22:30|The innocent shall be saved, and he shall be saved by the cleanness of his hands|Salvabitur innocens; salvabitur autem munditia manuum suarum]].

paras.t: Et purificate corda vestra per penitentiam ab omni simulatione, duplicitate, perversitate, ceterisque peccatis, qui duplices animo fuistis aut estis. De hac duplicitate dictum est copiose jam ante, super illud : Vir duplex animo, inconstans est in omnibus viis suis, etc. Hæc autem depuratio cordis est maxime appetenda. Siquidem, Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt. Atque in libro Proverbiorum inducitur : Qui diligit cordis munditiam, habebit amicum regem : illum utique regem, qui apud Malachiam testatur, Rex magnus ego sum. Denique propter hujus munditiæ cordis appetibilitatem loquitur Isaias, Hic est omnis fructus, ut auferatur iniquitas : quod maxime verum est, prout iniquitatis ablatio, caritatis et gratiæ infusionem includit, sine qua fieri nequit.
paras.en: [[4:8|and purify your hearts|Et purificate corda vestra]] by penance from all pretence, doubleness, perverseness and the other sins, you who have been or are [[4:8|double minded|duplices animo]]. Of this doubleness we spoke at length earlier, on the words: [[Jas 1:8|A double minded man is inconstant in all his ways|Vir duplex animo, inconstans est in omnibus viis suis]], etc. And this cleansing of the heart is to be desired above all, since [[Matt 5:8|Blessed are the clean of heart: they shall see God|Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt]]. And in the book of Proverbs it is said: [[Prov 22:11|He that loveth cleanness of heart|Qui diligit cordis munditiam]] [[Prov 22:11|shall have the king for his friend|habebit amicum regem]]: that King, namely, who testifies in Malachias: [[Mal 1:14|I am a great King|Rex magnus ego sum]]. Finally, because this cleanness of heart is so much to be desired, Isaias says: [[Is 27:9|this is all the fruit, that the sin thereof should be taken away|Hic est omnis fructus, ut auferatur iniquitas]] [Denis reads *iniquity* where the Vulgate has *peccatum ejus*, "the sin thereof"]; which is most true inasmuch as the taking away of iniquity includes the infusion of charity and grace, without which it cannot be done.

paras.t: Miseri estote. Duplex est miseria : Una culpæ, de qua legitur : Justitia elevat gentem, miseros facit populos peccatum. Altera est miseria pœnæ, de qua ait Propheta : Conversus sum in ærumna mea, dum configitur spina ; et Apostolus : Infelix ego homo ! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus? Unde S. Bernardus ait de Christo : Misericordiæ Domini multæ, sed et miseriæ Domini multæ. De utrisque autem his miseriis verificatur illud Job : Homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore, repletur multis miseriis. Hortatur ergo Apostolus ut miseri simus miseria pœnæ, corporales afflictiones, tribulationes, inopiam, famem, sitim, opera satisfactoria et laboriosa, sponte ac patienter pro nostris sustinendo excessibus, et pro gratia ampliori adipiscenda : qua deinceps vitemus peccata, atque ut Christo propter nos passo, aliquo modo conformemur, et futura evadamus supplicia. Et lugete pro vestris ac proximorum piaculis, pro desiderio regni cœlestis, et ex aliis piis causis, […].
paras.en: [[4:9|Be afflicted|Miseri estote]] [literally "be wretched": the Latin *miseri* gives the play on *miseria*, "misery", that follows]. Misery is twofold. One is the misery of guilt, of which we read: [[Prov 14:34|Justice exalteth a nation: but sin maketh nations miserable|Justitia elevat gentem, miseros facit populos peccatum]]. The other is the misery of punishment, of which the Prophet says: [[Ps 31:4|I am turned in my anguish, whilst the thorn is fastened|Conversus sum in ærumna mea, dum configitur spina]]; and the Apostle: [[Rom 7:24|Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?|Infelix ego homo ! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?]] Hence St Bernard says of Christ: Many are the mercies of the Lord, and many too the miseries of the Lord. And of both these miseries that word of Job is verified: [[Job 14:1|Man born of a woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries|Homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore, repletur multis miseriis]]. The Apostle therefore exhorts us to be wretched with the misery of punishment, bearing willingly and patiently bodily afflictions, tribulations, want, hunger, thirst, and works of satisfaction [that is, works done to make amends for sins already forgiven] and of toil, for our own excesses and to obtain greater grace, by which we may thereafter avoid sins; and so that we may in some way be conformed to Christ who suffered for us, and escape the punishments to come. [[4:9|and mourn|Et lugete]] for your own sins and your neighbours', out of desire for the heavenly kingdom, and from other devout causes, […].

paras.t: Risus vester inordinatus, ex mentis dissolutione et irrationabilibus causis proveniens, in luctum salubrem convertatur : quemadmodum per Joelem Dominus monet : Convertimini ad me in toto corde vestro, in jejunio et fletu et planctu ; et gaudium vestrum carnale, sæculare, inordinatum, vertatur in mærorem pœnitentialem, ut contrariis curentur contraria, et per quæ quis peccavit, per hæc puniat et castigat se ipsum.
paras.en: [[4:9|let your laughter|Risus vester]], disordered, springing from looseness of mind and from unreasonable causes, [[4:9|be turned into mourning|in luctum salubrem convertatur]], into a wholesome mourning, as the Lord warns through Joel: [[Joel 2:12|Be converted to me with all your heart, in fasting, and in weeping, and mourning|Convertimini ad me in toto corde vestro, in jejunio et fletu et planctu]]; [[4:9|and your joy|et gaudium]], your carnal, worldly, disordered joy, be turned [[4:9|into sorrow|in mærorem]], a penitential sorrow, so that contraries may be cured by contraries, and a man may punish and chastise himself by the very things by which he sinned.

paras.t: Est itaque risus illicitus, de quo ait Salvator : Væ vobis qui ridetis nunc, quia plorabitis et flebitis. De quo itidem in Ecclesiaste legitur : Sicut sonitus spinarum ardentium sub olla, sic risus stulti. Idcirco verum est vulgare illud proverbium : Per multum risum poteris cognoscere stultum. Hinc in Ecclesiastico scriptum est : Amictus corporis, et risus dentium, et incessus hominis, annuntiant de eo : quia videlicet per hæc tria exteriora conjicitur qualis sit homo interius. Vitandus est ergo risus immoderatus, quum rursus in Ecclesiastico dicitur : Fatuus in risu exaltat vocem suam ; vir autem sapiens vix tacite ridebit. Imo, secundum S. Basilium, a risu et omni irrefrenata lætitia nos cohibere debemus, quum quotidie tot peccata fiant in mundo, et Deus tam graviter inhonoretur ac offendatur, et tot animæ æternaliter condemnentur, et quilibet nostrum toties tamque enormiter peccet, atque in valle hac lacrimarum, in gravi exsilio, variisque periculis positi simus, et ignoremus an amore digni simus an odio, et utrum æternaliter simus damnandi. Verumtamen est aliquis moderatus ac licitus risus, de quo sanctus Job ait : Si quando ridebam ad eos, non credebant mihi. Qui risus ex laudabili causa oritur, ex gaudio spirituali, ex zelo justitiæ, aut causa penitus naturali, ut ex admiratione : ob quam homini naturale et proprium est, esse risibilem.
paras.en: There is, then, an unlawful laughter, of which the Saviour says: [[Luke 6:25|Woe to you that now laugh: for you shall mourn and weep|Væ vobis qui ridetis nunc, quia plorabitis et flebitis]]. Of it likewise we read in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 7:7|as the crackling of thorns burning under a pot, so is the laughter of a fool|Sicut sonitus spinarum ardentium sub olla, sic risus stulti]]. Therefore that common proverb is true: By much laughter thou mayest know a fool. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 19:27|The attire of the body, and the laughter of the teeth, and the gait of the man, shew what he is|Amictus corporis, et risus dentium, et incessus hominis, annuntiant de eo]]; because, namely, from these three outward things it is gathered what a man is within. Immoderate laughter, then, is to be avoided, since again in Ecclesiasticus it is said: [[Ecclus 21:23|A fool lifteth up his voice in laughter: but a wise man will scarce laugh low to himself|Fatuus in risu exaltat vocem suam ; vir autem sapiens vix tacite ridebit]]. Nay, according to St Basil, we ought to restrain ourselves from laughter and from all unbridled mirth, since every day so many sins are committed in the world, and God is so gravely dishonoured and offended, and so many souls are eternally condemned, and each of us sins so often and so enormously, and we are set in this vale of tears, in a grievous exile and amid various perils, and know not whether we are worthy of love or of hatred[[Eccles 9:1||]], and whether we are to be eternally damned. Yet there is a certain moderate and lawful laughter, of which holy Job says: [[Job 29:24|If at any time I laughed on them, they believed not|Si quando ridebam ad eos, non credebant mihi]]. Such laughter arises from a praiseworthy cause: from spiritual joy, from zeal for justice, or from a purely natural cause, as from wonder; by reason of which it is natural and proper to man to be risible [that is, able to laugh: in the schools the stock example of a property belonging to man alone].

paras.t: Denique est gaudium spirituale et sanctum, in actu virtutis consistens, de Creatore aut de creaturis in Deo conceptum. De quo ait Apostolus : Gaudete in Domino semper ; et Propheta : Lætamini in Domino, et exsultate, justi. Jacobus vero loquitur de illicito gaudio, actioni vitiosæ annexo. De quo ait Scriptura : Lætantur quum male fecerint, et exsultant in rebus pessimis. Et Christus quoque : Mundus, inquit, gaudebit. — Præterea his Jacobi verbis consonat quod in Ecclesiaste fertur : Melius est ire ad domum luctus, quam ad domum convivii : in illa enim finis cunctorum admonetur hominum, et vivens cogitat quid futurum sit. Et rursus : Cor sapientis ubi tristitia, et cor stultorum ubi lætitia. Hinc Salomon denuo ait : Risum reputavi errorem ; et gaudio dixi, Quid frustra deciperis?
paras.en: Lastly, there is a spiritual and holy joy, consisting in an act of virtue, conceived of the Creator, or of creatures in God. Of it the Apostle says: [[Phil 4:4|Rejoice in the Lord always|Gaudete in Domino semper]]; and the Prophet: [[Ps 31:11|Be glad in the Lord, and rejoice, ye just|Lætamini in Domino, et exsultate, justi]]. But James is speaking of the unlawful joy that is bound up with a vicious action. Of it Scripture says: [[Prov 2:14|Who are glad when they have done evil, and rejoice in the most wicked things|Lætantur quum male fecerint, et exsultant in rebus pessimis]]. And Christ too: [[John 16:20|the world|Mundus]], he says, [[John 16:20|shall rejoice|gaudebit]]. — Moreover, with these words of James agrees what is said in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 7:3|It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to the house of feasting: for in that we are put in mind of the end of all, and the living thinketh what is to come|Melius est ire ad domum luctus, quam ad domum convivii : in illa enim finis cunctorum admonetur hominum, et vivens cogitat quid futurum sit]]. And again: [[Eccles 7:5|The heart of the wise is where there is mourning, and the heart of fools where there is mirth|Cor sapientis ubi tristitia, et cor stultorum ubi lætitia]]. Hence Solomon says once more: [[Eccles 2:2|Laughter I counted error: and to mirth I said: Why art thou vainly deceived?|Risum reputavi errorem ; et gaudio dixi, Quid frustra deciperis?]]

paras.t: Humiliamini in conspectu Domini : id est, coram Deo unusquisque se deprimat, vitia sua inspiciat, defectus naturæ et culpæ quos habet in se intueatur, quam imperfecte serviat Deo perpendat. Ex his et aliis multis rite consideratis, unusquisque vilipendat se valde, et omni confusione, correptione et castigatione dignum se arbitretur, easque æquanimiter patiatur. Et exaltabit vos in vita præsenti per sublimia gratiæ dona, et in futuro per præcipua gloriæ munera. Ideo enim loquitur Christus : Beati pauperes spiritu, id est humiles (juxta unam expositionem), quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum ; et denuo, Qui se humiliat, exaltabitur. Hinc in Ecclesiastico scribitur : Noli te extollere in faciendo opere tuo ; et iterum, Sapientia humiliati exaltabit caput ipsius.
paras.en: [[4:10|Be humbled in the sight of the Lord|Humiliamini in conspectu Domini]]: that is, let each one lower himself before God, look into his vices, consider the defects of nature and of guilt that he has in himself, and weigh how imperfectly he serves God. When these and many other things have been duly considered, let each one hold himself very cheap, judge himself worthy of all confusion, reproof and chastisement, and bear them with an even mind. [[4:10|and he will exalt you|Et exaltabit vos]] in the present life by the sublime gifts of grace, and in the life to come by the surpassing rewards of glory. For this is why Christ says: [[Matt 5:3|Blessed are the poor in spirit|Beati pauperes spiritu]], that is, the humble (according to one exposition), [[Matt 5:3|for theirs is the kingdom of heaven|quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum]]; and again: [[Luke 14:11|he that humbleth himself shall be exalted|Qui se humiliat, exaltabitur]]. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:29|Extol not thyself in doing thy work|Noli te extollere in faciendo opere tuo]]; and again: [[Ecclus 11:1|The wisdom of the humble shall exalt his head|Sapientia humiliati exaltabit caput ipsius]] [the margin gives only Ecclus. x, 29; this second saying is Ecclus 11:1].

paras.t: Nolite detrahere alterutrum, fratres : id est, unus alteri non obloquatur, quum hoc sit contra caritatem atque justitiam, et ex suo genere peccatum valde mortale, multoque gravius furto, secundum doctores. Peccata namque in proximum tanto sunt graviora, quanto majus nocumentum inferunt ei. Quum ergo per detractionem unus auferat alteri bonum nomen, et lædat eum in fama, faciatque eum aliis contemptibilem aut despectum; ideo magis peccat quam fur, qui exteriorem tollit substantiam, qua bona fama est præstantior, juxta illud Ecclesiastæ : Melius est nomen bonum quam unguenta pretiosa.
paras.en: [[4:11|Detract not one another, my brethren|Nolite detrahere alterutrum, fratres]]: that is, let not one speak against another, since this is against charity and justice, and of its kind [that is, by the nature of the act, unless lightness of matter or want of full consent excuses it] a very mortal sin, and much graver than theft, according to the doctors. For sins against our neighbour are the graver the greater the harm they do him. Since, then, by detraction one takes from another his good name, wounds him in his reputation, and makes him contemptible or despised in the eyes of others, he sins more than a thief, who takes away outward goods, than which a good name is more excellent, according to that word of Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 7:2|A good name is better than precious ointments|Melius est nomen bonum quam unguenta pretiosa]] [the margin gives Ecclus. vii, 2; the words are Eccles 7:2].

paras.t: Hinc Scriptura detractionem vehementissime ac sæpissime prohibet, reprobat et condemnat. Scriptum est enim in Proverbiis : Labia detrahentia procul sint a te ; et in Ecclesiaste, Si mordeat serpens in occulto, nihil minus eo habet qui detrahit. Sed et Sapiens ait : Custodite vos a murmuratione, et a detractione parcite linguæ, quoniam sermo obscurus non ibit in vacuum. Denique S. Clemens Papa, martyr et doctor, refert quod beatissimus princeps Apostolorum dixit esse tria homicidii genera : unum corporale ; aliud dixit esse odium ; tertium, detractionem, per quam is cui detrahitur, occiditur in corde audientis detractionem, quantum ad esse bonæ reputationis, quod in eo habebat.
paras.en: Hence Scripture most vehemently and most often forbids, reproves and condemns detraction. For it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 4:24|let detracting lips be far from thee|Labia detrahentia procul sint a te]]; and in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 10:11|If a serpent bite in silence, he is nothing better that backbiteth secretly|Si mordeat serpens in occulto, nihil minus eo habet qui detrahit]]. And the Wise Man too says: [[Wis 1:11|Keep yourselves, therefore, from murmuring|Custodite vos a murmuratione]], [[Wis 1:11|and refrain your tongue from detraction, for an obscure speech shall not go for nought|et a detractione parcite linguæ, quoniam sermo obscurus non ibit in vacuum]]. Lastly St Clement, Pope, martyr and doctor, relates that the most blessed prince of the Apostles said there are three kinds of homicide: one bodily; the second, he said, is hatred; the third, detraction, by which he who is detracted is slain in the heart of the one who hears the detraction, as regards the good repute he had there.

paras.t: Præterea, de ista materia dicit Thomas in secunda secundæ : Sicut unus dupliciter nocet alteri facto (puta : aperte, ut in rapina ; et occulte, ut in furto et percussione dolosa); ita dupliciter nocet unus alteri verbis : primo, aperte, ut in contumelia; et secreto, ut in detractione, quæ est denigratio alienæ famæ per verba occulta. Dicitur autem homo detrahere, non quia semper de veritate diminuat, sed quia quantum in se est, alterius famam ex intentione corrumpit, et bonum nomen ejus diminuit. Quod fit pluribus modis : primo, falsum alteri imponendo ; secundo, peccatum alterius exaggerando ; tertio, peccatum ejus occultum inordinate prodendo; quarto, dum bonum dicit quis mala intentione esse peractum ; quinto, dum bona alterius negat, malitioseve reticet, quando rationabilis causa exigit ea manifestari. — Insuper, susurratio in hoc convenit cum detractione, quod occulte malum dicit de proximo : propter quod unum frequenter pro alio sumitur. Proprie tamen differunt : quoniam susurrator intendit proximorum mutuam dilectionem corrumpere, seminando discordias. Idcirco susurratio est gravius crimen quam detractio, quia amicitia majus bonum est quam fama, juxta illud in Ecclesiastico : Amico fideli nulla est comparatio. Et sicut rapina est gravior furto, sic contumelia detractione. Atque, ut ait Gregorius : Sicut contumelia oritur ex ira, sic detractio ex odio. Detractio quoque mentem detrahentis excæcat, ita ut detrahens, proprio vitio obtenebratus, incipiat verum putare quod dicit de alio, quamvis sit falsum.
paras.en: Moreover, on this matter Thomas says in the Secunda Secundæ [the second part of the second part of his *Summa theologiæ*, where detraction and tale-bearing are treated]: Just as one man harms another by deed in two ways (openly, as in robbery, and secretly, as in theft and a treacherous blow), so one man harms another by words in two ways: first, openly, as in contumely [that is, insult to a man's face]; and secretly, as in detraction, which is the blackening of another's good name by secret words. A man is said to detract, not because he always takes away from the truth, but because, as far as in him lies, he deliberately corrupts another's reputation and lessens his good name. This is done in several ways: first, by imputing something false to another; second, by exaggerating another's sin; third, by revealing his hidden sin without due cause; fourth, when someone says that a good deed was done with a bad intention; fifth, when he denies another's good deeds, or maliciously keeps silent about them when a reasonable cause requires them to be made known. — Further, tale-bearing [*susurratio*, "whispering"] agrees with detraction in this, that it speaks evil of one's neighbour in secret; and for this reason the one is often taken for the other. Properly, however, they differ: for the tale-bearer aims at destroying the mutual love of neighbours by sowing discord. Tale-bearing is therefore a graver crime than detraction, because friendship is a greater good than reputation, according to that word in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 6:15|Nothing can be compared to a faithful friend|Amico fideli nulla est comparatio]]. And as robbery is graver than theft, so contumely is graver than detraction. And, as Gregory says: As contumely springs from anger, so detraction springs from hatred. Detraction also blinds the mind of the detractor, so that the detractor, darkened by his own vice, begins to think true what he says of another, though it is false.

paras.t: Denique, detractor gravissime peccat : quia non solum occidit propriam animam, sed et animam audientis, quantum in se est, præbendo ei venenum mortiferum et consentiendi occasionem. Si enim audiens detractioni consentiat, mortaliter peccat, quum dicat Apostolus : Non solum morte digni sunt, qui faciunt mala, sed etiam qui consentiunt facientibus ea. Imo detractor, quantum in se est, illum quoque cui detrahit, spiritualiter perimit : quia si ille percipiat qualiter ei detractum sit, oritur ei occasio odiendi detractorem, et obloquendi eidem. Audiens ergo detractionem, increpet detrahentem, et vultum avertat, si congrue potest. Quod si convenienter non potest, increpet eum aliquo signo, videlicet tristem faciem ostendendo : quia ut in Ecclesiaste legitur, Per tristitiam vultus corrigitur animus delinquentis. In Proverbiis quoque asseritur : Ventus Aquilo dissipat pluvias, et facies tristis linguam detrahentem.
paras.en: Lastly, the detractor sins most grievously, because he slays not only his own soul but also, as far as in him lies, the soul of the hearer, offering him a deadly poison and an occasion of consenting. For if the hearer consents to the detraction, he sins mortally, since the Apostle says: Not only [[Rom 1:32|are worthy of death|morte digni sunt]] they that do evil things, [[Rom 1:32|but they also that consent to them that do them|sed etiam qui consentiunt facientibus ea]]. Nay, the detractor, as far as in him lies, also slays spiritually the one he detracts: for if that man learns how he has been detracted, an occasion arises for him of hating the detractor and of speaking against him in turn. Let the one, then, who hears detraction rebuke the detractor, and turn away his face, if he fittingly can. And if he cannot fittingly do so, let him rebuke him by some sign, namely by showing a sad face: for, as we read in Ecclesiastes, [[Eccles 7:4|by the sadness of the countenance the mind of the offender is corrected|Per tristitiam vultus corrigitur animus delinquentis]]. In Proverbs too it is asserted: [[Prov 25:23|The north wind driveth away rain, as doth a sad countenance a backbiting tongue|Ventus Aquilo dissipat pluvias, et facies tristis linguam detrahentem]].

paras.t: Abhorreamus ergo, jugiterque vitemus hæc vitia maledicta, videlicet verba contumeliosa, detractoria, susurratoria, et peccata ex eis nascentia. Et ut docet Isidorus, peccanti non obloquamur, sed compatiamur : formidantes ne et nos in eadem aut similia vel majora labamur. Qui enim proximis peccantibus mox indignantur, irascuntur ac detrahunt, merentur a Deo relinqui, et in eadem aut majora incidere.
paras.en: Let us therefore abhor and continually shun these accursed vices, namely contumelious, detracting and tale-bearing words, and the sins that spring from them. And, as Isidore teaches, let us not speak against one who sins, but have compassion on him, fearing lest we too fall into the same sins, or like ones, or greater. For those who at once grow indignant and angry with their neighbours when they sin, and detract them, deserve to be forsaken by God and to fall into the same sins or greater ones.

paras.t: Qui enim detrahit fratri, aut qui judicat fratrem suum, id est proximum judicio inordinato, temerario, suspicioso aut usurpato, detrahit legi divinæ, quæ prohibet detractionem et inordinata judicia, et judicat legem, id est, reprobat eam : non quod directe detrahat legi, aut reprobet eam, sed quoniam contra legem faciendo, ita se habet ac si sentiat eam esse iniquam, et quasi despiciat eam.
