Ait enim lex vetus : Non eris criminator, nec susurro in populo ; et rursus, Nolite facere iniquum aliquid in judicio, in regula, in pondere, in mensura. Si autem judicas legem, non es factor legis, id est, eam non imples, ejus præceptis obediendo, sed judex, id est, quasi superiorem te facis lege divina, eam transgrediendo, et juxta modum prætactum judicando : quod prorsus iniquum est.
paras.en: For [[4:11|He that detracteth his brother|Qui enim detrahit fratri]], [[4:11|or he that judgeth his brother|aut qui judicat fratrem suum]], that is, his neighbour, with a disordered, rash, suspicious or usurped judgment, [[4:11|detracteth the law|detrahit legi]], the divine law, which forbids detraction and disordered judgments, [[4:11|and judgeth the law|et judicat legem]], that is, condemns it: not that he directly detracts the law or condemns it, but because, by acting against the law, he behaves as if he thought it unjust, and as it were despises it. For the old law says: [[Lev 19:16|Thou shalt not be a detractor nor a whisperer among the people|Non eris criminator, nec susurro in populo]]; and again: [[Lev 19:35|Do not any unjust thing in judgment, in rule, in weight, or in measure|Nolite facere iniquum aliquid in judicio, in regula, in pondere, in mensura]]. [[4:11|But if thou judge the law, thou art not a doer of the law|Si autem judicas legem, non es factor legis]], that is, thou dost not fulfil it by obeying its precepts, [[4:11|but a judge|sed judex]], that is, thou makest thyself as it were superior to the divine law, by transgressing it and by judging in the manner touched on above: which is altogether unjust.

paras.t: Propter quod subditur : Unus est enim legislator et judex, videlicet Deus, qui est supremus dator legis divinæ. Moyses vero fuit legislator ministerialis. Deus autem legem quam condidit, habet judicare, interpretari et dispensare in ea, tanquam superior ipsa. Ejusdem namque est, legem condere atque exponere. Hinc Isaias dicit : Dominus judex noster, Dominus legifer noster, Dominus rex noster. Job quoque : Ecce Deus excelsus in fortitudine, et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus. Qui potest perdere, id est juste damnare, et liberare, id est misericorditer a peccato purgare, et ad salutem perducere. Qui in Deuteronomio testatur : Ego occidam, et ego vivere faciam ; in Exodo quoque, Miserebor cui voluero, et clemens ero in quem mihi placuerit. De quo ait Apostolus : Cujus vult miseretur ; et quem vult indurat.
paras.en: For which reason it is added: [[4:12|There is one lawgiver and judge|Unus est enim legislator et judex]], namely God, who is the supreme giver of the divine law; Moses was a lawgiver as His minister. And God has the right to judge, to interpret and to dispense in the law that He made, as being above it; for it belongs to the same one to make a law and to expound it. Hence Isaias says: [[Is 33:22|the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king|Dominus judex noster, Dominus legifer noster, Dominus rex noster]]. Job too: [[Job 36:22|Behold, God is high in his strength, and none is like him among the lawgivers|Ecce Deus excelsus in fortitudine, et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus]] [the margin gives Job xxxvi, 23, 24; the words are Job 36:22]. [[4:12|that is able to destroy|Qui potest perdere]], that is, to condemn justly, [[4:12|and to deliver|et liberare]], that is, to cleanse mercifully from sin and bring to salvation; who testifies in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 32:39|I will kill and I will make to live|Ego occidam, et ego vivere faciam]]; and in Exodus too: [[Ex 33:19|I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will be merciful to whom it shall please me|Miserebor cui voluero, et clemens ero in quem mihi placuerit]]. Of whom the Apostle says: [[Rom 9:18|he hath mercy on whom he will. And whom he will, he hardeneth|Cujus vult miseretur ; et quem vult indurat]].

paras.t: Tu autem quis es, id est cujus auctoritatis, qui judicas proximum tuum inordinato judicio? Sic et ad Romanos loquitur Paulus : Tu quis es qui judicas alienum servum? Suo domino stat aut cadit. Itemque : Tu quid judicas fratrem tuum? Omnes enim stabimus ante tribunal Christi. Itaque unusquisque pro se rationem reddet Deo. Non ergo amplius invicem judicemus.
paras.en: [[4:13|But who art thou|Tu autem quis es]], that is, of what authority, [[4:13|that judgest thy neighbour|qui judicas proximum tuum]] with a disordered judgment? So too Paul speaks to the Romans: [[Rom 14:4|Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? To his own lord he standeth or falleth|Tu quis es qui judicas alienum servum? Suo domino stat aut cadit]]. And again: [[Rom 14:10|why judgest thou thy brother|Tu quid judicas fratrem tuum]]? [[Rom 14:10|For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ|Omnes enim stabimus ante tribunal Christi]]. [[Rom 14:12|Therefore every one of us shall render account to God for himself|Itaque unusquisque pro se rationem reddet Deo]]. [[Rom 14:13|Let us not therefore judge one another any more|Non ergo amplius invicem judicemus]].

paras.t: Verumtamen ista non sunt intelligenda quasi non liceat prælatis, principibus et judicibus judicare subditos suos ; nec sic, quasi de his quæ manifeste sunt mala, nec bono animo fieri valent, non liceat unicuique bene disposito judicare, sed ne de incertis et dubiis quis præsumat temerarie judicare, affirmando seu definiendo aut puniendo. Aliud quoque est judicare personam, aliud actum. Sit ergo unusquisque diligens sui ipsius examinator, dijudicator et castigator, atque in primis emendet se ipsum. Sicque caritative, discrete et timorate, loco et tempore opportuno, exigenteque causa judicet et corripiat alium, prout hoc sibi incumbit aut licet. Qui enim in eisdem aut majoribus culpis est, indignus est alium judicare atque corripere de hujusmodi culpis in quibus ipsemet jacet. Quidam vero pessima consuetudine sunt infecti, qui alios judicare sunt proni, et negligunt semetipsos.
paras.en: Yet these words are not to be understood as though it were not lawful for prelates, princes and judges to judge their subjects; nor as though it were not lawful for anyone well disposed to judge of things that are manifestly evil and cannot be done with a good mind; but they mean that no one should presume to judge rashly of things uncertain and doubtful, by affirming, or deciding, or punishing. It is one thing, too, to judge the person, another to judge the act. Let each one, then, be a diligent examiner, judge and chastiser of himself, and first of all amend himself. And so, with charity, discretion and the fear of God, at a fitting place and time, and when the case requires it, let him judge and reprove another, as far as this falls to him or is lawful for him. For he who is in the same faults or greater ones is unworthy to judge and reprove another for such faults as he himself lies in. But some are infected with a most evil habit: they are prone to judge others, and neglect themselves.

paras.t: Consequenter sapientissimus Jacobus iste reprehendit incautam locutionem multorum. Ecce nunc, id est, errorem vestrum modo advertite, vos qui dicitis : Hodie aut crastino ibimus in illam civitatem, et faciemus quidem ibi annum, id est, uno anno stabimus ibi, aut mercabimur, et lucrum faciemus, id est, vendendo et emendo lucrabimur ; qui ignoratis, quid sit vobis in crastinum, id est, quid cras vobis eveniet, et an vivetis per diem, quia nescitis diem neque horam. Idcirco in Proverbiis scriptum est : Ne glorieris in crastinum, ignorans quid superventura pariat dies.
paras.en: Next this most wise James rebukes the incautious speech of many. [[4:13|Behold, now|Ecce nunc]], that is, take note now of your error, [[4:13|you that say: To-day or to-morrow we will go into such a city|qui dicitis : Hodie aut crastino ibimus in illam civitatem]], [[4:13|and there we will spend a year|et faciemus quidem ibi annum]], that is, we will stay there one year, [[4:13|and will traffic and make our gain|aut mercabimur, et lucrum faciemus]] [Denis reads *aut*, "or"; the margin notes the reading *et*, "and"], that is, by selling and buying we will make a profit; [[4:14|Whereas you know not what shall be on the morrow|qui ignoratis, quid sit vobis in crastinum]], that is, what will happen to you tomorrow, and whether you will live through the day, since [[Matt 25:13|you know not the day nor the hour|nescitis diem neque horam]]. Therefore it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 27:1|Boast not for to morrow, for thou knowest not what the day to come may bring forth|Ne glorieris in crastinum, ignorans quid superventura pariat dies]].

paras.t: Quæ est enim vita vestra, id est vita hæc corporalis ac temporalis ? Et respondet : Vapor est ad modicum parens, id est, similis est vapori seu fumo, brevi horula apparenti, ac protinus deficienti. Ideo subditur : et deinceps exterminabitur, id est, deficiet talis vapor, seu vita hæc præsens, quæ a nativitatis exordio est quasi continuus atque celerrimus cursus ad mortem. Propter quod sanctus Job dixit : Parce mihi, Domine, nihil enim sunt dies mei ; et rursus, Dies mei velocius transierunt quam a texente tela succiditur. David quoque primo Paralipomenon : Dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora ; et in Psalmo, Homo vanitati similis factus est, dies ejus sicut umbra prætereunt.
paras.en: [[4:15|For what is your life|Quæ est enim vita vestra]], that is, this bodily and temporal life? And he answers: [[4:15|It is a vapour which appeareth for a little while|Vapor est ad modicum parens]], that is, it is like a vapour or smoke, appearing for a brief little hour and straightway failing. Therefore it is added: [[4:15|and afterwards shall vanish away|et deinceps exterminabitur]], that is, such a vapour, or this present life, will fail, which from the beginning of birth is as it were a continuous and most swift course towards death. Wherefore holy Job said: [[Job 7:16|spare me|Parce mihi]], O Lord, [[Job 7:16|for my days are nothing|nihil enim sunt dies mei]]; and again: [[Job 7:6|My days have passed more swiftly than the web is cut by the weaver|Dies mei velocius transierunt quam a texente tela succiditur]]. David too, in the first book of Paralipomenon: [[1 Par 29:15|Our days upon earth are as a shadow, and there is no stay|Dies nostri quasi umbra super terram, et nulla est mora]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 143:4|Man is like to vanity: his days pass away like a shadow|Homo vanitati similis factus est, dies ejus sicut umbra prætereunt]].

paras.t: Consequenter docet Apostolus sapientem, timoratum ac sobrium modum loquendi. Pro eo ut dicatis : id est, tam insipientem modum loquendi habetis, pro eo quod merito diceretis ; vel ita supplendum est, Hæc doceo vos pro eo ut dicatis posthac : Si Dominus voluerit, et, Si vixerimus, faciemus hoc aut illud. Sic enim loquendo, memores estis propriæ fragilitatis atque incertitudinis vitæ præsentis, et insinuatis ac præsupponitis totum vitæ vestræ cursum, eventum et actum, ab omnipotentia et voluntate Dei indesinenter pendere. — Observemus ergo et nos hunc salubrem modum loquendi : quem, proh dolor ! multi non considerant neque observant ; sed ita de futuris sibi et faciendis a se loquuntur, quasi certi essent se tam diu victuros, vel a se ipsis vitam haberent, nec conservatione indigerent divina, nec providentiæ Creatoris cuncta subessent. Idcirco merentur improvise tolli de medio, et interdum sic accidit eis.
paras.en: Next the Apostle teaches a wise, God-fearing and sober manner of speaking. [[4:15|For that you should say|Pro eo ut dicatis]] [*pro eo ut*, "instead of", which Denis explains in two ways]: that is, you have so foolish a manner of speaking instead of what you might rightly say; or it is to be filled out thus: I teach you this so that you may say hereafter: [[4:15|If the Lord will, and, If we shall live, we will do this or that|Si Dominus voluerit, et, Si vixerimus, faciemus hoc aut illud]]. For by speaking so you are mindful of your own frailty and of the uncertainty of the present life, and you imply and presuppose that the whole course, outcome and action of your life hangs unceasingly on the almighty power and will of God. — Let us too, then, observe this wholesome manner of speaking, which, alas, many neither consider nor observe; but they speak of what is to come to them and what they are to do as though they were sure of living so long, or had life of themselves, and did not need God's preserving, nor were all things subject to the providence of the Creator. Therefore they deserve to be taken away suddenly from the midst, and sometimes it so befalls them.

paras.t: Nunc autem exsultatis in superbiis vestris, id est in superbis locutionibus et verbis præsumptuosis : quia ut in Proverbiis dicitur, Lætatur homo in sententia oris sui. Omnis exsultatio talis maligna est, id est vitiosa, et malæ libidinis igne accensa.
paras.en: [[4:16|But now you rejoice in your arrogancies|Nunc autem exsultatis in superbiis vestris]], that is, in proud speeches and presumptuous words: for, as it is said in Proverbs, [[Prov 15:23|A man rejoiceth in the sentence of his mouth|Lætatur homo in sententia oris sui]]. [[4:16|All such rejoicing is wicked|Omnis exsultatio talis maligna est]], that is, vicious, and kindled by the fire of evil desire.

paras.t: Scienti igitur bonum facere, et non facienti, id est, ei qui scit ad quæ obligetur, quid facere, quid vitare jam debeat, nec tamen juxta suam peritiam laudabiliter conversanti, peccatum est illi, id est, sua scientia est sibi majoris culpæ ac pœnæ occasio, et culpabilior est atque damnabilior : quemadmodum ait Salvator, Servus qui scit voluntatem domini sui, et non facit, plagis vapulabit multis ; et rursus, Cui plus datum est, plus requiretur ab eo. Hinc litterati specialiter obligantur esse coram Altissimo justi ac recti, et coram proximis exemplares. Propter quod gloriosissimus Archiapostolus contestatur : Melius est non cognoscere viam justitiæ, quam post agnitionem retrorsum reverti. Circa quæ verba inferius exponenda, plenior erit, si Deus concesserit, de horum intellectu verborum tractatus.
paras.en: [[4:17|To him therefore who knoweth to do good and doth it not|Scienti igitur bonum facere, et non facienti]], that is, to him who knows what he is bound to, what he ought now to do and what to avoid, and yet does not live in praiseworthy fashion according to his knowledge, [[4:17|to him it is sin|peccatum est illi]]: that is, his knowledge is for him the occasion of greater guilt and punishment, and he is the more culpable and the more damnable; as the Saviour says: [[Luke 12:47|that servant, who knew the will of his lord|Servus qui scit voluntatem domini sui]], [[Luke 12:47|and did not|et non facit]], [[Luke 12:47|shall be beaten with many stripes|plagis vapulabit multis]] [Denis has *plagis*, "with stripes", from the next verse]; and again: [[Luke 12:48|unto whomsoever much is given, of him much shall be required|Cui plus datum est, plus requiretur ab eo]]. Hence the learned are especially bound to be just and upright before the Most High, and an example to their neighbours. For which reason the most glorious Chief of the Apostles testifies: [[2 Pet 2:21|it had been better for them not to have known the way of justice than, after they have known it, to turn back|Melius est non cognoscere viam justitiæ, quam post agnitionem retrorsum reverti]]. On these words, which are to be expounded below, there will be, if God grants it, a fuller treatment of their meaning.

5.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI QUINTI : AGITE NUNC, DIVITES.
5.title_en: Explanation of the fifth chapter: Go to now, ye rich men.

paras.t: Sanctus apostolus Jacobus supra hortatus est eos quibus scripsit, ad patientiam in adversis, ad paupertatis amorem, ad humilitatem in omnibus, et inordinatum ad terrena reprehendit affectum. Nunc idem facit, ostendendo calamitatem ac periculosissimum statum divitum hujus sæculi : quorum fallacem prosperitatem acriter arguit, quatenus fideles pauperes in sua sint inopia patientiores. Quibusdam equidem nondum perfectis sua adversitas et paupertas molestæ sunt, dum iniquorum prosperitatem vident, nec vilipenduntur, sed aliquanti æstimant. In quorum imperfectorum persona ait Psalmista : Mei autem pene moti sunt pedes, pene effusi sunt gressus mei : quia zelavi super iniquos, pacem peccatorum videns. Unde rursus hortatur : Noli æmulari in malignantibus, etc.
paras.en: The holy apostle James above exhorted those to whom he wrote to patience in adversity, to the love of poverty, to humility in all things, and he rebuked an inordinate attachment to earthly things. Now he does the same by showing the calamity and most perilous state of the rich of this world, whose deceitful prosperity he sharply reproves, so that the faithful poor may be more patient in their want. For to some who are not yet perfect their adversity and poverty are grievous, when they see the prosperity of the wicked, who are not despised but held in some esteem. In the person of such imperfect men the Psalmist says: [[Ps 72:2|But my feet were almost moved; my steps had well nigh slipped.|Mei autem pene moti sunt pedes, pene effusi sunt gressus mei]] [[Ps 72:3|Because I had a zeal on occasion of the wicked, seeing the prosperity of sinners.|quia zelavi super iniquos, pacem peccatorum videns.]] Hence again he exhorts: [[Ps 36:1|Be not emulous of evildoers|Noli æmulari in malignantibus]], etc.

paras.t: Ait ergo Apostolus : Agite nunc, divites, id est, vitam corrigite, pœnitentiam facite, quum dicat Salvator : Nisi pœnitentiam egeritis, omnes similiter peribitis. Et Paulus : Dum tempus (inquit) habemus, operemur bonum ad omnes. Quidam exponunt sic : Agite nunc, divites, id est, voluntates vestras iniquas implete. Ut sit locutio ironica, quæ a contrario intelligenda est sensu, juxta quod in Apocalypsi scribitur : Qui in sordibus est, sordescat adhuc : et qui nocet, noceat adhuc. Sed prima expositio melior existimatur. Quum enim in generali dixisset Apostolus, Agite nunc, divites, mox adjecit quid agere debeant. Plorate ululantes, id est, vehementer dolete, et ex interioris contritionis vehementia in intensum ejulatum erumpite : juxta illud Michææ : Faciam planctum quasi draconum, et luctum quasi struthionum ; in miseriis [vestris] quæ advenient vobis, id est ex consideratione atque formidine metuendi judicii Dei, æternaliumque pœnarum imminentium vobis nisi interim dignum pœnitentiæ fructum feceritis.
paras.en: The Apostle therefore says: [[5:1|Go to now, ye rich men|Agite nunc, divites]], that is, amend your life, do penance; for the Saviour says: [[Luke 13:3|unless you shall do penance, you shall all likewise perish|Nisi pœnitentiam egeritis, omnes similiter peribitis]]. And Paul: [[Gal 6:10|whilst we have time|Dum tempus]] (he says), [[Gal 6:10|let us work good to all men|habemus, operemur bonum ad omnes]]. Some expound it thus: [[5:1|Go to now, ye rich men|Agite nunc, divites]], that is, fulfil your wicked wills; so that it would be an ironical expression, to be understood in the contrary sense, according to what is written in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 22:11|he that is filthy, let him be filthy still|Qui in sordibus est, sordescat adhuc]]: and [[Apoc 22:11|he that hurteth, let him hurt still|qui nocet, noceat adhuc]]. But the first exposition is thought the better. For when the Apostle had said in general, [[5:1|Go to now, ye rich men|Agite nunc, divites]], he at once added what they ought to do: [[5:1|weep and howl|Plorate ululantes]], that is, grieve vehemently, and from the vehemence of inward contrition break out into loud wailing, according to that of Micheas: [[Mich 1:8|I will make a wailing like the dragons, and a mourning like the ostriches|Faciam planctum quasi draconum, et luctum quasi struthionum]]; [[5:1|in your miseries|in miseriis]], [[5:1|which shall come upon you|quæ advenient vobis]], that is, from the consideration and dread of the fearful judgment of God, and of the eternal punishments that hang over you, unless meanwhile you bring forth fruit worthy of penance.

paras.t: Deinde subditur horum causa. Divitiæ vestræ naturales, videlicet frumenta, vina et consimilia, putrefactæ sunt ex diuturnitate et avara retentione : quoniam tempore apto non communicastis eas egenis, prout in Evangelio præcipit Christus, Quod superest, date eleemosynam. Ex eadem quoque causa, vestimenta vestra a tineis consumta sunt ; aurum et argentum vestrum æruginavit, id est, ex vetustate et cupida reservatione contraxit æruginem. Vestimenta autem, aurum et argentum, ad artificiales spectant divitias.
paras.en: Next the cause of these things is added: [[5:2|Your riches|Divitiæ vestræ]], your natural riches, namely corn, wine and the like, [[5:2|are corrupted|putrefactæ sunt]] through long keeping and covetous holding back, because at the fitting time you did not share them with the needy, as Christ commands in the Gospel: [[Luke 11:41|that which remaineth, give alms|Quod superest, date eleemosynam]]. From the same cause also [[5:2|your garments are motheaten|vestimenta vestra a tineis consumta sunt]]; [[5:3|Your gold and silver is cankered|aurum et argentum vestrum æruginavit]], that is, through age and greedy hoarding it has gathered rust. Now garments, gold and silver belong to artificial riches [that is, wealth made by human skill, as against natural riches, the fruits of the earth].

paras.t: Et ærugo eorum, similiter et naturalium divitiarum putrefactio, in testimonium vobis erit, id est, materialiter testimonium perhibebit adversus vos, quia a Judice summo assumetur in argumentum et signum vestræ cupiditatis ac justæ damnationis. Qui enim divitias suas taliter retinent, furtum et rapinam, imo nonnumquam etiam et homicidium perpetrant : quia sancti patres Ambrosius Basiliusque testantur : Non minoris criminis est habenti tollere, quam, quum possis et habeas, indigentibus denegare. Esurientium panis est, quem tu detines ; nudorum indumen[…]tum, quod includis ; miserorum redemptio, pecunia quam abscondis : tantorum te scias bona invadere, quantis possis nec vis præstare. Imo, ut ait Hieronymus : Eorum qui ex fame aut frigore obierunt, mortis reus teneris. Itaque Jacobus non divitias, sed eorum abusum et tenacitatem condemnat. Hinc super illud Psalmistæ, Divitiæ si affluant, nolite cor apponere, loquitur Augustinus : Qui non habet divitias, non ambiat eas ; qui autem habet, non de eis superbiat. Nec dicit Propheta, Nolite eas habere, sed, Nolite cor apponere. Non enim damnat divitias (per quas mereri possumus regnum cœlorum), sed cor appositum, quod eas misericorditer non expendit, sed avare recondit. Hinc quoque in Proverbiis dicitur : Qui abscondunt frumentum in tempore, maledicentur ; benedictio autem super caput vendentium.
paras.en: [[5:3|And the rust of them|Et ærugo eorum]], and likewise the rotting of the natural riches, [[5:3|shall be for a testimony against you|in testimonium vobis erit]], that is, will materially bear witness against you, because it will be taken up by the supreme Judge as a proof and sign of your cupidity and of your just damnation. For those who hold back their riches in this way commit theft and robbery, nay sometimes even murder, as the holy fathers Ambrose and Basil testify: It is no lesser crime to take from him who has than, when you can and have, to refuse those in need. It is the bread of the hungry that you hold back; the clothing of the naked […] that you lock away; the redemption of the wretched, the money that you hide: know that you invade the goods of as many as you could help and will not. Nay, as Jerome says: You are held guilty of the death of those who have died of hunger or cold. And so James condemns not riches, but their abuse and tight-fisted keeping. Hence on that verse of the Psalmist, [[Ps 61:11|if riches abound, set not your heart upon them|Divitiæ si affluant, nolite cor apponere]], Augustine says: He who has not riches, let him not seek after them; and he who has them, let him not be proud of them. The Prophet does not say, Do not have them, but, Set not your heart upon them. For he does not condemn riches (through which we can merit the kingdom of heaven), but the heart set upon them, which does not spend them mercifully but hoards them avariciously. Hence it is also said in Proverbs: [[Prov 11:26|He that hideth up corn, shall be cursed|Qui abscondunt frumentum in tempore, maledicentur]]; [[Prov 11:26|but a blessing upon the head of them that sell|benedictio autem super caput vendentium]].

paras.t: Et manducabit carnes vestras sicut ignis, id est, causa erit infernalis incendii, quod corpora vestra in inferno post diem judicii patientur. Non quod ærugo erit causa directa ac meritoria condemnationis, quum non sit peccatum, sed naturalis effectus ; sed culpa quam incurristis avare retinendo divitias, ex quarum reconditione æruginationem passæ sunt, meritoria erit vestræ afflictionis causa. De talibus scriptum est : Dominus omnipotens vindicabit in eis, in die judicii visitabit illos ; dabit ignem et vermes in carnes eorum, ut urantur et sentiant in sempiternum. Hinc in Ecclesiastico fertur : Humilia valde spiritum tuum, quoniam vindicta carnis impii ignis et vermis.
paras.en: [[5:3|And shall eat your flesh like fire|Et manducabit carnes vestras sicut ignis]], that is, it will be a cause of the fire of hell which your bodies will suffer in hell after the day of judgment. Not that the rust will be the direct and meritorious cause of damnation, since it is not a sin but a natural effect; but the fault which you incurred by avariciously holding back your riches, from whose hoarding they suffered rust, will be the meritorious cause [that is, the cause that deserves it] of your affliction. Of such it is written: [[Jdt 16:20|the Lord almighty will take revenge on them, in the day of judgment he will visit them|Dominus omnipotens vindicabit in eis, in die judicii visitabit illos]]; [[Jdt 16:21|he will give fire, and worms into their flesh, that they may burn, and may feel for ever|dabit ignem et vermes in carnes eorum, ut urantur et sentiant in sempiternum]] [the margin gives Job xx, 23, 24; the words are those of Judith 16:20–21]. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 7:19|Humble thy spirit very much: for the vengeance on the flesh of the ungodly is fire and worms.|Humilia valde spiritum tuum, quoniam vindicta carnis impii ignis et vermis]]

paras.t: Thesaurizastis vobis iram in novissimis diebus, id est, per tantam avaritiam vestram accumulastis vobis causam copiosissimam reprobationis ac condemnationis, quas in die judicii et deinceps sustinebitis in æternum. Juxta quem sensum dicitur ad Romanos : Secundum duritiam tuam et impœnitens cor tuum, thesaurizas tibi iram in die iræ et revelationis justi judicii Dei. Nempe in Ecclesiastico legitur : Avaro nihil est scelestius; nihil est iniquius quam amare pecuniam ; avarus enim animam suam habet venalem. Idcirco ait Salvator : Nolite thesaurizare vobis thesauros in terra, ubi ærugo et tinea demolitur. Hinc ad Timotheum scribit Apostolus : Divitibus hujus sæculi præcipe non sublime sapere, nec sperare in incerto divitiarum, sed divites fieri in operibus bonis, facile tribuere, communicare.
paras.en: [[5:3|You have stored up to yourselves wrath against the last days|Thesaurizastis vobis iram in novissimis diebus]], that is, by such great avarice you have heaped up for yourselves a most abundant cause of reprobation and damnation, which you will undergo on the day of judgment and thereafter for ever. In this sense it is said to the Romans: [[Rom 2:5|according to thy hardness and impenitent heart, thou treasurest up to thyself wrath, against the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God|Secundum duritiam tuam et impœnitens cor tuum, thesaurizas tibi iram in die iræ et revelationis justi judicii Dei]]. Indeed in Ecclesiasticus we read: [[Ecclus 10:9|nothing is more wicked than the covetous man|Avaro nihil est scelestius]]; [[Ecclus 10:10|There is not a more wicked thing than to love money: for such a one setteth even his own soul to sale|nihil est iniquius quam amare pecuniam ; avarus enim animam suam habet venalem]]. Therefore the Saviour says: [[Matt 6:19|Lay not up to yourselves treasures on earth: where the rust, and moth consume|Nolite thesaurizare vobis thesauros in terra, ubi ærugo et tinea demolitur]]. Hence the Apostle writes to Timothy: [[1 Tim 6:17|Charge the rich of this world not to be highminded nor to trust in the uncertainty of riches|Divitibus hujus sæculi præcipe non sublime sapere, nec sperare in incerto divitiarum]], but [[1 Tim 6:18|to be rich in good work, to give easily, to communicate|divites fieri in operibus bonis, facile tribuere, communicare]].

paras.t: Consequenter describit Apostolus quoddam crimen enorme, quod ex avaritia oritur, quod est subtractio justæ mercedis operariorum. Ecce merces operariorum vestrorum, qui messuerunt regiones vestras, id est, terræ nascentia agrorum quos in vestris regionibus possidetis, deposuerunt, quæ fraudata est a vobis, id est, quam mercedem illis injuste atque fallaciter subtraxistis, clamat, id est, materialiter vos accusat, et ultionem contra vos expetit ; et clamor eorum, videlicet præmiorum quæ operariis vestris tenemini, seu clamor operariorum dolentium et conquerentium de tanta injustitia eis facta, in aures Domini Sabaoth introivit, id est, ab omnipotente Deo judicatus est justus. Talium enim operariorum querelam Deus reputat esse justissimam, atque injuriam eis illatam judicat esse gravissimam. Dicitur autem Deus, Dominus Sabaoth, id est exercituum, sive omnipotens. Quod verbum magnificum apposuit Jacobus, ad perterrendum iniquos, qui ita se habent circa egenos, quasi non habeant protectorem ac judicem ; quum tamen Deus omnipotens, angelicorum exercituum Dominus, sit illorum specialis pater, exauditor, tutor et judex, secundum illud in Psalmo : Tibi derelictus est pauper, orphano tu eris adjutor.
paras.en: Next the Apostle describes a certain enormous crime which springs from avarice, namely the withholding of the just wages of labourers. [[5:4|Behold the hire of the labourers|Ecce merces operariorum vestrorum]], [[5:4|who have reaped down your fields|qui messuerunt regiones vestras]], that is, have cut down the produce of the lands which you possess in your regions, [[5:4|which by fraud has been kept back by you|quæ fraudata est a vobis]], that is, the wages which you have unjustly and deceitfully withheld from them, [[5:4|crieth|clamat]], that is, materially accuses you and demands vengeance against you; [[5:4|and the cry of them|et clamor eorum]], namely of the wages you owe your labourers, or the cry of the labourers grieving and complaining of so great an injustice done to them, [[5:4|hath entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth|in aures Domini Sabaoth introivit]], that is, has been judged just by almighty God. For God reckons the complaint of such labourers most just, and judges the wrong done to them most grievous. Now God is called the Lord of Sabaoth, that is, of hosts, or almighty. James set down this magnificent word to terrify the wicked, who behave towards the needy as if these had no protector and judge; whereas almighty God, the Lord of the angelic hosts, is their special father, hearer, guardian and judge, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 9:35|To thee is the poor man left: thou wilt be a helper to the orphan|Tibi derelictus est pauper, orphano tu eris adjutor]] [the margin gives Ps. x, 14, according to the Hebrew; in the Vulgate numbering Ps 9:35].

paras.t: Denique ut ex Scripturis elicitur, quatuor sunt peccata, quæ propter suam enormitatem dicuntur clamare ad Deum. Primum est homicidium, juxta illud Geneseos : Vox sanguinis fratris tui clamat ad me de terra. Secundum est oppressio miserabilium personarum, quemadmodum in Exodo loquitur Dominus : Clamor filiorum Israel venit ad me, vidique afflictionem eorum. Tertium est vitium contra naturam. Unde in Genesi loquitur Dominus: Clamor Sodomorum et Gomorrhæorum multiplicatus est. Quartum est defraudatio mercedis operariorum, ut patet hoc loco. Estque peccatum istud tam grave, ut in Ecclesiastico dicatur: Qui effundit sanguinem, et qui fraudem facit mercenario, fratres sunt. Hinc Scriptura peccatum hoc multipliciter prohibet: quia in Levitico ait Deus per Moysen, Non morabitur merces operariorum apud te usque mane; et Tobias, Quicumque tibi aliquid operatus fuerit, statim mercedem ei restitue, et merces operarii tui apud te omnino non remaneat. Hinc sanctus Job ait: Si adversum me terra mea clamat, si fructus ejus comedi absque pecunia, et animam agricolarum ejus afflixi, pro frumento oriatur mihi tribulus, et pro hordeo spina.
paras.en: Further, as is gathered from the Scriptures, there are four sins which, because of their enormity, are said to cry to God. The first is murder, according to that of Genesis: [[Gen 4:10|the voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me from the earth|Vox sanguinis fratris tui clamat ad me de terra]]. The second is the oppression of wretched persons, as the Lord says in Exodus: [[Ex 3:9|the cry of the children of Israel is come unto me: and I have seen their affliction|Clamor filiorum Israel venit ad me, vidique afflictionem eorum]]. The third is the vice against nature; hence the Lord says in Genesis: [[Gen 18:20|The cry of Sodom and Gomorrha is multiplied|Clamor Sodomorum et Gomorrhæorum multiplicatus est]]. The fourth is the defrauding of labourers of their wages, as is plain in this place. And this sin is so grave that it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 34:27|He that sheddeth blood, and he that defraudeth the laborer of his hire, are brothers.|Qui effundit sanguinem, et qui fraudem facit mercenario, fratres sunt.]] Hence Scripture forbids this sin in many ways: for in Leviticus God says through Moses, [[Lev 19:13|The wages of him that hath been hired by thee shall not abide with thee until the morning|Non morabitur merces operariorum apud te usque mane]]; and Tobias: [[Tob 4:15|If any man hath done any work for thee, immediately pay him his hire, and let not the wages of thy hired servant stay with thee at all.|Quicumque tibi aliquid operatus fuerit, statim mercedem ei restitue, et merces operarii tui apud te omnino non remaneat]] And so holy Job says: [[Job 31:38|If my land cry against me|Si adversum me terra mea clamat]], [[Job 31:39|If I have eaten the fruits thereof without money, and have afflicted the son of the tillers thereof|si fructus ejus comedi absque pecunia, et animam agricolarum ejus afflixi]], [[Job 31:40|Let thistles grow up to me instead of wheat, and thorns instead of barley|pro frumento oriatur mihi tribulus, et pro hordeo spina]].

paras.t: Insuper, ex temporalium affluentia solent oriri carnalia vitia: quia, ut ait Valerius: Dives currit ad libitum, corruit ad illicitum; et dum abundat divitiis, abundat et carnalibus vitiis. Ideo subjungitur: Epulati estis super terram, id est, delicate et gulose vos refecistis, et in luxuriis enutristis corda vestra, id est, desideriis carnalibus vestri cordis, sensitivo appetitui consentientes, satisfecistis, incontinenter vivendo absque freno. Tales sunt qui non solum ex passione seu infirmitate, sed ex proposito et habitu vitioso vivunt turpissime, qui teste Philosopho, sunt brutis incomparabiliter viliores atque pejores. In talium persona ait Salomon in Ecclesiaste: Non prohibui cor meum, quin frueretur omni voluptate. Istis eveniet quod de divite epulone in Evangelio legitur, cui in infernali incendio constituto, negata est una aquæ gutta; et quod in Apocalypsi ait Judex cœlestis, Quantum glorificavit se, et in deliciis fuit, tantum date ei tormentum et luctum.
paras.en: Moreover, carnal vices are wont to arise from an abundance of temporal goods; for, as Valerius says: The rich man runs to what he likes, and falls into what is unlawful; and while he abounds in riches, he abounds also in carnal vices [in the Latin the clauses rhyme: *libitum … illicitum*, *divitiis … vitiis*]. Therefore it is added: [[5:5|You have feasted upon earth|Epulati estis super terram]], that is, you have fed yourselves daintily and gluttonously, [[5:5|and in riotousness you have nourished your hearts|et in luxuriis enutristis corda vestra]] [*luxuriis*, which the Douay-Rheims renders "riotousness", means also lust, and Denis takes it so], that is, consenting to the sensitive appetite, you have satisfied the carnal desires of your heart, living incontinently without a bridle. Such are those who live most shamefully not only from passion or weakness, but of set purpose and from a vicious habit; who, as the Philosopher [that is, Aristotle] testifies, are incomparably viler and worse than the brutes. In the person of such men Solomon says in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 2:10|I withheld not my heart from enjoying every pleasure|Non prohibui cor meum, quin frueretur omni voluptate]]. To these will happen what we read in the Gospel of the rich glutton, to whom, set in the fire of hell, one drop of water was denied; and what the heavenly Judge says in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 18:7|As much as she hath glorified herself and lived in delicacies, so much torment and sorrow|Quantum glorificavit se, et in deliciis fuit, tantum date ei tormentum et luctum]].

paras.t: Horum carnalium jam innumerabiles sunt imitatores. Quibus in Evangelio ait Salvator: Væ vobis divitibus qui habetis consolationem vestram; væ vobis qui saturati estis. Qui et per Prophetam Amos loquitur: Væ qui dormitis in lectis eburneis, et lascivitis in stratis vestris. Unde et Judas asserit: Hi sunt in epulis suis convivantes, sine timore, semetipsos pascentes. Contra quod loquitur Paulus: Non in comessationibus et ebrietatibus, non in cubilibus et impudicitiis.
paras.en: Of these carnal men there are now innumerable imitators. To them the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Luke 6:24|woe to you that are rich: for you have your consolation|Væ vobis divitibus qui habetis consolationem vestram]]; [[Luke 6:25|Woe to you that are filled|væ vobis qui saturati estis]]. He speaks also through the prophet Amos: Woe to you [[Amos 6:4|that sleep upon beds of ivory, and are wanton on your couches|qui dormitis in lectis eburneis, et lascivitis in stratis vestris]]. Hence Jude too declares: [[Jude 1:12|These are|Hi sunt]] [[Jude 1:12|in their banquets, feasting together without fear, feeding themselves|in epulis suis convivantes, sine timore, semetipsos pascentes]]. Against this Paul says: [[Rom 13:13|not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and impurities|Non in comessationibus et ebrietatibus, non in cubilibus et impudicitiis]].

paras.t: Denique congruo ordine præmisit Apostolus, Epulati estis; protinusque subjunxit, Et in luxuriis enutristis corda vestra: quoniam gulam sequi solet luxuria, præbetque ei incentivum, dicente Hieronymo: Venter æstuans vino, cito spumat libidinem. Ideo testatur Scriptura: Qui amat vinum et pinguia, non erit sapiens, sed lascivus.
paras.en: Then too, in fitting order the Apostle put first, [[5:5|You have feasted|Epulati estis]], and straightway added, [[5:5|and in riotousness you have nourished your hearts|Et in luxuriis enutristis corda vestra]]: because lust usually follows gluttony, which gives it its incentive, as Jerome says: The belly boiling with wine soon foams out in lust. Therefore Scripture testifies: [[Prov 21:17|he that loveth wine, and fat things|Qui amat vinum et pinguia]], shall not be wise, but wanton [the Douay-Rheims has "shall not be rich"; "shall not be wise" seems to come from Prov 20:1, "whosoever is delighted therewith, shall not be wise"].

paras.t: Quia et Judæi ex suis carnalitatibus et ambitionibus moti fuerunt ad Christi invidiam, deinde ad ejus occisionem (juxta illud Sapientiæ: Dixerunt impii: Circumveniamus justum, quoniam contrarius est operibus nostris; promittit se scientiam Dei habere, et Filium Dei se nominat; morte turpissima condemnemus eum); hinc subditur: In die occisionis, id est in die Parasceves, adduxistis ad tribunal Pilati, et occidistis, id est, occidi procurastis, justum, videlicet Christum, qui est Sanctus Sanctorum: qui antonomastice Justus vocatur, quia secundum quod Deus, est essentialiter sanctus et justus; atque ut homo, omnibus justior fuit per concreatam sibi justitiam, qua tota suæ humanitatis capacitas fuit repleta. De quo in Actibus Stephanus ait: Patres vestri occiderunt eos qui de adventu Justi annuntiaverunt, cujus vos nunc proditores et homicidæ fuistis. Et non restitit vobis, sed ut ab Isaia est prædictum, sicut ovis ad occisionem ductus est, et tanquam agnus coram tondente se obmutuit. De istis Christus ante suam passionem locutus est apud Joannem: Quum exaltaveritis Filium hominis, tunc scietis quia ego sum, […], sicut in Actibus Apostolorum probatur, multa turba sacerdotum et Pharisæorum crediderunt in Christum : qui tamen ejus occisionem specialiter procurasse leguntur.
paras.en: Since the Jews too were moved by their carnal desires and ambitions to envy of Christ, and then to his killing (according to that of Wisdom: The wicked said: [[Wis 2:12|Let us, therefore, lie in wait for the just|Circumveniamus justum]], because [[Wis 2:12|he is contrary to our doings|contrarius est operibus nostris]]; [[Wis 2:13|He boasteth that he hath the knowledge of God, and calleth himself the son of God|promittit se scientiam Dei habere, et Filium Dei se nominat]]; [[Wis 2:20|Let us condemn him to a most shameful death|morte turpissima condemnemus eum]]), it is added: [[5:5|in the day of slaughter|In die occisionis]], that is, on the day of the Parasceve [that is, Good Friday, the day of preparation], [[5:6|You have condemned|adduxistis]] [Denis reads *adduxistis*, "you have brought", for the Vulgate's *addixistis*, "you have condemned"] him before the tribunal of Pilate, [[5:6|and put to death|et occidistis]], that is, you procured his death, [[5:6|the Just One|justum]], namely Christ, who is the Holy of Holies: who by antonomasia [that is, by way of eminence, the common name used as his own] is called the Just One, because as God he is essentially holy and just, and as man he was more just than all, through the justice created together with him, with which the whole capacity of his humanity was filled. Of him Stephen says in the Acts: [[Acts 7:52|your fathers|Patres vestri]] [[Acts 7:52|have slain them who foretold of the coming of the Just One|occiderunt eos qui de adventu Justi annuntiaverunt]]: [[Acts 7:52|of whom you have been now the betrayers and murderers|cujus vos nunc proditores et homicidæ fuistis]]. [[5:6|And he resisted you not|Et non restitit vobis]], but, as was foretold by Isaias, [[Is 53:7|he shall be led as a sheep to the slaughter|sicut ovis ad occisionem ductus est]], [[Is 53:7|and shall be dumb as a lamb before his shearer|et tanquam agnus coram tondente se obmutuit]] [Denis gives the prophecy in the past: "he was led … he was dumb"]. Of these men Christ spoke before his passion, in John: [[John 8:28|When you shall have lifted up, the Son of man|Quum exaltaveritis Filium hominis]], [[John 8:28|then shall you know that I am he|tunc scietis quia ego sum]], […], as is shown in the Acts of the Apostles, [[Acts 6:7|A great multitude also of the priests|multa turba sacerdotum]] and of the Pharisees believed in Christ [Acts 6:7 names the priests; believing Pharisees appear at Acts 15:5], who yet are read to have procured his death in particular.

paras.t: Quidam exponunt hunc locum de justis communiter, intelligendo per justum, justos pluraliter, ut ponatur singulare pro plurali. Nam in primitivæ Ecclesiæ exordio, justi ab impiis passim ad judicia trahebantur, et absque sua renisione occidebantur. Juxta quem modum Isaias ait : Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet; et viri misericordiæ tolluntur, et non est qui intelligat.
paras.en: Some expound this place of the just in general, understanding by *the just one* the just in the plural, so that the singular is put for the plural. For at the beginning of the primitive Church the just were everywhere dragged before the courts by the wicked, and were slain without resisting. In this manner Isaias says: [[Is 57:1|The just perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart|Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet]]; [[Is 57:1|and men of mercy are taken away|et viri misericordiæ tolluntur]], [[Is 57:1|because there is none that understandeth|et non est qui intelligat]].

paras.t: Consequenter Apostolus vertit sermonem ad bonorum consolationem. Patientes ergo estote, fratres. Potest tamen istud ad præfatos divites jam conversos referri, ut sit sensus : Quoniam ante conversionem vestram ad Christum, tot scelera commisistis, ideo quidquid adversitatis vobis nunc accidit, patientissime ferre debetis : siquidem culpæ debetur pœna. Et Deus in hac vita per reprobos purgat electos, quemadmodum per Isaiam contestatur : Væ Assur, virga furoris mei et baculus ipse est. Itaque, Patientes estote usque ad adventum Domini, id est usque ad horam judicii vestri particularis, statim post mortem, vel universalis judicii, quando justa retributio fiet. Nam et Sanctis qui sub ara Dei clamabant, Usquequo, Domine, non vindicas sanguinem nostrum de his qui habitant super terram? responsum est, ut requiescant tempus adhuc modicum, donec impleatur numerus conservorum eorum et fratrum, qui interficiendi sunt sicut et ipsi.
paras.en: Next the Apostle turns his discourse to the consolation of the good. [[5:7|Be patient therefore, brethren|Patientes ergo estote, fratres]]. This may, however, be referred to the rich already spoken of, now converted, so that the sense is: Since before your conversion to Christ you committed so many crimes, you ought therefore to bear most patiently whatever adversity now befalls you; for punishment is due to guilt. And God in this life purges the elect through the reprobate, as he declares through Isaias: [[Is 10:5|Woe to the Assyrian, he is the rod and the staff of my anger|Væ Assur, virga furoris mei et baculus ipse est]]. Therefore, [[5:7|Be patient|Patientes estote]] [[5:7|until the coming of the Lord|usque ad adventum Domini]], that is, until the hour of your particular judgment, straight after death, or of the general judgment, when just retribution will be made. For to the Saints too who cried beneath the altar of God, [[Apoc 6:10|How long, O Lord|Usquequo, Domine]], [[Apoc 6:10|dost thou not judge and revenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?|non vindicas sanguinem nostrum de his qui habitant super terram]] it was answered [[Apoc 6:11|that they should rest for a little time|ut requiescant tempus adhuc modicum]], [[Apoc 6:11|till their fellow servants and their brethren, who are to be slain even as they|donec impleatur numerus conservorum eorum et fratrum, qui interficiendi sunt sicut et ipsi]].

paras.t: Insuper terreno exemplo inducit eos ad patientiam istam. Ecce agricola expectat pretiosum fructum terræ, patienter ferens dilationem fructuum sui laboris, donec accipiat temporaneum, id est primi temporis fructum, et serotinum, id est ultimi temporis terræ nascentia. Terra quippe promissionis (ut fertur, et de qua nunc loquitur) bis in anno fructificat, videlicet in Aprili atque Septembri. Sic Sancti accipiunt fructum temporaneum. Statim quippe post corporis resolutionem, eorum animæ coronantur in cœlis, et fructum serotinum sortientur in die judicii, in corporum suorum glorificatione. Quum ergo fructus æternæ salutis sit omni fructu terreno incomparabiliter dulcior, præstantior, jucundior, plenior, diuturnior, patientissime ferre debemus omnem præsentis vitæ afflictionem, propter æternam remunerationem. Nec enim condignæ sunt passiones hujus temporis ad gloriam illam.
paras.en: Moreover, he leads them to this patience by an earthly example. [[5:7|Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth|Ecce agricola expectat pretiosum fructum terræ]], [[5:7|patiently bearing|patienter ferens]] the delay of the fruits of his labour, [[5:7|till he receive the early|donec accipiat temporaneum]], that is, the fruit of the first season, [[5:7|and latter rain|et serotinum]], that is, the produce of the earth of the last season [the Douay-Rheims supplies "rain"; Denis takes *temporaneum* and *serotinum* of the early and the late crop]. For the land of promise (as is reported, and of it he is now speaking) bears fruit twice a year, namely in April and in September. So the Saints receive the early fruit: for straight after the dissolution of the body their souls are crowned in heaven; and they will obtain the late fruit on the day of judgment, in the glorification of their bodies. Since, then, the fruit of eternal salvation is incomparably sweeter, more excellent, more delightful, fuller and more lasting than any earthly fruit, we ought most patiently to bear every affliction of the present life for the sake of the eternal reward. For [[Rom 8:18|the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory|Nec enim condignæ sunt passiones hujus temporis ad gloriam illam]].

paras.t: Hinc subditur : Patientes estote et vos, et confirmate corda vestra, id est, virtuosis operibus roborate, et per futuræ beatitudinis fiduciam, per divinæ justitiæ contemplationem, per considerationem æternalis supplicii reproborum, per quotidianum profectum virtutum, per fortitudinem mentis, constabilite, atque in Deo defigite ac firmate animas vestras : juxta illud ad Ephesios : Confortamini in Domino, et in potentia virtutis ejus ; induite armaturam Dei, ut possitis stare adversus insidias diaboli. Unde de Josue loquebatur Dominus : Confortare et esto robustus valde, ut custodias omnem legem. Quia adventus Domini appropinquabit : imo indesinenter appropinquat. Propter quod in Apocalypsi ait : Ecce venio cito, et merces mea mecum est, dare unicuique juxta opera sua. Habacuc quoque propheta inducit : Apparebit in finem, et non mentietur; si moram fecerit, exspecta eum, quia veniens veniet, et non tardabit. Porro Deus venire dicitur in morte singulorum, per judicii exhibitionem et retributionem mercedis. Unde apud Marcum legitur : Vigilate (nescitis enim quando Dominus veniat, sero, an media nocte, an galli cantu, an mane), ne quum venerit repente, inveniat vos dormientes.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[5:8|Be you therefore also patient|Patientes estote et vos]] [[5:8|and strengthen your hearts|et confirmate corda vestra]], that is, fortify them with virtuous works; and by confidence in the beatitude to come, by contemplation of the divine justice, by consideration of the eternal punishment of the reprobate, by daily progress in the virtues, by fortitude of mind, make your souls steadfast, and fix and settle them in God; according to that to the Ephesians: [[Eph 6:10|be strengthened in the Lord and in the might of his power|Confortamini in Domino, et in potentia virtutis ejus]]; [[Eph 6:11|Put you on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil|induite armaturam Dei, ut possitis stare adversus insidias diaboli]]. Hence the Lord spoke thus of Josue: [[Jos 1:7|Take courage therefore, and be very valiant|Confortare et esto robustus valde]], [[Jos 1:7|that thou mayst observe and do all the law|ut custodias omnem legem]]. [[5:8|for the coming of the Lord is at hand|Quia adventus Domini appropinquabit]] [Denis reads *appropinquabit*, "will draw near"]: nay, it draws near unceasingly. Wherefore he says in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 22:12|Behold, I come quickly: and my reward is with me, to render to every, man according to his works|Ecce venio cito, et merces mea mecum est, dare unicuique juxta opera sua]]. The prophet Habacuc too brings in: [[Hab 2:3|it shall appear at the end, and shall not lie: if it make any delay, wait for it: for it shall surely come, and it shall not be slack|Apparebit in finem, et non mentietur; si moram fecerit, exspecta eum, quia veniens veniet, et non tardabit]]. Now God is said to come in the death of each one, by the holding of judgment and the paying of the reward. Hence we read in Mark: [[Mark 13:35|Watch ye therefore (for you know not when the lord of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cock crowing, or in the morning|Vigilate (nescitis enim quando Dominus veniat, sero, an media nocte, an galli cantu, an mane]]), [[Mark 13:36|Lest coming on a sudden, he find you sleeping|ne quum venerit repente, inveniat vos dormientes]].

paras.t: Nolite ingemiscere, fratres, in alterutrum, id est, unus ex zelo amaro aut displicentia passionata contra alium nullatenus ingemiscat ; sed alter alterius onera portate, et invicem caritative ac dulciter supportate. Vel, Nolite in alterutrum ingemiscere, id est mutuo gemere et dolere propter adversa quæ sustinetis, quasi injustus sit Deus, qui fidelibus tot adversa largitur, impios vero in hoc sæculo prosperari permittit. Imo unus alium ad patientiam provocet, et consoletur in Domino, quemadmodum ad Hebræos scribitur : Adhortamini vosmetipsos per singulos dies, ut non obduretur quis ex vobis fallacia peccati ; et alibi, Consideremus invicem in provocatione caritatis et bonorum operum. Ita fecerunt septem fratres Machabæi cum matre, qui se mutuo ad martyrium hortabantur, prout secundo Machabæorum plenius continetur. Conformiter et nos debemus nos invicem animare, accendere, roborare, tanquam ejusdem regis commilitones, ejusdem viæ ambulatores, eisdem hostibus circumvallati, et ad eamdem patriam gradientes, quemadmodum ad Hebræos monet Apostolus : Deponentes omne peccatum, per patientiam curramus ad propositum nobis certamen, adspicientes in Jesum, qui proposito sibi gaudio, sustinuit crucem. Recogitate eum qui talem sustinuit adversus semetipsum a peccatoribus contradictionem, ut non fatigemini animis vestris. Nempe ut ait Gregorius : Nihil est quod non æquanimiter toleretur, si Christi passio ad memoriam revocetur.
paras.en: [[5:9|Grudge not, brethren, one against another|Nolite ingemiscere, fratres, in alterutrum]], that is, let no one by any means groan against another out of bitter zeal or passionate displeasure; but [[Gal 6:2|Bear ye one another's burdens|alter alterius onera portate]], and bear with one another charitably and gently. Or, [[5:9|Grudge not, brethren, one against another|Nolite in alterutrum ingemiscere]], that is, do not groan and grieve among yourselves over the adversities you endure, as though God were unjust, who bestows so many adversities on the faithful but allows the wicked to prosper in this world. Rather, let one stir up another to patience and comfort him in the Lord, as is written to the Hebrews: [[Heb 3:13|exhort one another every day|Adhortamini vosmetipsos per singulos dies]], [[Heb 3:13|that none of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin|ut non obduretur quis ex vobis fallacia peccati]] [the margin gives Hebr. x, 11; the words are Heb 3:13]; and elsewhere: [[Heb 10:24|let us consider one another, to provoke unto charity and to good works|Consideremus invicem in provocatione caritatis et bonorum operum]]. So did the seven Machabee brothers with their mother, who exhorted one another to martyrdom, as is related more fully in the second book of Machabees[[2 Mach 7:1||]] [the margin gives only II Machab.; the story is in chapter 7]. In like manner we too ought to rouse, kindle and strengthen one another, as fellow soldiers of the same king, travellers on the same road, beset by the same enemies, and journeying to the same fatherland; as the Apostle admonishes in Hebrews: [[Heb 12:1|laying aside|Deponentes]] every [[Heb 12:1|sin|omne peccatum]], [[Heb 12:1|let us run by patience to the fight proposed to us|per patientiam curramus ad propositum nobis certamen]], [[Heb 12:2|Looking on Jesus|adspicientes in Jesum]], [[Heb 12:2|who, having joy set before him, endured the cross|qui proposito sibi gaudio, sustinuit crucem]]. [[Heb 12:3|think diligently upon him that endured such opposition from sinners against himself that you be not wearied|Recogitate eum qui talem sustinuit adversus semetipsum a peccatoribus contradictionem, ut non fatigemini]] [[Heb 12:3|in your minds|animis vestris]] [the margin gives Hebr. xi, 1–3; the words are Heb 12:1–3]. Indeed, as Gregory says: There is nothing that may not be borne with equanimity, if the passion of Christ is called to mind.

paras.t: Nolite igitur tam infideliter et inique in alterutrum ingemiscere, ut non judicemini judicio reprobationis, id est, ne condemnemini. De quo judicio ait Salvator : Qui verbum meum audit, et credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam æternam, et in judicium non venit. Apostolus quoque : Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur. Ecce judex ante januam adsistit, id est, proximus adest, et adjuvare, judicare et remunerare paratus est. Unde in Apocalypsi loquitur : Ego sto ad ostium et pulso.
paras.en: [[5:9|Grudge not|Nolite]], then, so faithlessly and wickedly [[5:9|one against another|in alterutrum ingemiscere]], [[5:9|that you may not be judged|ut non judicemini]] with the judgment of reprobation, that is, that you be not condemned. Of this judgment the Saviour says: [[John 5:24|he who heareth my word and believeth him that sent me hath life everlasting: and cometh not into judgment|Qui verbum meum audit, et credit ei qui misit me, habet vitam æternam, et in judicium non venit]]. The Apostle also: [[1 Cor 11:31|if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged|Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur]]. [[5:9|Behold the judge standeth before the door|Ecce judex ante januam adsistit]], that is, he is close at hand, and ready to help, to judge and to reward. Hence he says in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:20|I stand at the gate and knock|Ego sto ad ostium et pulso]].

paras.t: Verumtamen, quia sancti patres non solum verbo, sed et exemplo nos docuerunt, Jacobus exemplo illorum hortatur nos ad patientiam indesinentem. Exemplum accipite, fratres, exitus mali, id est mortis, quæ est malum pœnale, et longanimitatis, id est longæ dilationis seu exspectationis cœlestis retributionis, laboris, qui in exercitiis virtuosis solet consistere (propter quod ait vir sanctus : Propter verba labiorum tuorum ego custodivi vias duras ; atque Apostolus, Labora, inquit, sicut bonus miles Christi Jesu), et patientiæ, id est æquanimis tolerantiæ in adversis, Prophetas, qui locuti sunt in nomine Domini, id est, ex divino instinctu vere prophetaverunt hominibus. Qui utique Prophetæ, quamvis essent viri tam sancti et præelecti, nihilo minus exitum malum, id est violentam per martyrium mortem, multiplicemque sustinuerunt laborem : et erant valde patientes atque longanimes, ut patet de Abraham, Noe, David, Isaia, Jeremia, ac aliis. Unde ad Hebræos ait Apostolus : Juxta fidem defuncti sunt omnes isti, non acceptis repromissionibus, sed a longe eas adspicientes et salutantes, et confitentes quia hospites et peregrini sunt super terram. Judith quoque asseruit : Sic Isaac, sic Jacob, Moyses, et omnes qui Deo placuerunt, per multas tribulationes transierunt fideles.
paras.en: But since the holy fathers taught us not only by word but also by example, James exhorts us by their example to unceasing patience. [[5:10|Take, my brethren, for example of suffering evil|Exemplum accipite, fratres, exitus mali]] [literally "of an evil end"], that is, of death, which is a penal evil, and of long-suffering [*et longanimitatis*, words of Denis's text not in the Douay-Rheims], that is, of long delay or waiting for the heavenly reward; [[5:10|of labour|laboris]], which is wont to consist in virtuous exercises (wherefore the holy man says: [[Ps 16:4|for the sake of the words of thy lips, I have kept hard ways|Propter verba labiorum tuorum ego custodivi vias duras]]; and the Apostle: [[2 Tim 2:3|Labour|Labora]], he says, [[2 Tim 2:3|as a good soldier of Christ Jesus|sicut bonus miles Christi Jesu]]); [[5:10|and patience|et patientiæ]], that is, of even-minded endurance in adversity, [[5:10|the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord|Prophetas, qui locuti sunt in nomine Domini]], that is, who truly prophesied to men by divine inspiration. These Prophets, though they were men so holy and chosen, nonetheless underwent an evil end, that is, a violent death by martyrdom, and manifold labour; and they were very patient and long-suffering, as is plain of Abraham, Noe, David, Isaias, Jeremias and others. Hence the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 11:13|All these died according to faith, not having received the promises but beholding them afar off and saluting them and confessing that they are pilgrims and strangers on the earth|Juxta fidem defuncti sunt omnes isti, non acceptis repromissionibus, sed a longe eas adspicientes et salutantes, et confitentes quia hospites et peregrini sunt super terram]]. Judith too declared: [[Jdt 8:23|So Isaac, so Jacob, so Moses, and all that have pleased God, passed through many tribulations, remaining faithful|Sic Isaac, sic Jacob, Moyses, et omnes qui Deo placuerunt, per multas tribulationes transierunt fideles]].

paras.t: Ecce beatificamus eos qui sustinuerunt adversa patienter : sicut etiam asserit Christus, Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum. De quibus scriptum est : Sapientiam Sanctorum narrant populi, et laudem eorum nuntiat Ecclesia ; corpora eorum in pace sepulta sunt, et nomina eorum vivent in generationem et generationem ; in paucis vexati, in multis bene disponentur. Et Job ait : Beatus homo qui corripitur a Domino.
paras.en: [[5:11|Behold, we account them blessed who have endured|Ecce beatificamus eos qui sustinuerunt]] adversities patiently: as Christ also declares, [[Matt 5:10|Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.|Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum]] Of whom it is written: [[Ecclus 44:15|Let the people shew forth their wisdom, and the church declare their praise|Sapientiam Sanctorum narrant populi, et laudem eorum nuntiat Ecclesia]]; [[Ecclus 44:14|Their bodies are buried in peace, and their name liveth unto generation and generation|corpora eorum in pace sepulta sunt, et nomina eorum vivent in generationem et generationem]]; [[Wis 3:5|Afflicted in few things, in many they shall be well rewarded|in paucis vexati, in multis bene disponentur]] [the passage joins Ecclus 44:15 and 44:14 with Wis 3:5]. And Job says: [[Job 5:17|Blessed is the man whom God correcteth|Beatus homo qui corripitur a Domino]].

paras.t: Sufferentiam Job audistis, id est admirabilem patientiam ejus : qui quamvis omnium sit exemplar virtutum, præsertim tamen patientiæ forma est. Unde de Tobia habetur : Hanc tentationem permisit Dominus evenire ei (puta Tobiæ), ut posteris daretur exemplum patientiæ ejus, sicut et sancti Job. Et finem Domini vidistis, id est, quam gratiose Deus finaliter egit cum Job, non solum post vitam præsentem, sed etiam in sæculo isto eum remunerando, vidistis per fidem, id est, ex sacra libri ejus historia credidistis. De qua visione Apostolus: Videmus, inquit, nunc per speculum in ænigmate. Verumtamen quod dictum est, Finem Domini vidistis, communiter de Christo exponitur, ut sit sensus: Finem Domini, id est mortem Christi in cruce, vidistis, quia adstantes suæ cruci fuistis tunc adhuc increduli. Quoniam misericors est Dominus in sua natura, id est naturaliter bonus et pius: non tamen compassionis affectum in deitatis suæ natura habens, imo quoad hoc, misericors appellatur, quantum ad similitudinem effectus, non quoad veritatem affectus: et miserator in effectu. Hoc Jacobus dicit: primo, quia electis suis Deus in tribulationibus misericordissime adfuit, eos quoque eripuit, et gloriosissime coronavit; secundo, quoniam summa misericordia Dei fuit, quod proprium Filium suum pro nostra pati voluit salute.
paras.en: [[5:11|You have heard of the patience of Job|Sufferentiam Job audistis]], that is, his wonderful patience: for though he is a model of all the virtues, he is above all the pattern of patience. Hence it is said of Tobias: [[Tob 2:12|this trial the Lord therefore permitted to happen to him|Hanc tentationem permisit Dominus evenire ei]] (that is, to Tobias), [[Tob 2:12|that an example might be given to posterity of his patience, as also of holy Job|ut posteris daretur exemplum patientiæ ejus, sicut et sancti Job]]. [[5:11|And you have seen the end of the Lord|Et finem Domini vidistis]], that is, how graciously God dealt with Job in the end, rewarding him not only after the present life but in this world too[[Job 42:10||]]; you have seen it by faith, that is, you have believed it from the sacred history of his book. Of this seeing the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 13:12|We see|Videmus]], he says, [[1 Cor 13:12|now through a glass in a dark manner|nunc per speculum in ænigmate]]. Yet the words [[5:11|you have seen the end of the Lord|Finem Domini vidistis]] are commonly expounded of Christ, so that the sense is: [[5:11|the end of the Lord|Finem Domini]], that is, the death of Christ on the cross, [[5:11|you have seen|vidistis]], because you stood by his cross, being then still unbelievers. [[5:11|that the Lord is merciful|Quoniam misericors est Dominus]] in his nature, that is, naturally good and kind: not that he has the affection of compassion in the nature of his Godhead; rather, in this respect he is called merciful by a likeness of the effect, not by the reality of the affection [that is, God does what the merciful do, without the passion of pity]; [[5:11|and compassionate|et miserator]] in effect. James says this, first, because God stood by his elect most mercifully in their tribulations, delivered them too, and most gloriously crowned them; secondly, because it was the supreme mercy of God that he willed his own Son to suffer for our salvation.

paras.t: Ante omnia autem, fratres mei, nolite jurare, neque per cœlum, neque per terram, neque aliud quodcumque juramentum. Sit autem sermo vester: Est, est; Non, non: ut non sub judicio decidatis. His consonat quod in Matthæo loquitur Christus: Ego dico vobis, non jurare omnino, neque per cœlum, neque per terram. Sit autem sermo vester: Est, est; Non, non.
paras.en: [[5:12|But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, nor by the earth, nor by any other oath|Ante omnia autem, fratres mei, nolite jurare, neque per cœlum, neque per terram, neque aliud quodcumque juramentum]]. [[5:12|But let your speech be: Yea, Yea: No, No|Sit autem sermo vester: Est, est; Non, non]]: [[5:12|that you fall not under judgment|ut non sub judicio decidatis]]. With this agrees what Christ says in Matthew: [[Matt 5:34|I say to you not to swear at all, neither by heaven|Ego dico vobis, non jurare omnino, neque per cœlum]], [[Matt 5:35|Nor by the earth|neque per terram]]. [[Matt 5:37|But let your speech be yea, yea: no, no|Sit autem sermo vester: Est, est; Non, non]].

paras.t: Sed quomodo intelligenda sunt ista? quum in Deuteronomio dicatur, Dominum Deum timebis, et per nomen ejus jurabis; et in Psalmo, Laudabuntur omnes qui jurant in eo; itemque, Juravi et statui custodire judicia justitiæ tuæ; secundo quoque Paralipomenon, In omni corde suo juraverunt Domino, et invenerunt eum. Elias quoque et Eliseus in libris Regum jurasse leguntur, dicendo: Vivit Dominus, in cujus conspectu sto hodie; et Paulus in suis epistolis, Testis (inquiens) est mihi Deus. — Sed omnium horum solutio atque concordia patent ex eo quod scriptum est in Exodo: Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum: non enim habebit insontem Dominus eum qui assumpserit nomen Domini Dei sui frustra. Christus igitur et ejus apostolus Jacobus non absolute prohibuerunt jurationem, sed jurationem indiscretam, injustam et falsam, et ne assuescamus jurare; et rursus, quia frequentatio jurandi periculosa est, quum perjurationi approximet.
paras.en: But how are these words to be understood, since it is said in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 6:13|Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God|Dominum Deum timebis]], [[Deut 6:13|and thou shalt swear by his name|et per nomen ejus jurabis]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 62:12|all they shall be praised that swear by him|Laudabuntur omnes qui jurant in eo]]; and again: [[Ps 118:106|I have sworn and am determined to keep the judgments of thy justice|Juravi et statui custodire judicia justitiæ tuæ]]; and in the second book of Paralipomenon: [[2 Par 15:15|with all their heart they swore|In omni corde suo juraverunt]] to the Lord, [[2 Par 15:15|and they found him|et invenerunt eum]]? Elias too and Eliseus are read in the books of Kings to have sworn, saying: [[3 Kings 17:1|As the Lord liveth|Vivit Dominus]], [[4 Kings 3:14|in whose sight I stand|in cujus conspectu sto]] this day [*this day* is from Elias's oath at 3 Kings 18:15]; and Paul in his epistles, saying: [[Rom 1:9|God is my witness|Testis (inquiens) est mihi Deus]][[Phil 1:8||]]. — But the solution and reconciliation of all these is plain from what is written in Exodus: [[Ex 20:7|Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain|Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum]]: [[Ex 20:7|for the Lord will not hold him guiltless that shall take the name of the Lord his God in vain|non enim habebit insontem Dominus eum qui assumpserit nomen Domini Dei sui frustra]]. Christ, therefore, and his apostle James did not forbid swearing absolutely, but swearing that is indiscreet, unjust and false; and they forbade it lest we grow used to swearing, and again because frequent swearing is dangerous, since it comes close to perjury.

paras.t: Præterea super illud Jeremiæ, Jurabis, Vivit Dominus, in veritate et judicio et justitia, scribit Hieronymus, quod tres sunt comites juramenti, videlicet veritas, judicium seu discretio, et justitia, id est justa et rationabilis causa: quia hæc tria requiruntur ad hoc ut juramentum sit licitum; et quodcumque eorum defuerit, erit illicitum juramentum. Si enim veritas desit, est falsa juratio; si discretio, est temeraria et incauta. Si desit justitia, juratio est iniqua, inutilis et levis atque vana, quia non subest ad jurandum rationabilis causa. Per creaturas vero secundum se consideratas, non licet jurare, sed in quantum divina veritas atque potestas relucet in eis. Si itaque ipsa juratio debitis virtutum circumstantiis vestiatur, ut scilicet fiat loco et tempore opportunis, causa rationabili exigente, debito fine, tunc est actus virtutis quæ latria appellatur, per quam cultus Deo impenditur. Nam qui sic jurat, Deum honorat, quoniam præsupponit eum esse infallibilem veritatem, ac omnium rerum habere certissimam cognitionem, providentiamque infallibilem. Qui vero aliter jurat, non excusatur a culpa, quamvis quod jurat sit verum. Cedit namque ad irreverentiam omnipotentis et superdignissimi Dei, eum sine rationabili causa et discretione, in testem veritatis verborum propriorum assumere.
paras.en: Moreover, on that saying of Jeremias, [[Jer 4:2|thou shalt swear: As the Lord liveth, in truth, and in judgment, and in justice|Jurabis, Vivit Dominus, in veritate et judicio et justitia]], Jerome writes that an oath has three companions, namely truth, judgment or discretion, and justice, that is, a just and reasonable cause: for these three are required for an oath to be lawful, and if any one of them is lacking, the oath will be unlawful. For if truth is lacking, it is a false oath; if discretion, it is rash and heedless. If justice is lacking, the oath is wicked, useless, light and vain, because there is no reasonable cause beneath it for swearing. By creatures considered in themselves it is not lawful to swear, but only inasmuch as the divine truth and power shine forth in them. If, then, the oath itself is clothed with the due circumstances of the virtues, that is, if it is made at a fitting place and time, when a reasonable cause requires it, and for a due end, then it is an act of the virtue called latria [that is, the worship due to God alone], by which worship is paid to God. For he who swears thus honours God, since he presupposes that God is infallible truth, and has the most certain knowledge of all things, and an infallible providence. But he who swears otherwise is not excused from fault, even though what he swears is true. For it turns to the irreverence of the almighty and most supremely worthy God to take him, without reasonable cause and discretion, as witness to the truth of one's own words.

paras.t: Quum ergo ita jurare sit contra divinum præceptum, et per consequens ex suo genere peccatum mortale, constat quam enormiter peccent qui consuetudinem habent jurandi, et qui jurant mendose, aut non implent quod juraverint, dummodo juraverint licite. Verumtamen supergravissime peccant, et quasi blasphemi sunt reputandi, qui per membra Christi et intestina ipsius, sceleratissime jurant. Idcirco in Ecclesiastico scribitur: Jurationi non assuescat os tuum; multi enim casus in ea. Vir multum jurans, replebitur iniquitate, et non deficiet de domo illius plaga. Unde quum Jacobus prohibuisset jurare, adjecit: Ut non sub judicio decidatis, id est, ne condemnationis judicium incurratis. Hinc dicit Albertus: Quum jurare non sit aliud quam Deum testem invocare, idcirco: primo, ex parte rei quæ juramento firmatur, requiritur veritas; secundo, ex parte causæ pro qua juratur, debet esse necessitas (juramentum quippe non debet fieri nisi pro justa et legitima causa); tertio, ex parte jurantis debet esse discretionis maturitas: quia ne homo incurrat perjurium, debet magnam cautelam ac maturitatem in jurando servare, ne ex linguæ lubricitate contingat eum aliquando inordinate aut false jurare. Sit igitur omnis homo verax, ad jurandum tardissimus, atque tam verax semper in verbis suis, ut suo simplici verbo quasi juramento credatur: quod sibi exstat salubre, et aliis exemplare.
paras.en: Since, then, to swear in this way is against the divine commandment, and consequently a mortal sin in its kind [that is, by the nature of the act itself], it is clear how grievously they sin who have the habit of swearing, and who swear falsely, or do not fulfil what they have sworn, provided they swore lawfully. Yet those sin most grievously of all, and are to be counted as blasphemers, who most wickedly swear by the members of Christ and by his bowels. Therefore it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 23:9|Let not thy mouth be accustomed to swearing|Jurationi non assuescat os tuum]]: [[Ecclus 23:9|for in it there are many falls|multi enim casus in ea]]. [[Ecclus 23:12|A man that sweareth much, shall be filled with iniquity, and a scourge shall not depart from his house|Vir multum jurans, replebitur iniquitate, et non deficiet de domo illius plaga]]. So when James had forbidden swearing, he added: [[5:12|that you fall not under judgment|Ut non sub judicio decidatis]], that is, lest you incur the judgment of condemnation. Hence Albert says: Since to swear is nothing else than to call God as witness, therefore: first, on the part of the thing confirmed by the oath, truth is required; second, on the part of the cause for which one swears, there must be necessity (for an oath ought not to be made except for a just and lawful cause); third, on the part of the one swearing, there must be the ripeness of discretion: for lest a man fall into perjury, he must keep great caution and deliberation in swearing, so that it may not happen through a slip of the tongue that he sometimes swears inordinately or falsely. Let every man, then, be truthful, most slow to swear, and always so truthful in his words that his simple word is believed as if it were an oath: which is wholesome for himself, and an example to others.

paras.t: Tristatur aliquis vestrum? Oret æquo animo, et psallat. De duplici tristitia loquitur sacra Scriptura, videlicet de inordinata et sæculari tristitia, quæ est immoderata mœstitia de temporali damno, aut corporali incommodo, seu exteriori adversitate. De qua in Ecclesiastico legitur: Tristitiam longe expelle a te; multos enim occidit tristitia, et non est utilitas in ea. In Proverbiis quoque, Sicut tinea vestimento, ita tristitia nocet cordi. Alia est tristitia spiritualis, bona et ordinata, qua homo de propriis aut proximorum dolet peccatis, præsertim de inhonoratione et offensa summi ac sancti Dei; vel de propria imperfectione, aut dilatione felicitatis perpetuæ. De qua Salomon ait: Cor sapientium ubi tristitia; et Psalmista, Tota die contristatus ingrediebar. Atque Apostolus ad Romanos: Tristitia mihi magna est, et dolor continuus cordi meo, videlicet propter excæcationem Judæorum. Et rursus Apostolus utramque tristitiam tangit, dicendo: Quæ secundum Deum est tristitia, pœnitentiam in salutem stabilem operatur; sæculi autem tristitia mortem operatur.
paras.en: [[5:13|Is any of you sad?|Tristatur aliquis vestrum?]] [[5:13|Let him pray|Oret]] with an even mind, and [[5:13|let him sing|psallat]] [Denis reads *Oret æquo animo, et psallat*, "let him pray with an even mind, and sing"; the Vulgate has *oret. Æquo animo est? psallat*, which the Douay-Rheims renders: Let him pray: Is he cheerful in mind? Let him sing]. Sacred Scripture speaks of two kinds of sadness. One is inordinate and worldly sadness, which is immoderate grief over a temporal loss, a bodily hardship or some outward adversity. Of this we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 30:24|drive away sadness far from thee|Tristitiam longe expelle a te]]; [[Ecclus 30:25|For sadness hath killed many, and there is no profit in it|multos enim occidit tristitia, et non est utilitas in ea]]. In Proverbs too: [[Prov 25:20|As a moth doth by a garment|Sicut tinea vestimento]], [[Prov 25:20|so the sadness of a man consumeth the heart|ita tristitia nocet cordi]]. The other is spiritual sadness, good and ordered, by which a man grieves for his own sins or his neighbours', above all for the dishonour and offence done to the most high and holy God; or for his own imperfection, or for the delay of everlasting happiness. Of this Solomon says: [[Eccles 7:5|The heart of the wise is where there is mourning|Cor sapientium ubi tristitia]] [*tristitia*, the same word as "sadness" here]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 37:7|I walked sorrowful all the day long|Tota die contristatus ingrediebar]]. And the Apostle to the Romans: [[Rom 9:2|I have great sadness and continual sorrow in my heart|Tristitia mihi magna est, et dolor continuus cordi meo]], namely because of the blinding of the Jews. And again the Apostle touches on both kinds of sadness, saying: [[2 Cor 7:10|For the sorrow that is according to God worketh penance, steadfast unto salvation: but the sorrow of the world worketh death|Quæ secundum Deum est tristitia, pœnitentiam in salutem stabilem operatur; sæculi autem tristitia mortem operatur]].

paras.t: Qui ergo tristatur tristitia inordinata, oret Deum ut auferatur ab eo; et psallat, quatenus psallendo incipiat spiritualiter delectari, et a prava relevari mæstitia, quæ non solum animæ, sed et corpori præcipue nocet, naturam lædit, et vitam abbreviat, juxta illud in Proverbiis: Spiritus tristis exsiccat ossa; animus autem gaudens ætatem floridam facit. Porro, qui tristatur bona et virtuosa tristitia, oret Deum, ut conservetur in ea; et psallat ac spiritualiter jucundetur ex consideratione Dei, cœlestisque præmii et beneficiorum ac operum Christi: quia et illa tristitia, quamvis sit bona, est tamen quandoque interrumpenda per gaudium spirituale, ne homo se nimis dejiciat aut affligat. — Quidam hoc loco per tristitiam intelligunt acediam, quæ est torpor et mœror de exercitio virtuoso, seu de Dei obsequio. Idcirco orare Deum debet, qui acediæ vitio tangitur, ut ab ea protinus liberetur, et fervens alacerque reddatur.
