paras.en: So whoever is sad with an inordinate sadness, let him pray God that it be taken from him; and let him sing, so that by singing he may begin to delight in spiritual things and be lifted out of that evil grief, which harms not only the soul but the body above all: it injures nature and shortens life, according to that saying in Proverbs: [[Prov 17:22|a sorrowful spirit drieth up the bones|Spiritus tristis exsiccat ossa]]; [[Prov 17:22|A joyful mind maketh age flourishing|animus autem gaudens ætatem floridam facit]]. But whoever is sad with a good and virtuous sadness, let him pray God that he be kept in it; and let him sing and rejoice spiritually in the thought of God, of the heavenly reward, and of the benefits and works of Christ: for that sadness too, good though it is, must at times be broken off by spiritual joy, lest a man cast himself down or afflict himself too much. — Some understand sadness in this place as acedia [that is, spiritual sloth], which is torpor and gloom about the practice of virtue, or about the service of God. Therefore whoever is touched by the vice of acedia ought to pray God to be freed from it at once, and to be made fervent and eager.

paras.t: Itaque oratio et psalmodia remedia sunt contra tristitiam et acediam. Est enim admirabilis virtus psalmorum et orationum, et ex sua natura habent mentem orantis ac psallentis dulcedine quadam perfundere. Nam in psalmis et orationibus homo attendit Dei omnipotentiam, pietatem, liberalitatem et perfectionem, propriam quoque imperfectionem, et Christi mysteria, quorum consideratio est jucunda, in quantum veritas naturaliter est delectans. Per gratiam vero hæc dulcius sapiunt. Angeli etiam sancti orantibus psallentibusque adsistunt, et eos exhilarant. Hinc ait Psalmista: Exsultabunt labia mea cum cantavero tibi. Et Gregorius: Dum vox psalmodiæ per intentionem cordis agitur, tunc aut prophetica mysteria revelantur, aut compunctionis gratia inspiratur. — Itaque, qui tristatur, non se ad carnales vilesque consolationes effundat, non murmuret, nec loquacitatibus vacet, nec pusillanimis efficiatur, neque a bonis cesset operibus; sed faciat quod est in se, et oret ac psallat, quamvis in hoc spiritualem non experiatur saporem. Imo Deum pro spirituali consolatione stabiliter deprecetur, et eam longanimiter præstoletur, sicque eam citius obtinebit, secundum quod apud Tobiam dicitur Deo: Non delectaris in perditionibus nostris, quia post tempestatem tranquillum facis, et post fletum exsultationem infundis.
paras.en: Prayer and psalmody, then, are remedies against sadness and acedia. For wonderful is the power of psalms and prayers, and by their nature they pour a certain sweetness through the mind of the one who prays and sings. For in psalms and prayers a man attends to God's omnipotence, mercy, generosity and perfection, to his own imperfection as well, and to the mysteries of Christ, the thought of which is pleasant, inasmuch as truth by its nature delights. And through grace these things taste sweeter still. The holy angels too stand by those who pray and sing, and gladden them. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 70:23|My lips shall greatly rejoice, when I shall sing to thee|Exsultabunt labia mea cum cantavero tibi]]. And Gregory: When the voice of psalmody is uttered with the intention of the heart, then either prophetic mysteries are revealed, or the grace of compunction is breathed in. — So let him who is sad not pour himself out on carnal and base consolations, nor murmur, nor give himself to chatter, nor grow faint-hearted, nor cease from good works; but let him do what lies in him, and pray and sing, even though he tastes no spiritual savour in it. Rather let him pray God steadily for spiritual consolation and wait for it with long patience, and so he will obtain it the sooner, according to what is said to God in Tobias: [[Tob 3:22|thou art not delighted in our being lost, because after a storm thou makest a calm, and after tears and weeping thou pourest in joyfulness|Non delectaris in perditionibus nostris, quia post tempestatem tranquillum facis, et post fletum exsultationem infundis]].

paras.t: Consequenter apostolus Jacobus consulit graviter ægrotanti. Infirmatur quis in vobis? id est, si aliquis vestrum graviter infirmatur, ita ut probabiliter æstimetur cito moriturus, inducat presbyteros Ecclesiæ, id est, sacerdotes faciat sibi adduci, si plures sint ibi presbyteri, et convenienter possint habere, ut multorum oratione infirmus copiosius adjuvetur. Sufficit tamen unus sacerdos ad ungendum: imo quamvis plures adducantur et adsint, tamen ab uno fit unctio. Istud autem sacramentum Extremæ unctionis, est exeuntium. Et orent super eum, id est, omnes invocent misericordiam Dei super infirmum, ungentes eum oleo consecrato, ex debita materia confecto: ita tamen quod unus faciat unctionem realiter, et alii suo modo cooperentur. In nomine Domini. Hoc refertur ad ungentes. Unctio enim fieri debet sub certa et congrua forma verborum; et nunc communiter fit cum invocatione nominis Dei seu pietatis divinæ per modum orationis, quum dicitur: Per istam unctionem, et suam piissimam misericordiam, indulgeat tibi Deus quidquid peccasti per visum, etc.
paras.en: Next the apostle James counsels one who is gravely ill. [[5:14|Is any man sick among you?|Infirmatur quis in vobis?]] that is, if any of you is gravely ill, so that he is thought likely to die soon, [[5:14|Let him bring in the priests of the church|inducat presbyteros Ecclesiæ]], that is, let him have priests brought to him, if there are several priests there and they can conveniently be had, so that the sick man may be helped more abundantly by the prayer of many. Yet one priest suffices for the anointing: indeed, although several are brought and are present, the anointing is done by one. And this sacrament of Extreme Unction is the sacrament of those departing this life. [[5:14|and let them pray over him|Et orent super eum]], that is, let them all call down the mercy of God upon the sick man, [[5:14|anointing him with oil|ungentes eum oleo]] that is consecrated and made from the due matter: in such a way, however, that one actually performs the anointing, and the others cooperate in their own way. [[5:14|in the name of the Lord|In nomine Domini]]. This refers to those who anoint. For the anointing must be done under a fixed and fitting form of words; and now it is commonly done with the invocation of the name of God, or of the divine mercy, by way of prayer, when it is said: Through this anointing and his most tender mercy may God pardon thee whatever sin thou hast committed by sight, etc.

paras.t: Et oratio fidei, id est oratio ungentis facta in fide catholica, atque ex fide procedens, salvabit infirmum, id est, ad salutem cooperabitur ei, præsertim virtute sacramenti: quoniam sacramenta evangelicæ legis sunt medicinalia vasa, gratiæ contentiva, et effectiva salutis, quia efficiunt quod designant; et alleviabit eum Dominus a corporis infirmitate, illam tollendo aut minuendo. Et si in peccatis sit, dimittentur ei: quia virtute hujus sacramenti venialia dimittuntur, contra quæ creditur institutum, et etiam cetera de quibus non recordatur.
paras.en: [[5:15|And the prayer of faith|Et oratio fidei]], that is, the prayer of him who anoints, made in the Catholic faith and proceeding from faith, [[5:15|shall save the sick man|salvabit infirmum]], that is, shall cooperate with him towards salvation, above all by the power of the sacrament: for the sacraments of the law of the Gospel are healing vessels, containing grace and bringing about salvation, because they effect what they signify; [[5:15|And the Lord shall raise him up|et alleviabit eum Dominus]] [*alleviabit*, literally "shall lighten" or relieve him] from the infirmity of the body, by taking it away or lessening it. [[5:15|and if he be in sins, they shall be forgiven him|Et si in peccatis sit, dimittentur ei]]: for by the power of this sacrament venial sins are forgiven, against which it is believed to have been instituted, and also the others which the sick man does not remember.

paras.t: Itaque ad sacramentum Extremæ unctionis, quinque de necessitate concurrunt: primum, quod unctionem faciens, sit sacerdos; secundum est intentio ejus; tertium, materia, utpote oleum infirmorum; quartum est forma verborum; quintum, locus inungendi. Potest et sextum addi, quoniam a solis episcopis potest hoc oleum consecrari seu confici. Nec datur sacramentum hoc nisi adultis, qui venialia habere videntur. — Porro effectus hujus sacramenti, est multiplex, utpote duplex sanitas, scilicet: spiritualis, quæ est liberatio a spirituali infirmitate, contracta ex mortalibus venialibusque peccatis, estque infirmitas illa quædam debilitas ad actum virtutis. Hinc dicitur sacramentum hoc institutum contra reliquias peccatorum. Sanat quoque a venialibus quæ invenit in eo qui ungitur. Secunda est sanitas corporalis, quam causat in parte aut toto, si expediat ad salutem, nec obex ponatur. Causat etiam sacramentum hoc quamdam spiritualem lætitiam, et valet ad continuandam devotionem, atque ad celeriorem ingressum in patriam.
paras.en: Thus five things necessarily concur in the sacrament of Extreme Unction: first, that the one who anoints be a priest; the second is his intention; the third, the matter, namely the oil of the sick; the fourth is the form of words; the fifth, the place of anointing. A sixth may be added, since this oil can be consecrated or made only by bishops. Nor is this sacrament given except to adults, who are thought to have venial sins. — The effect of this sacrament, moreover, is manifold, namely a twofold health. The first is spiritual: freedom from the spiritual infirmity contracted from mortal and venial sins, which infirmity is a certain weakness for acts of virtue. Hence this sacrament is said to have been instituted against the remains of sins [that is, the weakness left in the soul after the sins themselves are forgiven]. It also heals from the venial sins it finds in the one anointed. The second is bodily health, which it causes in part or in whole, if this is expedient for salvation and no obstacle is put in the way [that is, by the will of the one receiving it]. This sacrament also causes a certain spiritual gladness, and avails to continue devotion and for a swifter entry into the heavenly fatherland.

paras.t: Et quia ad remissionem peccatorum actualium mortalium, requiritur sacramentalis confessio in facto vel proposito, sine qua non est quis aptus sacramentum Extremæ unctionis suscipere, subditur: Confitemini ergo alterutrum peccata vestra, id est, unus alteri propria peccata confiteatur. Verumtamen, sacramentalis confessio soli facienda est sacerdoti. Tamen in casu necessitatis potest non sacerdoti confessio fieri de quibuscumque peccatis: quæ tamen confessio non est perfecte sacramentalis, estque reiteranda, seu sacerdoti postmodum facienda, si ad hoc detur facultas. Venialium vero confessio potest alterutrum non sacerdotibus fieri, quum non sit de necessitate salutis. Quæ omnia super quartum Sententiarum doctores declarant. Hinc Beda hic scribit: Quotidiana leviaque peccata alterutrum coæqualibus confiteamur; graviorem vero lepram, id est mortalia, sacerdoti pandamus. Nec hoc sic intelligendum est quasi non debeamus venialia sacerdotibus confiteri, sed quia non ita necessarium est ea sacerdotibus confiteri sicut mortalia.
paras.en: And because for the remission of actual mortal sins sacramental confession is required, in deed or in intention [that is, made, or at least purposed where it cannot be made], without which no one is fit to receive the sacrament of Extreme Unction, he adds: [[5:16|Confess therefore your sins one to another|Confitemini ergo alterutrum peccata vestra]], that is, let each confess his own sins to another. Sacramental confession, however, is to be made to a priest alone. Yet in case of necessity confession of any sins whatever may be made to one who is not a priest: but this confession is not perfectly sacramental, and is to be repeated, that is, made afterwards to a priest, if the opportunity is given. Confession of venial sins, though, may be made to one another, to those who are not priests, since it is not necessary for salvation. All of which the doctors explain on the fourth book of the Sentences [of Peter Lombard, which treats the sacraments]. Hence Bede writes here: Let us confess our daily and light sins to one another, to our equals; but the graver leprosy, that is, mortal sins, let us lay open to the priest. Nor is this to be understood as though we ought not to confess venial sins to priests, but because it is not as necessary to confess them to priests as it is mortal sins.

paras.t: Et orate pro invicem ut salvemini. Hoc namque exigit caritas, qua proximorum tenemur desiderare ac procurare salutem quemadmodum propriam. Oratio quippe desiderii est interpres. Hinc Christus orationem quam docuit, in plurali formavit, insinuans ut pro proximis sicut pro nobis ipsis oremus: ita ut interdum eadem oratio pro se aliisque fundatur; interdum vero oret quis, nunc pro se et specialibus indigentiis suis, nunc pro aliis, et præsertim pro communi bono Ecclesiæ, pro reformatione ejus in omnibus, pro parentibus, propinquis, commissis et benefactoribus, pro cunctis fidelibus defunctis, pro vivis ac mortuis, pro universorum salute et infidelium conversione. Qui enim pro omnibus orat, particeps est omnium bonorum quæ fiunt: et bonum quanto communius, tanto divinius perhibetur. Hinc debet unusquisque orationes aliorum humiliter ac ferventer appetere, et eos, ut pro se orent, rogare. Quo enim alios humilius atque ferventius, ut pro nobis orent, rogamus, eo capaciores efficimur fructus orationis illorum. Potissimum tamen hominum devotorum et notabiliter virtuosorum est appetenda oratio.
paras.en: [[5:16|and pray one for another, that you may be saved|Et orate pro invicem ut salvemini]]. For charity requires this, by which we are bound to desire and to work for our neighbours' salvation as for our own. For prayer is the interpreter of desire. Hence Christ framed the prayer that he taught in the plural[[Matt 6:9||]], suggesting that we should pray for our neighbours as for ourselves: so that sometimes one and the same prayer is poured out for oneself and for others; and sometimes a man prays now for himself and his own particular needs, now for others, and above all for the common good of the Church, for its reform in all things, for parents, kinsfolk, those in his charge and benefactors, for all the faithful departed, for the living and the dead, for the salvation of all and the conversion of unbelievers. For he who prays for all is a sharer in all the good things that are done: and the more common a good is, the more divine it is held to be. Hence each one ought humbly and fervently to seek the prayers of others, and to ask them to pray for him. For the more humbly and fervently we ask others to pray for us, the more capable we are made of the fruit of their prayer. Above all, however, the prayer of devout and notably virtuous men is to be sought.

paras.t: Propter quod subditur: Multum enim valet deprecatio justi assidua. Justus namque est Dei amicus, ejusque filius adoptivus, et ei consimilis atque amabilis. Siquidem justus Dominus, et justitias dilexit. Amicorum autem est eadem velle et nolle. Ideo scriptum est: Oratio justi penetrat cælos; itemque, Voluntatem timentium se faciet, etc. Et bene ait Apostolus, quod assidua justi oratio valeat multum, seu magni vigoris ac meriti seu præcipuæ exaudibilitatis sit apud Deum: quia una conditio ad orationis exaudibilitatem requisita est, ut sit perseverans. Propter quod ait Salvator: Oportet semper orare, et non deficere. Porro orationes ministrorum Ecclesiæ, quamvis injustorum, tamen in persona Ecclesiæ fusæ, quamdam efficaciam sortiuntur pro plebe.
paras.en: That is why he adds: [[5:16|For the continual prayer of a just man availeth much|Multum enim valet deprecatio justi assidua]]. For the just man is God's friend and his adopted son, like him and lovable to him. For [[Ps 10:8|the Lord is just, and hath loved justice|justus Dominus, et justitias dilexit]]. And friends will and refuse the same things. Therefore it is written: The prayer of the just pierces the heavens[[Ecclus 35:21||]] [Denis's wording; the verse reads: The prayer of him that humbleth himself shall pierce the clouds]; and again: [[Ps 144:19|He will do the will of them that fear him|Voluntatem timentium se faciet]], etc. [the margin's psalm number is lost and its verse is read as 16; the words are Ps 144:19]. And the Apostle says well that the continual prayer of a just man avails much, that is, is of great strength and merit, or is especially sure to be heard by God: because one condition required for a prayer to be heard is that it be persevering. That is why the Saviour says: [[Luke 18:1|we ought always to pray and not to faint|Oportet semper orare, et non deficere]]. Moreover, the prayers of the ministers of the Church, even unjust ones, since they are poured out in the person of the Church, obtain a certain efficacy for the people.

paras.t: Quod autem multum valeat justorum oratio, probat exemplo. Elias homo erat similis nobis passibilis, id est mortalis, qui timore mortis fugit a facie Jezabel; et oratione oravit. Ista est proprietas idiomatis Hebræorum, per talem ingeminationem effari, sicut in Isaia: Dissipatione dissipabitur terra, agitatione agitabitur terra, confractione confringetur terra. Vel ideo ait, Oratione oravit, quoniam una oratione impetravit quod subditur, ut Beda hic loquitur. Itaque, Oratione oravit, ut non plueret super terram decem tribuum Israel, propter eorum facinora, videlicet idololatrias regis eorum et ipsorum. Hoc enim oravit Elias zelo justitiæ, ut per adversa retraherentur a vitiis vexatione edocti. Et non pluit annos tres et menses sex.
paras.en: That the prayer of the just avails much he proves by an example. [[5:17|Elias was a man passible like unto us|Elias homo erat similis nobis passibilis]] [Denis's order: "a man like us, passible"], that is, mortal, for in fear of death he fled from the face of Jezabel[[3 Kings 19:1||]]; [[5:17|and with prayer he prayed|et oratione oravit]]. It is a property of the Hebrew idiom to speak with such a doubling, as in Isaias: [[Is 24:3|With desolation shall the earth be laid waste|Dissipatione dissipabitur terra]], [[Is 24:20|With shaking shall the earth be shaken|agitatione agitabitur terra]], [[Is 24:19|With breaking shall the earth be broken|confractione confringetur terra]]. Or else he says, [[5:17|with prayer he prayed|Oratione oravit]], because by one prayer he obtained what follows, as Bede says here. So, [[5:17|with prayer he prayed|Oratione oravit]], [[5:17|that it might not rain upon the earth|ut non plueret super terram]] of the ten tribes of Israel, because of their crimes, namely the idolatries of their king and their own. For Elias prayed this out of zeal for justice, that through adversity they might be drawn back from their vices, taught by affliction. [[5:17|And it rained not for three years and six months|Et non pluit annos tres et menses sex]].

paras.t: Ista historia tertio Regum diffuse describitur. Et rursus oravit. Quum enim vidisset eos humiliatos et nimis afflictos, condoluit eis, orans Deum ut pluviam condonaret. Et cœlum dedit pluviam, id est, sua virtute influentiali concurrit ad hoc; et terra dedit fructum suum.
paras.en: This story is told at length in the third book of Kings[[3 Kings 17:1||]]. [[5:18|And he prayed again|Et rursus oravit]]. For when he saw them humbled and sorely afflicted, he had compassion on them, praying God to grant the rain[[3 Kings 18:1||]]. [[5:18|And the heaven gave rain|Et cœlum dedit pluviam]], that is, concurred in this by its own influential power [that is, the influence of the heavens on things below, as the natural philosophy of the day held]; [[5:18|and the earth brought forth her fruit|et terra dedit fructum suum]].

paras.t: Fratres mei, si quis ex vobis erraverit a veritate, id est, aliquis vestrum a fidei rectitudine, aut a veritate doctrinæ, vitæ sive justitiæ declinaverit, et converterit quis eum per veram informationem, caritativam exhortationem, justam increpationem, fraternam correptionem; scire debet quoniam qui converti fecerit peccatorem ab errore viæ suæ, id est, a via perditionis ad viam salutis, seu observantiam præceptorum, reduxerit, salvabit animam ejus a morte, id est, a condemnatione gehennæ, quæ est mors æternæ miseriæ, animam peccatoris conversi præservabit ac eruet. Revocando enim eum a culpa, eruit eum a pœna perpetua. Et operit multitudinem peccatorum, id est, peccata peccatoris conversi facit sic tegi, ut a Judice summo non videantur ad condemnandum. Nempe per hoc quod peccatorem ad contritionem et emendationem inducit, cooperatur ad remissionem culparum illius: quæ remissio est peccatorum opertio sive tectio vel deletio, juxta illud, Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, et quorum tecta sunt peccata.
paras.en: [[5:19|My brethren, if any of you err from the truth|Fratres mei, si quis ex vobis erraverit a veritate]], that is, if any of you has turned aside from the rightness of faith, or from the truth of doctrine, of life or of justice, [[5:19|and one convert him|et converterit quis eum]] by true instruction, charitable exhortation, just rebuke, fraternal correction; [[5:20|He must know that he who causeth a sinner to be converted from the error of his way|scire debet quoniam qui converti fecerit peccatorem ab errore viæ suæ]], that is, has brought him back from the way of perdition to the way of salvation, or the keeping of the commandments, [[5:20|shall save his soul from death|salvabit animam ejus a morte]], that is, shall preserve and rescue the soul of the converted sinner from the condemnation of hell, which is the death of eternal misery. For by calling him back from guilt, he rescues him from everlasting punishment. [[5:20|and shall cover a multitude of sins|Et operit multitudinem peccatorum]], that is, he causes the sins of the converted sinner to be so covered that they are not seen by the supreme Judge for condemnation. For by leading the sinner to contrition and amendment, he cooperates in the remission of his faults: and this remission is a covering, or hiding, or blotting out of sins, according to that saying: [[Ps 31:1|Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered|Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates, et quorum tecta sunt peccata]].

paras.t: Aliqui textus habent: Salvabit animam suam a morte: quia qui alium ex caritate admonet, corripit et convertit, sibi ipsi maximum præmium promeretur, et caritatis suæ fervore quotidiana et propria sua incendit peccata, dimittunturque ei. Imo et præteritorum suorum excessuum obtinet remissionem, quantum ad pœnam, omnino aut partim, secundum quod caritatis fervor fuerit in eo major aut minor. Idcirco in Proverbiis scribitur: Universa delicta operit caritas. Et princeps Apostolorum: Caritas, inquit, operit multitudinem peccatorum. Idcirco de beatissima Magdalena locutus est Dominus: Dimissa sunt ei peccata multa, quoniam dilexit multum. Verumtamen si quis impie vivens, non agens quod docet, prædicare præsumpserit, et prædicando quosdam quasi convertens, sua peccata sibi indulgeri non promeretur: imo gravius peccat, et suas transgressiones multiplicat, prædicationis officium indigne exercens.
paras.en: Some texts have: [[5:20|shall save his soul from death|Salvabit animam suam a morte]] [Latin *suam*, "his own" soul, that is, the soul of the one who converts the sinner]: because he who out of charity admonishes, corrects and converts another merits the greatest reward for himself, and by the fervour of his charity burns up his own daily sins, and they are forgiven him. Indeed he also obtains the remission of his past excesses as to their punishment, wholly or in part, according as the fervour of charity in him is greater or less. Therefore it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 10:12|charity covereth all sins|Universa delicta operit caritas]]. And the prince of the Apostles: [[1 Pet 4:8|charity|Caritas]], he says, [[1 Pet 4:8|covereth a multitude of sins|operit multitudinem peccatorum]]. Therefore the Lord said of the most blessed Magdalen: [[Luke 7:47|Many sins are forgiven her, because she hath loved much|Dimissa sunt ei peccata multa, quoniam dilexit multum]]. But if anyone living wickedly, not doing what he teaches, presumes to preach, and by preaching as it were converts some, he does not merit to have his own sins forgiven him: rather he sins more gravely and multiplies his transgressions, exercising the office of preaching unworthily.

paras.t: Ex præinductis demum sancti apostoli Jacobi verbis docemur, quam salubre et magnum sit apud Deum, peccantes fraterne corripere, pie instruere, caritative convertere. Nam, ut divinus Dionysius fassus est, omnium divinorum divinissimum est, Deo cooperari in conversione iniquorum ad eum. Atque ut asserit Augustinus, ille in caritate Dei est perfectior, qui ad ejus amorem plures convertit. Gratissimumque Deo sacrificium, zelus est animarum. Et sicut Christus graviorem pati non potest persecutionem, quam ut quis verbo aut exemplo, animas suo sanguine liberatas, ab ipso avertat: sic ampliorem honorationem ei impendere non valemus, quam animas deviantes convertendo ad ipsum. Fraternam ergo correptionem, ad quam omnes tenentur, in quantum est caritatis effectus, efficaciter ac discrete cum omni fervore et humilitate exerceamus, errantes et lapsos erigamus pro posse et informemus. Taliterque vivamus, et tam timorate ac fructifere jugiter conversemur, ut alios corripere, informare, convertere simus idonei. Nec verbis dumtaxat, sed oratione quoque et exemplo, pro aliorum conversione conemur. Imo pro illis oremus instantius, quos incorrigibiliores conspicimus. Deficiente quippe humana virtute, ad Omnipotentis auxilium seriosius est confugiendum. Postremo, ut in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Unicuique Deus mandavit de proximo suo, ut eripiat eum ab omni iniquo. Errori quoque cui non resistitur, consentitur. Zelo ergo divini honoris ac fraternæ salutis simus semper accensi. Quumque anima sit incomparabiliter corpore præstantior, et æterna felicitas omni temporali sanitate inæstimabiliter desiderabilior, infernalisque mors omni corporali præsentis vitæ languore formidabilior; propterea incomparabiliter sollicitiores operosioresque simus pro conversione et salute animarum errantium proximorum, quam pro curatione corporum aut relevamine corporalium incommodorum illorum, ut sit in omnibus nostra caritas ordinata. Nec dubium quin omnia ista ad prælatos ac præsidentes potissimum spectent. Omni igitur modo possibili pro propria ac proximorum laboremus salute. Ad laudem et gloriam Omnipotentis, qui est super omnia Deus sublimis et benedictus. Amen.
paras.en: From these words of the holy apostle James, finally, we are taught how wholesome and how great a thing it is before God to correct sinners as brothers, to instruct them with kindness, and to convert them with charity. For, as the divine Dionysius declared, of all divine things the most divine is to cooperate with God in the conversion of the wicked to him. And as Augustine asserts, he is more perfect in the charity of God who converts more people to his love. And the sacrifice most pleasing to God is zeal for souls. And just as Christ can suffer no heavier persecution than that someone, by word or example, should turn away from him the souls set free by his blood, so we can pay him no greater honour than by converting straying souls to him. Let us therefore practise fraternal correction, to which all are bound inasmuch as it is an effect of charity, effectively and with discretion, with all fervour and humility; let us raise up and instruct, as far as we can, those who stray and have fallen. And let us live in such a way, and always conduct ourselves with such fear of God and such fruitfulness, that we may be fit to correct, instruct and convert others. And let us strive for the conversion of others not with words only, but also with prayer and example. Indeed let us pray the more earnestly for those whom we see to be the less corrigible. For when human strength fails, we must flee the more earnestly to the help of the Almighty. Lastly, as it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 17:12|he gave to every one of them commandment concerning his neighbour|Unicuique Deus mandavit de proximo suo]], that he should rescue him from all iniquity [the words "that he should rescue him from all iniquity" are not in the Vulgate text of the verse]. Error, too, that is not resisted is consented to. Let us then be always on fire with zeal for the honour of God and the salvation of our brethren. And since the soul is incomparably more excellent than the body, and eternal happiness inestimably more desirable than any temporal health, and the death of hell more dreadful than any bodily sickness of this present life, let us therefore be incomparably more anxious and more active for the conversion and salvation of the souls of our straying neighbours than for the healing of their bodies or the relief of their bodily hardships, so that our charity may be ordered in all things. Nor is there any doubt that all these things concern prelates and superiors most of all. Let us therefore labour in every way possible for our own salvation and that of our neighbours. To the praise and glory of the Almighty, who is God above all things, exalted and blessed. Amen.
